Mr. Md. Nazibur Rahman with Mr. H. M. Mushfiqur Rahman ----- For the petitioners in all the Civil Revisions
Mr. S.S. Halder ----- For the opposite parties in all the Civil Revisions
parties:
Md. Obaidur Rahman & ors (in C. R. No. 2804/94)
Md. Delower Hossan & ors.(in C. R. No. 2805/ 94)
Md. Abdul Majid & ors.(in C. R. No. 2785/94)
Md. Abdul Majid & ors.(in C. R. No. 2786/94)
Md. Anwar Hossan & ors.(in C. R. No. 2787/ 94)
Vs.
Bijay Kumar Roy and others
full_judgment:
Sikder Maqbul Huq, J:- These Rules involving common questions of law and facts and arising out of a consolidated judgment disposing of 5 Miscellaneous Appeals confirming the judgment and orders passed in Misc. Case Nos. 59 of 1988, 60 of 1988, 61 of 1988, 62 of 1988 and 63 of 1988 were issued upon the opposite parties asking them to show cause as why the aforesaid orders passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Thakurgaon should not be set aside. 

2. Opposite party No. 1 Bijoy Kumar Roy, as preemptor, instituted Misc. Case Nos. 59-63 of 1988 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Thakurgaon, under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act against the present petitioners and opposite party Nos. 2-9 contending inter alia that the opposite party No. 3 namely Sankar Barman transferred 1.13 acres of land recorded in the C.S. plot 4955 under C.S. khatian No. 852 corresponding to S.A. khatian No. 744 of Mouza Hariharpur, P. S. and District Thakurgaon to the preemptee opposite parties by 5 kabalas dated 24.3.88, 28.3.88 and 31.3.88; that the petitioner is a holder of land contiguous to the case land and the purchaser opposite parties were strangers thereto; that the petitioner has 8/9/10 acres of land and that he is legally entitled to preempt the case land.

3. The preemptee opposite parties filed written objections in all the 5 cases denying the material allegations of the petitioner and contending inter alia that the petitioner and his other brothers and sisters are members of the joint family headed by his father Narendra Nath Roy having more than 500 acres of land and as such the petitioner had no right to acquire the land contiguous the case land by Ext. 5(chha) dated 1.6.82; that the petitioner being a member of the joint family having the aforesaid quantum of land cannot preempt the case land; that the said Narendra Nath Roy fraudulently with a view to conceal the area of land held by him filed 3 uniform returns to the office of the Circle Officer (Revenue) for himself and his sons Indra Nath Roy and Bijoy Kumar Roy each owning 33.00 acres of land and the C. O. (Revenue), after hearing both the sides; passed an order treating and consolidating the returns in the name of Narendra Nath Roy and asking him to surrender the excess land held by him in pursuance of P.O. No. 98 of 1972 but subsequently the successor in office of the concerned C.0. (Revenue) accepted the 3 returns in the name of aforesaid 3 persons by reviewing the earlier order holding them to be members of separate families in view of the fact that they are guided by Mitakshara School of Hindu law and each son, on the date of birth, became owner of land with his father in contravention of the provisions of the aforesaid Ordinance; that the petitioner according to his own showing in Return Case No. 75/7243. had 33.94 acres of land and also 12.23 acres of land on the basis of another return; that Basudev Das, son of Radha Moni Dasi had no interest in the land appertaining of plot Nos. 5613 and 5955 adjacent to the case plot and the petitioner also did not acquire any interest therein by subsequent purchase from the alleged transferee of Basudev and that all the holders of land contiguous to the case land have not been impleaded as opposite parties in the cases and that all the Misc. cases, under circumstances, are liable to be disallowed. 

4. The learned Assistant Judge allowed all the Misc. cases holding that the petitioner having not more than 60 bighas of land and having impleaded all the necessary parties in the case and also being a holder of land contiguous the case land is legally entitled to preempt the same. 

5. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid appellate judgment and orders, the preemptee opposite parties preferred Misc. Appeal Nos. 7-11 of 1992 before the learned District Judge, Thakurgaon, who having heard all appeals analogously, dismissed the same and upheld the judgment and orders passed by the trial court. 

6. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and orders, the preemptee petitioners have preferred the instant revisional applications being revisional application Nos. 2804-05 of 1994 and 2745-47 of 1994. 

7. Heard the learned Advocates of both the sides Perused the record. 

8. Mr. Md. Nazibar Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners in all revisional applications, submits that the learned trial court committed errors of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in allowing the Misc. cases holding that the opposite parties could not prove that the petitioners have more than 60 bighas of land and that the learned court of appeal below also committed error of law in holding that the petitioner being the owner of less than 60 bigas of land is entitled to preempt the case land. Secondly the learned Advocate subunits that the courts below committed error of law in holding that the petitioner is owner of land contiguous to the case land; 3rdly the learned Advocate submits that both the courts below committed errors of law in allowing the Misc. cases and holding that the petitioner has not more than or he has less than 60 bigas of land without calculating the area of land transferred by the petitioner vide Exts. 5 (Ka)(kha)(ga)(gha) and came to an erroneous finding of fact resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice; 4thly the learned Advocate submits that both the courts below committed error of law in finding that the petitioner being a member of Mitakshara Hindu sect cannot be treated as member of joint family and further submits that the definition of family has been given in P.0.98 of 1972 without any ambiguity and that both the courts below committed errors of law and facts in not holding that the petitioner was minor at the time of return; 5thly the learned Advocate submits that both the courts below failed to consider the documentary evidence Exts. ga and gha and came to an erroneous finding regarding the date of birth and lastly submits that both the courts below misinterpreted law and decisions referred to in the judgment. 

9. Mr. S. S. Halder, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 1 in all the revisional applications, on the other hand, submits that both the courts below concurrently came to a finding that the petitioner is not a member of a joint family as alleged by the opposite parties and that the courts below were legally justified in allowing the preemption cases holding that the petitioner, having land contiguous to the case land, is legally entitled to preempt the same. Controverting the submissions made by the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties regarding the validity of the deeds of gift Exts. 5- 5(kha) dated 18.3.1988, the learned Advocate further submits that the concurrent findings of the courts below in this regard being based on material evidence on record cannot be interfered with by this Court in revisional jurisdiction and that both the courts below were legally justified in holding that the pre-emptee-petitioners cannot challenge those deeds of gift without instituting regular suit in competent court having jurisdiction for annulment of those documents. The learned advocate further submits that both the courts below concurrently found that the petitioner is a holder of contiguous land and this court in its revisional jurisdiction cannot term of documents in the name of petitioner and his predecessor in respect of plot Nos. 4955 and 5613 as fraudulent and void. It is also submitted by the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party that the preemptee petitioners nowhere in their written objections or in the memo of appeal made any assertion that the petitioner has more than 60 bighas of land and as such the petitioners cannot legally raise such question during the course of hearing of the revisional applications. The learned advocate further summits that both the courts below were legally justified in passing the impugned judgment and orders and allowing the Misc. cases and they have not misinterpreted any law or misapplied the decisions as referred to by the learned Advocate appearing for the preemptee petitioners.

10. There is no dispute about the fact that the opposite party No. 2 Sankar Borman transferred the case land vide 5 kabalas dated 24.3.88, 28.3.88 and 31.3.88 Exts.1, 1(ka), 1 (kha), 1(ga) and 1(gha) to the pre-emptee petitioners. 

11. The moot points to be decided in the cases are that whether the petitioner was a member of an undivided family headed by Narendra Nath Roy and whether the petitioner held more than 60 bighas of land at the relevant time. 

12. It appears from the record that Narendra Nath Roy had wife, 3 sons and 2 daughters who were living in a joint family headed by him at the time of filing of the returns in compliance with the provisions of P.O.No.98 of 1972 and the learned Advocate for the petitioners in this connection submits that both the courts below committed error of law in not considering Exts. Ga and Gha. It appears from the record that Ext. Ga, the certificate issued by the Head Master and Ext. Gha the registration certificate of Indra Nath Roy have not been considered either by the trial court or the appellate court. It appears from the judgments that those courts have not uttered a single word about the certificate which is a very important of piece of evidence and that Bejoy Kumar Roy is younger to said Indra Nath Roy and Bijoy Kumar Roy passed S.S.C Examination and such an important certificate regarding the date of birth of the petitioner was not produced to prove his age. Exts. ga and gha are the best evidence of the fact that Indra Nath Roy was born in 1958. It further appears from the record that Bejoy Kumar as P.W.1 has stated in his deposition that he has passed the S.S.C. examination in 1979 /1980 and he could not say whether the S.S.C certificate contains his date of birth. Thus definitely his evidence goes to support the submission that he has suppressed the fact regarding his date of birth and he has suppressed with ulterior motives. Indra Nath Roy, the elder son of Narendra Kumar Roy, might have been born at least 1 or 2 years before the birth of Bijoy Kumar Roy. In that view of the matter Bijoy Kumar Roy was minor at the time of submission of returns in pursuance of P.0.98 of 1972. It is apparent that they were at the relevant time members of a joint family headed by Narendra Nath Roy and both the courts below committed errors of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in holding that the petitioner had not more than 60 bighas or he had less than 60 bigas of land as mentioned above. 

13. The next important point to be decided is whether the deeds of gift Exts.5 and 5(ka) are sham documents. Both the courts below concurrently found that the pre-emptee petitioners cannot legally challenge the validity of those documents without their annulment in the Civil Court and as such these are legal documents. The learned advocate appearing for the petitioners has referred to the decision in the case of Shall Khan Vs. Mannujan Hossain wife of A.Z.M. Delwar Hossain Advocate and others reported in 35 DLR(AD) 225 wherein it has held that if the transaction is a colorable one, a mere paper transaction, then there has been no real retransfer and preemption right will prevail and to the case of Ashwini Kumar Karmaker being dead his heirs; Sree Radha Raman Karmaker & ors Vs. Hari Mohan & ors and Sufi Golam Mohiuddin Vs. Hafizur Rahman Munshi & ors reported in 36 DLR(AD) page 1, wherein it has been held that question of benami nature not to be agitated in preemption proceeding but if in fact no transfer of the land had taken place and the alleged vendor continuing to be in possession, such a question can be gone into. Thus the claim of pre-emption can be resisted on the ground that no transfer has taken place under the relevant kabala simply made as a document of transfer for any purpose and in the case of Balali Chand Mondal Vs. Nibaran Chandra Das reported in 51 CWN page 644 it has been held that such a transfer whether being colourable one, may be gone into. This decision lends support to the contention of the learned advocate for the petitioners and neither of the courts below found that the deeds of gift Exts. 5(ka) and 5 (kha) are genuine documents and the pre-emptees can not rely on this decision on the ground that the pre-emptees had to file an independent suit in competent court for annulment of the documents and such proposition of law is not applicable in view of the fact as submitted by the learned Advocate for the petitioners that the pre-emptee petitioners have no locus standi to institute independent suit for cancellation of the above documents inasmuch as they are not parties to the instruments and not directly affected by them and this contention of the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners could not be controverted by the learned Advocate for the opposite party. The learned Advocate for the petitioners in this connection referred to section 258 of Hindu law and submits that a member of joint family governed by Mitakshara School of Hindu law cannot transfer any property without the consent of other coparceners and any such transfer being altogether void there is no estoppel or other kind of personal bar which precludes the donor from asserting his right to recover the transferred property and in that view of the matter the learned Advocate further submits that the pre-emptor did not divest himself of the land transferred by him by way of gift vide Exts.5 and 5(kha) and such a legal position also could not be assailed by the learned Advocate for the opposite parties. 

14. It appears from the record that the Ext. 5 contains 9.98 acres, Ext. 5(kha) 9.95 acres of land and in Ext. 5 (ka) the donee is Aujamul Huq and in Ext. 5(kha) the donee is Mozammel Hoq the son and son-in-law respectively of Mr. Nurul Huq, the learned Advocate of the petitioner in the trial court. It appears from the recitals in those documents that the donees are in no way related to the donor and without any doubt they also belong to a different community and religion and the donees were not examined by the preemptor. It appears from the record that both the deeds of gift are dated 18.3.88 but were presented for registration on 4.5.88 after a long and unreasonable delay. The kabalas under preemption are dated 24.3.88, 28.3.88 and 31.3.88 and all those documents were preseined for registration on the respective date of their execution. The registration of 5 deeds were completed on 7.8.88 and 2.8.88 and 9.8.88 under section 60 of the Registration Act. The relevant deeds of gift were presented for registration on 4.5.88 long after the kabalas in favour of the pre-emtee petitioners were presented for registration and in this connection the learned advocate for the petitioners submits that the pre-emptor opposite party with an ulterior motive by practicing fraud created those deeds of gift in violation of section 258 of the Hindu law on 4.5.88 by antedating which are sham transactions in order to create right of preemption as holder of land below 60 bighas. The two deeds of gift do not find mention in the preemption application and execution of those deeds was not even proved but they were marked exhibits in spite of the objection by the pre-emptee and the pre-emptor cannot be given a premium for his illegal activities and both the courts below committed error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in finding that the pre-emptee petitioners are to file independent suit for annulling those documents to entitle them to challenge pre-emptor's locus standi for preemption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

15. The only inference regarding the deeds of gift is that the aforesaid deeds are collusive creation and the petitioner has not divested himself of the property allegedly donated and he as per section 258 is entitled to recover the property any time from the denees. Those are mere paper transactions and not acted upon and created to show that the pre-emptor had less than 60 bighas land. 

16. The pre-emptor according to his own showing was holding more than 100 bigas of land at the time of the alleged returns in 1973 and there is no evidence on record that he transferred more than 40 bighas of land in between the date of submission of the return and filing of the application for preemption. The pre-emptor further asserted to have transferred .99 acre of land vide Exts. 5(ka) dated 7.4.88 and 5(ga) dated 29.9.83 and there is no allegation of the pre-emptor having transferred any other land. Thus it is apparent that neither of the courts below correctly calculated land transferred and also took into consideration the admitted returns that the pre-emptor had more than 100 bighas of land at the time of submission of the aforesaid returns. In view of the aforesaid circumstances, it is apparent that the pre-emptor must have more than 6o bighas of land at the relevant time of filing 5 preemption cases and thus even if it is conceded that the petitioner is not a member of the joint family still then, he is not legally entitled to preempt the case land according to law as he was holding land exceeding 60 bighas at the relevant time. 

17. The learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner further submits that the petitioner having owned more than 100 bighas of land was not entitled to acquire more land by Ext. 5 (chha) in 1982. The petitioners have taken definite defence in their written objection to that effect. In view of the aforesaid findings it cannot be said that the pre-emptor acquired any interest.in the land contiguous to the case land by virtue of Ext. 5 (chha). Thus the contention of the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners that the pre-emptor acquired no interest in the land by Ext. 5(chha) cannot be brushed aside. 

18. The learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners further submits that the trial court admitted Exts. 5 and -5(kha) and other documents even without proof of custody or their proof of execution in spite of objection raised by the opposite parties of the Misc. cases and objection to that effect was also raised before the appellate court but both the courts below ignored the legality of those objection and thereby committed errors of law and facts. Mr. S.S. Halder, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties referring to the decision in the case of Abdullah & 3 others Vs. Abdul Karim and others reported in 20 DLR (SC) 205 submits that the objections as to formal proof of document is to be taken at the earliest point of time and relied on the decision in the said case. He further submits that the Court of revision should not disturb the concurrent findings of facts unless such findings are based on no evidence or upon misreading or misconstruction of the evidence on record. In the instant case objection, as it appears from record, regarding admission of the said documents in the trial Court was taken at the initial stage and also at the appellate stage and as such the submissions of the learned Advocate for the opposite parties so far as it relates to admission of documents in evidence has no merit at all and so far as concurrent findings of fact are concerned the same are not the result of proper consideration of the evidence and materials on record as discussed above rather result of mis-appreciation of evidence and law as well. So the decision does not help the opposite parties. 

19. The learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties has also referred to the case of Nayeb Ali and others Vs. Akhtar Rahman & others reported in 29 DLR 153 wherein it has been held that onus is on the person who seeks to repurchase the land sold to show that the area of land in his possession does not exceed the maximum he is entitled to retain under section 90 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The learned Advocate for the opposite parties further referred to the decision in the case of Md. Abbas Ali Vs. Md. Osman Ali (minor) and others reported in 1985 BCR (HCD) 236 wherein it has been held that the assertion as to the maximum ceiling of area of the land not having been denied in the written objection by the vendee opposite parties, there is no bar of section 90 for the petitioner to pre-empt the case land. This submission of the learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 1 appears to be without substance in view of the fact that the petitioners although asserted that the preemptor being a member of a joint family having 500 acres of land besides the assertion that the petitioner according to his own showing being in possession of more than 60 bighas of land is not entitled to preempt the case land. The decision in the case of Hatem Ali Mollah & ors Vs. Hayet Khan & ors reported in 1985 BLD (AD) 183 does not appear to be relevant for the purpose of the disposal of these rules. The learned Advocate for the opposite parties lastly referred to the decision in the case of Abul Kalam (Md.) and others Vs. Md. Shamsuddin reported in 49 DLR page 502 wherein it has been held that mere omission to Make an assertion in his application or to adduce evidence to this effect, in the absence of any averment to the contrary, will not render pre-emption application liable to be dismissed. This decision also does not appear to be relevant for the purpose of decision in the cases before me in view of the fact that evidence has been adduced regarding the land held by the petitioner and evidence to that effect has not been challenged. No other point has been raised in this case. The court of appeal below in its judgment referred to the decision in the case of S.M. Basiruddin Vs. Zahirul Islam Chowdhury and another reported in B.C.R (A.D) 1983 at page 224 in which it is held that in a case for preemption Court cannot go beyond the decision given by the C.O. (Rev.) regarding the return and land held by the petitioner and his father and other brother Indra Nath Roy. The facts and circumstances of the said reported case are quite distinguishable. Even if it is conceded that the petitioner as held by the C.O. Rev. was a member of a separate family still then he is not entitled to preempt the case land for reasons detailed earlier. 

20. It has been held in the case of Abseruddin Mondol Vs. Md. Toyezuddin Dewan reported in 44 DLR, 105 that the deed of gift though executed earlier was registered after registration of the disputed sale deed sought to be preempted cannot have the effect of destroying the right of pre-emption nor can it affect the right of pre-emption inasmuch as a party at his own will cannot exclude the operation of the statute providing for pre-emption. From this decision it can be said that a right of pre-emption cannot be created by creating certain sham and colorable documents so as to bring the quantum of land of the petitioner within permissible limit in order to entitle him to apply for preemption. 

21. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case, it is apparent that the Court of appeal below was not legally justified in passing the judgment and order and committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. 

22. In the result these rules are made absolute without any order as to costs and the judgment and orders passed by the courts below are hereby set aside.
 
Send down the lower court records. 

Communicate the order to the Courts below at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Sheikh Rezowan Ali, J: This single judgment will dispose of Death Reference No. 33 of 2004, Crl. Appeal No. 887 of 2004, Jail Appeal No. 313 of 2004, Jail Appeal No. 172 of 2005 and Crl. Misc. Case No. 1195 of 2005.

2. Learned Speedy Trial Tribunal, Barisal by his judgment and order dated-01-03-2004 passed in Speedy Tribunal Case No. 62 of 2003 convicted condemned prisoners (1) Tipu Gazi, (2) Moti Gazi (3) Sohel Gazi and (4) Mizanur Rahman of the offence punishable under section 302/34 of the Penal Code and sentenced them there under to death by hanging subject to confirmation by the High Court Division and made the reference to this Coma under section 374 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for confirmation of the said sentence.

3. Being aggrieved by the impugned judment and order of conviction and sentence condemned prisoners (1) Tipu Gazi (2) Sohel Gazi and (3) Mizanur Rahman preferred Criminal Appeal No 887 of 2004. Earlier to this, the said three condemned prisoners preferred Jail Appeal No. 313 of 2004. On the other hand, condemned prisoner (4) Moti Gazi preferred Jail Appeal No 172 of 2005 and later preferred Criminal Misc. Case No 1195 of 2005, a proceeding under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, seeking quashment of the impugned judgment order of conviction. Accordingly a rule was issued.

4. PW.1 Mokbul Gazi appeared in the local police station at Patuakhali on 24.3.2003 at 10.15 in the morning and lodged a written FIR alleging that during the last Union Parishad election accused Abul Kalam and another Habibur Rahman contested for the office of member of Badarpur Union. His (PW 1's) son Gazi Harun-Or-Rashid (deceased) did not support accused Abul Kalam and worked for Habibur Rahman. Accused Abul Kalam was defeated in the said election. Being annoyed at this, accused Abul Kalam along with the terrorist elements of his party was making conspiracy to murder him and was looking for opportune moment. On the date of occurrence on 23.03.2003 in the evening, the day being Sunday, accompanied by his Bhatija (brother's son) PW.2 Faisal deceased Harun- or- Rashid went to New Market at Patuakhali. After finishing his business he proceeded for home along with PW.2 Faisal. After crossing the Khalishakali ferry when they disembarked on the other bank of the river at 10-30 at night and reached north-west road crossing all the FIR column named accused i.e. 1) Tipu, 2) Moti Gazi, 3) Sohel, 4) Rustom Gazi, 5)Kabir, 6) Faruque,7) Delowar Gazi,8) Abul Kalam, 9) Kalam, Son of Eraf Ali, 10) Mostafa, 11) Yusuf, 12) Mizanur Hawlader and 13) Nasir along with 5/7 other unknown persons who lay in wait armed with ramdao, gachh Kata dao (tree taping dao) and other deadly weapons surrounded deceased Harun and dragged him to the road on the southern side of the nursery of one Montu Mia and chopped him indiscriminately causing grievous injuries on his person. PW. 2 Faisal managed his escape tactfully and reached home running and apprised him (informant PW.1) that the said accused captured the deceased for murder. On hearing this accompanied by his son PW.3 Jahirul Huq, wife PW.4 Lal Banu and some of the witnesses he reached the place of occurrence and by flashing electric torch he found the deceased lying on the northern slope of the road. He heard from him (the deceased) about the occurrence in details and carried him to Patuakhali General Hospital by the engine driven trawler of one Bazlur Rahman. The Emergency Medical Officer, then on duty, examined him and declared him dead. He further stated in the FIR that he narrated to the other witnesses of the details of the occurrence which he heard from his deceased son while he was still alive. It was further stated in the FIR that the deadbody was lying at Patuakhali Hospital.

5. Names of 6 witnesses were also mentioned in the FIR. They were PW.2 Md. Faisal, PW.3 Jahirul Islam, PW.4 Lal Vanu, PW.7 Dulal Gazi, PW.5 Nannu Hawlader and PW.6 Hatem Gazi.

6. On receipt of a typewritten FIR containing the aforesaid allegation on 24.3.2003 at 10-15 am duty officer of the police station registered Patuakhali Police Station Case No. 25 dated 24.3.2003 and filled in the formal column of the FIR. PW.18 S. 1. Md. Shahjahan  was entrusted by the officer in charge with investigation into the case. During the course of investigation he visited the place of occurrence and prepared a sketch map along with an index thereof. He also held inquest on the deadbody of the deceased and sent the same to the morgue for post mortem examination. He also seized alamats under proper 'seizure list and examined witnesses under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. A prima facie case having been proved he submitted charge sheet for prosecution of 12 accused namely 1). Md. Tipu Gazi, 2) Md. Moti Gazi, 3) Sohel, 4) Kabir, 5) Mostafa, 6) Yusuf, 7) Mizanur Rahman, 8) Rustam, 9) Delowar, 10) Kalam Son of Eraf Ali, 11) Sikandar and 12) Niranjan for. the offence punishable under section 302/34 of the Penal Code while he submitted FRT recommending discharge of 3 FIR named accused namely, Faruk Khan, Abul Kalam and Nasir and 7 other accused who were arrested during the course of investigation as suspects.

7. After completion of necessary formalities in terms of the provision of section 339 B (1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure for trial of the absconding accused in absentia the learned Magistrate sent the record of the case to the learned Sessions Judge, Patuakhali who registered it as Sessions Case No.73 of 2003 and after necessary cognizance transferred it to the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Patuakhali for disposal. Charge was framed by him against the instant condemned prisoners who were absconding and other accused for the offence punishable under section 302/34 of the Penal Code by his order dated 6.10.2003. Ultimately, the record of the case was transferred to the Speedy Trial Tribunal, Barisal and the learned tribunal by his order dated-20-10-2003 registered it as Druto Bichar Tribunal Mamla No.62 of 2003. Learned Speedy Trial Tribunal by his order dated 05-11-2003 fixed on 11.11.2003 for examination of prosecution witnesses. Offence under section 302 of the Penal Code having provided capital punishment, learned tribunal appointed advocate Mr. Mokhlesur Rahman Khan as the state defence lawyer for the undefended absconding accused.

8. In order to bring home the charge against the instant condemned prisoners and other accused prosecution produced 18 witnesses before the tribunal below. After the closure of the evidence of the prosecution witnesses other accused who were present before the tribunal were examined under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The instant condemned prisoners being absconding they could not be examined under section 342 of the Code of Criminal procedure. The learned tribunal then heard arguments of both the sides and by his impugned judgment and order found the instant 4 condemned prisoners, namely 1) Tipu Gazi, 2) Moti Gazi, 3) Sohel Gazi and 4) Mizanur Rahman guilty of the offence under section 302/34 of the Penal Code and sentenced them to death by hanging and made a reference to this court for confirmation of the death sentence while he acquitted the rest of the 8 accused.

9. We have mentioned earlier that being aggrieved by the impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence the condemned prisoners preferred the aforesaid Crl. Appeals, Jail Appeal and a Criminal Misc. Case under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

10. Mr. Yusuf Hossain Humayun, the learned Senior advocate who has represented all the 4 condemned prisoners, has taken us through the FIR, charge sheet, inquest report, seizure lists, the evidence of the witnesses recorded by the tribunal below and also the impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence. He has submitted that the learned tribunal below did not take into consideration of the contradictions and improbabilities appearing in the prosecution case during the course of trial. He has submitted that the learned tribunal below placed reliance upon the evidence of PW.6 Sultan Hawlader as an eyewitness to the occurrence corroborated by PW.5 Nannu Hawlader as another eyewitness. He also placed reliance upon the evidence of PW.7 Md. Dulal Gazi who was a hearsay witness from the mouth of informant PW.1 Mokbul Gazi. Learned advocate has further submitted that electric torches which were allegedly the means of recognition of the condemned prisoners were not seized at the earliest opportunity though the investigating officer could have seized them on the very first day of his seizure of other materials from the place of occurrence; but instead he seized them 2 days thereafter without any cogent explanation of the delay, which made the prosecution case quite doubtful about recognition of the accused in the darkness of night. He has further submitted that the 18 injuries which were found on the person of the deceased were so grievous in nature that it was beyond physical ability of the deceased to make any dying declaration naming as many as 12/13 accused. He has submitted that as per FIR murder took place as a sequel to conspiracy by accused Abul Kalam who lost election to one Habibur Rahman because of the support given by the deceased Harun-Or-Rashid to the said Habibur Rahman. But the said accused Abul Kalam, learned advocate submits, had been favoured with FRT. So the motive of murder relegated to the background making the prosecution case quite doubtful. In his assessment learned tribunal below had not materials enough before him to convict the condemned prisoners, not to speak of sentencing them to capital punishment. 27. In his cross-examination he stated that whatever might be the size of injuries a patient would not die unless there was bleeding. In reply to courts' query he stated that if the injures were present on the vital parts death was usual. He was not aware how long the deceased remained without any treatment. The deceased was struck blows at random without aiming at any particular place of his body. Before holding post-mortem examination he also went through the inquest report. Half digested food was found in his stomach. Person of the sort of the deceased could digest food within 2-4 hours. He held inquest on 24.3.2003 at 3 in the afternoon. He denied the defence suggestion that he did not hold post mortem examination properly. The injuries were of different kinds being incised and bruises. He did not find any penentrating, perforated or stab wounds. Bruises we caused by blunt weapons like lathi.

28. P.W.12 Hatem Gazi stated in his deposition that on 24.3.2003 investigating officer seized some bloodstained earth and bark of plantain tree from a place towards the southern side of nursery of Montu Mia in his presence. He proved his signature on the seizure list as ext. 3/3. In his cross examination he stated that the informant was his Chachato Bhagnipoti. They lived in the same dwelling house. They received information that the deceased lay murdered at ferry ghat. At the time of occurrence he was ill and did not go to the place of occurrence.

29. PW.13 Md. Kanchon Howlader stated in his deposition that on 24.3.2003 at 12.15 pm investigating officer seized from the corridor of Patuakhali General Hospital a bloodstained chocolate coloured full pant. (in tatters) a bloodstained cream coloured full sleeve shirt (in tatters) and a bloodstained sando ganjee and a bloodstained V-necked ganjee, green in colour and another ash coloured bloodstained sando ganjee in his presence. He proved his signature on the seizure list as ext. 4/2. In his cross examination he stated that he was bhaira of informant PW.1 Mokbul Gazi. He saw the informant his wife, son and grandson in the hospital. Habibur Rahman member was also present there. He did not accompany the informant to the police station. He further stated that all those persons who signed the seizure list were related to the informant.

30. PW.14 Abdul Sattar Sikder stated in his deposition that on 26.3.2003 at 10-30 am investigating officer seized 3 electric torches from the place of occurrence. He proved the said seizure list as ext. 6 and his signature thereon as ext.6/1. He also proved the signature of PW.9 Sentu Biswas thereon as ext. 6/2. He stated that both PW.2 Faisal and PW.5 Nannu Hawlader were present at the place of occurrence on 26.3.2003 at 10-30. He went to the place of occurrence on the following day when police appeared there.

31. PW.15 Md. Shamsul Alam S. I. stated in his deposition that he was, attached as a S.I. of police with Patuakhali Sadar Police Station (on the date of occurrence). On 24.3 (inadvertently recorded as 1). 2003 he was holding the charge of the officer-in- charge. On receipt bf the written FIR of the informant on the said date he registered the case. He proved his signature on the FIR as ext. 1/2, 1/3 and 1/4. He stated in his cross-examination that Police Station was 2 kilometre away from the place of occurrence. There was a delay of 11 hours and 45 minutes in lodging the Ejahar. It did not contain the name of the scribe.

32. PW.16 Nuruzzaman Sharif stated in his deposition that he was working as TNO at Kaliakoir within Gazipur District. On 8-04-2003 he worked as NDC and Magistrate of the first Class, at the same collectorate. He recorded the statements of Bazlu as a witness on the same date (8-04-2003), of Shahajahan on 5.4.2003 and of Mahbub on 20.4.2003 by observing all the formalities under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. He proved those statements and his signatures thereon as ext. 7 and 7/1, 8 and 8/1, 9 and 9/1 respectively. He also stated that the witnesses put their signatures in his presence. He stated in his cross examination that he was not aware if witnesses Shahajahan and Mahbub Gazi withdrew their statements. He further stated that the witnesses were not known to him. Investigating officer identified them. He denied the defence suggestion that the said 3 witnesses did not make statements voluntarily before him. He further stated that he did not record any certificate in the statements of the said Bazlu, Shahjahan and Mahbub that they made statements voluntarily.

33. PW. 17 Md. Rezaul Karim stated in his deposition that on 23.3.2003 he was attached as a sepoy with Patuakhali Police Station. On the said date on the basis of a challan prepared by S. I. Shahjahan (PW.18) he carried the deadbody of the deceased Harun Gazi to the morgue from the hospital corridor and handed over the same to the doctor on duty. He proved the challan as ext.10 and his signature thereon as ext.10/1. Defence declined to cross examine him.

34. PW.18 Md. Shahjahan stated in his deposition that he retired from service. On 24.3.2003 he was attached as a S. I. of police with Patuakhali Police Station. On that date officer in charge of the police station registered Patuakhali Police Station Case No. 25 and entrusted him with investigation into the said case. Accordingly, he visited the place of occurrence and prepared a sketch map along with an index thereof. He recorded the statements of witnesses under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. He seized alamats. He proved the seizure list prepared by him on 24.3.2003 at 12.15 pm and another seizure list prepared by him on 26.3.2003 at 10-30 a.m. He obtained signatures of witnesses thereon. He arrested accused. Further he prepared inquest report. During the course of investigation he also sent the dead body to the morgue under challan. He proved his signature on the challan as ext.10/2. A primafacie case having been proved against 12 accused persons he submitted charge sheet against them on approval of his higher authority. He proved the sketch map as ext. 11 and ext. 11/1. He proved the index thereof and his signature thereon as ext.12/ and his signature thereon as ext. 12/1 respectively. He further proved his signature on .3 seizure lists (proved earlier) as ext.3/3, 4/3 and 6/3 respectively. Again he proved his signature on the inquest report as ext.2/4. He further stated that the alamats were present before the tribunal. In his cross examination he stated that he visited the place of occurrence on the following day of the occurrence. He did not happen to meet PW.2 Faisal at the place of occurrence on 24.3.2003. The said PW.2 did not state to him that he had an electric torch in his hand or that he witnessed the occurrence in the light of electricity. He came to know during the course of investigation that the deceased expired in the hospital no sooner had he reached there. PW.4 (Lal Vanu) did not state to him that she saw the deceased lying beside the road in the light of electricity or at the flash of torch light. He knew Habibur Rahman member who was a witness to the inquest report. In the FIR he did not find any mention that the occurrence took place under the leadership of accused Kamal but there was mention in the FIR about his conspiracy. In the inquest report there was mention that the deceased was murdered by miscreants. He did not know who wrote out the FIR. He denied the defence suggestion that the Member Habibur Rahman handed over the FIR to him. He examined Bazlur Rahman of the ferry ghat. There was engine driven trawler named ferry boat for crossing the river. Place of occurrence was about 2 kilometres away from the police station. It took 15 minutes for him to cover 2 kilometres' distance. FIR was recorded on 24.3.2003 at 10-15 in the morning. He denied the defence suggestion that before retirement from service he submitted a false charge sheet. He further stated that PW.3 (Jahurul) did not state to him that PW. 2 Faisal informed him that the deceased was being chopped and that he also proposed to rush to the place of occurrence. PW.3 did not state to him that he made any query to the deceased as to who brought him to such a state. PW.5 did not state to hith that the inmates of his house did not allow him to go outside nor did he state that he accompanied PW.2 Faisal for the second time to the place of occurrence. He further stated that he examined PW.6 on 24.3.2003. In the sketch map letters "Ga" "Umo" "Cha" and "Neo" indicated 4 shops while letter "Chha" "Tha" indicated 3 dwelling houses. Letter "Chha" indicated the shop of Shahjahan Gazi. Letter "Cha" indicated tea-stall of accused Yusuf Sardar while letter "Neo" indicated the shop of Jamal Howlader. He did not find any such thing during the investigation that the informant had any electric torch in his hand. He did not examine Nazrul Howlader, Ruhul, Baruk, Akhtar and Bachchu who were not charge sheet listed witness. He denied the defence suggestion that he did not submit charge sheet by holding investigation properly. He further stated that in the FIR there was no mention of the name of accused Sikendar. He was not aware if accused Sikandar and Kalam kept in mortgage landed property of the informant, his wife and their sons. He denied the defence suggestion that he was gained over by the informant or that because of their previous enmity with the informant he falsely implicated the accused. The deceased was not a person of immoral character. He was not addicted to Ganja, He denied the defence suggestion that he was removed from service.

35. We have placed above the whole of the evidence of the prosecution witnesses in material particulars. We have noticed that the learned tribunal suffered from a suspicion about the truth of the dying declaration allegedly made by the deceased to his father PW.1 Mokbul Gazi, his mother PW.3 Lal Vanu, his brother PW.3 Jahurul Islam and also to PW.2 Faisal. We have also noted that when the said PW.2 returned to the place of occurrence by taking with him the aforesaid 3 witnesses on an information to them that the deceased was being chopped, the accused had already left the place by accomplishing their mission. The deceased was found lying with as many as 18 incised bleeding injuries, soma of them being on vital parts of his body like his right ear, neck, shoulder and back. The injuries were grievous in nature with sufficient depth, bleeding continuously. Learned advocate for the condemned prisoners has submitted before us that uttering anything in such a physical condition by the deceased was beyond human ability. It would be unusual to believe that he could mate a dying declaration mentioning names of as many as 12/13 accused with details of the occurrence in such a physical condition. Learned tribunal below also considered it difficult to place reliance on such dying declaration allegedly made by the deceased but he posed a question why should then his father, mother and brother undertake the pains and make a futile attempt to carry him to the hospital if he had been really dead when they saw him. In our view the body of the deceased was still warm with pulsating of life in it that made them hopeful of regaining his life by providing necessary treatment in the hospital. But alas the was declared dead when he was arrived at the hospital. When cross examined PW.1 Mokbul Gazi could not even tell when the deceased breathed his last. From the aforesaid circumstances, we have reason to hold that the remnant of life that was still pulsating in the deceased when he was found by the informant party was not strong enough for him to make such a dying declaration pronouncing names of as many as 12/13 accused.

36. The dying declaration was not also free from suspicion. As alleged in the FIR accused Abul Kalam member who lost the last union parishad election to one Habibur Rahman because of the deceased's active support for the said Habibur Rahman was the main culprit conspiring for his murder. His name also transpired as one of the assailants in the dying declaration. But the investigating officer submitted FRT in favour of the said Abul Kalam and 2 other accused, namely Faruk and Nasir whose names were disclosed by him in his dying declaration. Informant did not prefer any narajee petition against the said FRT. Further, 2 other new persons, namely Sikandar and Niranjon were made accused in the charge sheet though their names did not appear in the FIR nor their names were disclosed by the deceased in the dying declaration. But what is peculiar is that PW.2 Faisal included the names of the said Sikandar and Niranjon in his deposition as having been disclosed in the dying declaration made by the deceased. PW.3 Jahurul Islam also included in his deposition the names of said Sikandar and Niranjan as accused allegedly mentioned by the deceased in his dying declaration. Dying declaration of this sort varying at times was quite suspicious and appears to us to have been invented by the prime prosecution witnesses for the purpose of implicating the accused including the condemned prisoners whom they suspected. It is not worthy of credence.

37. The learned tribunal below placed reliance upon the evidence of PW.6 Sultan Howlader as an eyewitness to the occurrence corroborated by PW.5 Nannu Hawlader and also upon the evidence of PW.7 Dula Gazi, a hearsay witness from PW.1 Mokbul Gazi. The occurrence as told in the prosecution case took place at about 10-30 at night. Eye-witnessing an occurrence with recognition of accused was not thus possible without sufficient light. PW. 2 Faisal who was allegedly accompanying his deceased uncle Harun-or-Rashid at the time of occurrence did not disclose the means of recognition of the accused in the FIR which was lodged by his grandfather PW.1 Mokbul Gazi. Means of recognition was introduced for the first time during the course of trial by the said PW.2 Faisal Gazi as saying;-

চাচাকে আসামীরা উপযুপরী কোপাতে থাকে। আমি পিছন হতে অনুসরন করে বিদ্যুত ও আমার হাত থাকা টর্চের আলোতে পুর্বোক্ত সকল আসামীকে চিনে ফেলি।

(The aforesaid accused were chopping my uncle at random. By following them from behind I recognized all those accused in the light of the electricity and also in the flash of electric torch which I had in my hand). In his cross examination he stated:

রাত ঘুটঘুটে অন্ধকার ছিল কি না আমার স্মরণ নাই। আমার হাতে টর্চ না থাকলে ও বিদ্যুতের আলো না থাকলে আসামী কাউকে চিনতে পারতাম না।

(I do not remember if the night was pitch-black. I could not have recognized any of the accused had there been no light of electricity or if I had not an electric torch light in my hand). It was suggested to him in cross examination that he did not make any such statement to the investigating officer that he had any electric torch light in his hand or that he witnessed the occurrence in the light of electricity but he denied the suggestion straight away. ঞ.0 PW. 18 S. I. Shahjahan's attention was then drawn during his cross examination to the said statement of PW.2 Faisal but he categorically stated that the said PW.2 did not state to him that he had any electric torch in his hand or that he recognized any accused in the light of electricity. Under the circumstances his statement regarding witnessing the occurrence with recognition of all the accused in the light of electricity and also in the focus of electric torch was certainly an act of embellishment during the course of trial. Further, we have found that the dead body was found lying in a banana cluster towards the southern direction of the nursery of one Montu Mia. PW.1 Mokbul Gazi stated in his cross examination that there was no light post at the place where the deceased was found. So, how could the occurrence of chopping of the deceased could be viewed and the accused recognized when it was going on in a dark place by indiscriminate blows as is apparent from the number of injuries appearing on the deceased.

38. We have 2 other eyewitness of the occurrence. They were PW.5 Nannu Hawlader and PW.6 Sultan Hawlader. Both of them were sons of Mohammad Ali Howlader and were, therefore, full brothers. They also stated in their depositions that they witnessed the occurrence of chopping in the light of electricity and also in the flash of the electric torches which they had in their hands. It, however, deserves mention here that they did not state any such thing that they were witnessing the occurrence from the same place. The place of occurrence was a dark place as we have noticed earlier. There was no electric post there as stated by PW.1 himself. So, witnessing the occurrence in the light of electricity was but unusual unless it was a deliberate attempt to prop up the prosecution case.

39. Now, let us come to the case of recognition by electric torch 3 electric torches were allegedly seized by the investigating officer, one belonging to PW.2 Faisal, another belonging to PW.5 Nannu Hawlader and the other belonging to PW. 6 Sultan Hawlader from the place of occurrence on 26.3.2003 at 10-30 in the morning. It was not stated in the seizure list (ext-6) if those items were handed over to him (I. 0) by the said 3 witnesses or he got the same by picking up from the place of occurrence finding them lying I there. Learned advocate for the condemned prisoners has submitted that the investigating officer seized bloodstained 'earth and bloodstained bark of plantain tree from the place of occurrence on 24.3.2003 at 10-45 in the morning by preparing a seizure list (ext.3). Why then those 3 items of electric torch, should not also be found and seized from the same place on the same date and at the same time on 24.3.2003? Why further 2 days' delay should occur in seizing those 3 items? According to him belated seizure of those 3 items is an afterthought affair to give the prosecution case an acceptable shape. His argument does not appear to us to be unsubstantial if we consider it in the light of the evidence on record. PW.5 Nannu Hawlader stated in his cross examination that he had communication with the investigating officer after one month of the occurrence, that his electric torch lay deposited with the police and that he did not remember on which date he deposited the electric torch. If the said PW.5 had occasion to meet the investigating officer for the first time after one month of the occurrence he must have met him 23-4-2003 (the occurrence having taken place on 23-3-2003). The said electric torch must have then been deposited or handed over to him approximately on 23.4.2003. Then how could it be shown to have been seized on 26.3.2003? Does it not render the seizure list quite dodgy? PW.6 Sultan Hawlader stated in his cross examination that he made statement to the investigating officer on the following day of the occurrence. The occurrence, we have found, took place on 23-3-2003 and he made statement to the investigating officer on 24-3-2003. Then it was but usual that the electric torch held by- him, in the flash of which he allegedly recognized the accused, should be handed over to him on 24.3.2003 but why should it be seized after 3 days of the occurrence on 26-3-2003 and not on 24.3.2003 at least? When the investigating officer showed sufficient promptness in seizing other materials like blood stained earth and bloodstained plantain tree bark from the place of occurrence immediately on taking over investigating on 24.3.2003, we find no reason why even the least delay should take place on his part in seizing those means of recognition which had a vital impact upon the whole case of the prosecution. We have also found earlier that PW.2 Faisal who was allegedly accompanying the deceased introduced the story of recognition of the accused in the light of electricity and flash of electric torch during the course of trial to embellish the prosecution case. So, seizure of an electric torch from him was a planned affair. The seizure list which showed seizure of three electric torches belonging to 3 PWs was quite dubious.

40. Now, we shall also consider how far the evidence of PW.5 Nannu Hawlader and PW.6 Sultan Hawlader was credible regarding their witnessing the occurrence of chopping with their own eyes. As stated by PW.5 Nannu Hawlader in his deposition he also crossed the river in the same ferry with the deceased Harun-or-Rashid and PW. 2 Faisal on 23.3.2003 at 10-15 at night; their dwelling houses being in the same locality they are proceeding in the same direction; he fell a little behind; when the deceased and PW.2 Faisal reached the middle portion of the road running from east to west all those accused (names mentioned) caught hold of him (deceased) and dragged him to the road beside the nursery of Montu Mia and started chopping him at random; he witnessed the occurrence in the flash of the electric torch and also in the light of electricity; on his query to accused Moti Gazi why they were so chopping him, he (Moti Gazi) threatened him whereupon he ran away for fear of life to his house and narrated the occurrence to the other inmates of his house; then again he followed PW.2 Faisal, PW.4 Lal Vanu, PW.1 Mokbul Gazi and PW.3 Jahurul Islam when they were proceeding towards the place of occurrence; he also accompanied the deceased in the same trawler on way to Patuakhali General Hospital and was also present in the hospital. This was affirmed by him in his cross examination. Was it not then usual for him to disclose the fact of his having witnessed the occurrence with recognition of the accused to the informant PW.1 Mokbul Gazi, PW.2 Faisal, PW.3 Jahurul Islam, PW.4 Lal Vanu and PW.7 Dulal Gazi with whom he was accompanying the deceased in the same trawler? Then should not such fact of vital importance find place in the FIR itself which was lodged by PW.1 after the deceased was declared dead in the hospital? Should not such fact be deposed to by PW.1, PW.2, PW.3, PW.4 and PW.7 during the course of trial? But we find conspicuous absence of it in the FIR and also in the evidence of the aforesaid 5 witnesses. Why this witness should conceal the fact of his being an eyewitness to the occurrence to the said witnesses if he had really seen the occurrence? We thus find it difficult to place reliance upon his evidence as an alleged eyewitness to the occurrence, this being beyond human expectation under the circumstances found by us above.

41. Similar is the case of eyewitness PW.6 Sultan Hawlader. We have noticed that PW.5 Nannu Hawlader was his full brother. His evidence regarding his witnessing the occurrence was in the same line of his other brother PW.5 Nannu Hawlader. This witness also on being threatened by accused Moti Gazi ran home for fear of life and narrated the entire occurrence to the inmates of his house. Both of them being inmates of the same house and both of them having run home at the threat of accused Moti Gazi and both of them having disclosed the occurrence to the inmates of their house, both of them must have heard each other about the manner of occurrence and recognition of the accused. In that event it was but usual that PW.5 should narrate this occurrence of his other brother PW.6 Sultan Hawlader having witnessed the occurrence to the informant PW.1 Mokbul Gazi, PW.2 Faisal, PW.3 Johurul Islam, PW.4 Lal Vanu and PW.7 Dulal Gazi with whom he was travelling in the same trawler carrying the deceased to the hospital. But we do not find such disclosure. Neither of the said PW.5 Nannu Hawlader and PW.6 Sultan Hawlader stated in his deposition about the other having witnessed the occurrence. So, their non disclosure of such an important fact which had a vital bearing upon the whole case of the prosecution made their evidence incredible.

<u>42. In the instant case before us statements of 3 witnesses namely Bazlu, Shahjahan and Mahbub Gazi were recorded by a competent Magistrate under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. But they were not examined by the prosecution during the course of trial. A single sentence statement was, however, made by PW.1 Mokbul Gazi in his examination-in-chief that Bazlu, Mahbub and Shajahan were gained over by the defence. But this was not sufficient to prevent the prosecution agency from producing the said 3 witnesses before the tribunal below. If they resiled from the statements made by them under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure prosecution could have contradicted them to impeach their credit in terms of provision of section 155 of the Evidence Act. At any rate they should not have been withheld. It thus raised a presumption under section 114 (g) of the Evidence Act to the effect that had they been produced they would not have supported the case of the prosecution. Of course the instant 4 condemned prisoners were absconding from the very beginning but ascension itself could not be a ground for conviction when there was lack of sufficient evidence against them.</u>

43. Learned tribunal below Without appreciating the evidence on record in their true perspective and without taking into consideration of the statements made by the vital witnesses in their cross examination making the prosecution quite shaky most illegally convicted and sentenced them under section 302/34 of the Penal Code. His impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence is not sustainable in law and is liable to be set aside.

44. In the result, Criminal Appeal No. 887 of 2004 be and is allowed with rejection of Death Reference No. 33 of 204. The rule issued in Crl. Misc. Case No.1195 of 2005 be and is Made absolute. Jail Appeal Nos.313 of 2004 and 172 of 2005 are disposed of accordingly.

45. The impugned judgment and order dated 01-03-2004 passed by the learned Speedy Trial Tribunal, Barisal in Speedy Tribunal Case No. 62 of 2003 convicting the condemned Prisoners of the offence punishable under section 302/34 of the Penal Code and sentencing them there under to death by hanging is set aside hereby.

46. Condemned prisoners Tipu Gazi, Moti Gazi, Sohel Gazi and Mizanur Rahman be acquitted of the charge levelled against them under section 302/34 of the Penal Code. They be set at liberty at once, if not wanted in any other connection.

47. Send down lower tribunal records along with a copy of this, judgment expeditiously.

End.

Minhaz Uddin

full_judgment:
Salma Masud Chowdhury, J: This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2(Gha) to show cause as to why the order no. 54 dated 14.10.2002 passed by the Assistant Judge, Nawabganj Court, Dhaka in Title suit No. 8 of 2000 allowing the application under order 26 Rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure filed by the plaintiff for local investigation of the suit land should not be set aside and/or pass such other orders or further order or orders as to this court may seem fit and proper.

2. The opposite party No. 1-2 as plaintiffs filed Title suit No. 8 of 2000 against the petitioner and others for declaration of title.

3. The petitioner as defendant contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint.

4. On 7.9.2002 the plaintiff opposite party filed an application under order 26 Rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure for local investigation and the defendant petitioners filed a written objection against it. The trial court by the order dated 14.10.2002 allowed the said application and an Advocate Commissioner was appointed for the purpose.

5. Being aggrieved thereby the defendant as petitioner filed an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure before this Court an obtained the present Rule.

6. None appears to support the Rule.

7. Mr. Md. Ibrahim Mollah, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties opposes the Rule and submits that the Court committed no illegality in appointing the Advocate Commissioner for local investigation which was necessary for proper adjudication of the matter.

<u>8. I have perused the revisional application along with the materials on record and heard the learned Advocate appearing on be-half of the opposite parties. The object of the local investigation under Order 26 Rule 9 of the Case of Civil Procedure is to obtain evidence which from its peculiar nature can best be had from the spot itself. Such evidence enables the court to properly and correctly understand and assess the evidence on record. The Court has wide discretion in the matter of rejection or acceptance of a report submitted by an Advocate Commissioner.</u>

9. I am of the view that under revisional jurisdiction, this court may not interfere with the discretion of the trial court to appoint an Advocate Commissioner for local investigation. Under the Circumstances, I find that the court below has committed no illegality in passing the impugned order.

10. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The order of stay granted earlier stands vacated.

11. Communicate the order to the court concerned.

End.

A.K.M. Mozammel huq
Vs.
Chancellor of the National University, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Education, Bangladesh Secretariat, Dhaka and others.
case_source: arising out of Writ Petition No. 5125 of 2004
full_judgment:
A.H.M. Shamsuddin Choudhury, J.- The Rule under adjudication, issued on 13th July 2010 was in following terms:

"Let a Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 22.8.2006 passed by a Division Bench of this Division in Writ Petition No.5125 of 2004 discharging the Rule should not be reviewed and/or pass such other or further order orders as this Court may deem fit and proper"

2. Relying on the following averments the petitioner seeks for review of the judgment and order dated 22.08.2006 passed by the Hon'ble High Court Division in writ petition No.5125 of 2004:

3. The Writ Petitioner and the present Petitioner are not the same person. The present petitioner is an elected Member of the Parliament of our country. He is also the Chairman of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on the Ministry of Land and the President of Bangladesh Awami League (AL), Gazipur District.

4. The previous Vice-Chancellor of the National University, Professor Aftab Ahmed joined as Vice-Chancellor on 05.07.2003. Thereafter from 17.11.2003 to 04.01.2004 he appointed 331 persons without any advertisement, without any selection committee and without maintaining the quota system. This was done in exercise of the unguided and unfettered powers under Section 12(10) of the National University Act, 1992. In this way during his term the said Vice-Chancellor appointed a total of 1222 persons in violation of various recruitment Rules, which are stated below. Most of these violations are internal in nature and at the time of hearing of Writ Petition No.5125 of 2004 neither the writ-petitioner nor the present petitioner had enough specific evidence to substantiate the allegations. Subsequently new evidence came to light through investigation by the National University authority and the University Grants Commission (UGC) and criminal cases have also been filed. Hence the present application for review.

5. The violations of recruitment rules by the Respondents were done in many ways-National Policy of maintaining quota was violated and the basic need for prior advertisement under the provisions of Services (Re-organization and Conditions) Act, 1975 was not complied with. On the other hand, several persons were given advance increments making them senior to previously appointed persons. They were arbitrary, unjustified, illegal and were done for unlawful gain. Some examples of such illegal appointment have been cited in paragraph No. 4 of the above mentioned Writ Petition. In paragraph No. 5 of the said Writ Petition a list of appointees is given, who were appointed in exercise of the extra ordinary power under Section 12(10) of the National University Act. Thus, all these appointments were made with no proper advertisement, no proper interview and with the exception of a few, most of the appointees joined on the day of the appointment or on the following date violating all norms and rules. This indicated that there were private arrangements of incentives not recognized by law. But at that stage the Writ Petitioner or the present petitioner did not have specific and conclusive evidence to prove these illegalities.

6. After making the impugned appointments during 17.11.2003 to 04.01.2004, there was a 'sham' advertisement bearing No.01 (740) NU/Admn./2004/1/2946 dated 04.01.2004, which was published in the `Daily Sangbad' on 05.01.2004. It would be seen from the said advertisement that though 30 categories of posts were mentioned nothing was mentioned as to how many persons would be recruited from each category nor was it mentioned if appointments were being made on a 'regular or temporary' basis. This was a clear violation of the law.

7. It was a farce of a public advertisement made more to deceive than to inform or illuminate. The impugned appointments were made prior to the publication of the advertisement. The petitioner learnt that the aforesaid illegal appointees were subsequently interviewed as Departmental candidates and allowed to continue indefinitely.

39. The questions we are to address are whether, (1) in the absence of explicit constitutional mandate, the High Court Division can entertain an application to review a judgment it passed earlier under Article 102 of the Constitution (2) if the first question in resolved affirmatively, the instant review petition is destined to succeed or not.

40. Article 105 of the Constitution stipulates provision for review, but that Article is meant for the Appellate Division only. No corresponding Article is inscripted in our Constitution to explicitly confer power of review to the High Court Division.

41. Does this absence denote this Division's incompetence to review it's own decision?

42. Case laws of high preponderance suggest otherwise.

43. This Division's jurisdiction as to review it's own judgment has been comprehensively and meticulously laid down by our Appellate Division, the Supreme Courts of India and Pakistan in a myriad of cases. The ratio decidendi in all these cases throw illuminated becon to guide us.

44. The first case that deserves reliance is that of Serajuddin Ahmed and others Vs. AKM Saiful Alam and other reported at page 41 of 56 DLR (AD). In describing the High Court Division's power in reviewing it's own previous judgment, the Appellate Division, quite unequivocally stated, "It is true in the constitution there is no provision empowering the High Court Division to review it's own judgment and order, but it is also true that there was no provision precluding the High Court Division from exercising power of review. The Court's inherent power to do justice to the parties before it, is an accepted one and for that the form in which the court shall dispense justice is a matter for the Court or, in other words, it may either by way of review of its judgment or, upon revising it's judgment in the background of the materials brought before it subsequent to the pronouncement of the judgment since the Court is the master of it's own procedure and it will exercise both its procedural and substantive discretion only on the ground of justice, equity and good conscience."

45. The Appellate Division in the same case continued to assert the proposition of law in the following terms, "There being no dispute that the court is for the dispensation of justice and in doing so, is competent to exercise it's discretion to advance the cause of justice upon resorting to procedure that would advance the cause of justice, equity and good conscience and, as there in nothing in Article 102 of the Constitution to preclude the High Court Division from exercising the power of review, we are of the view that the High Court Division is very much competent to entertain an application for review and to revise it's judgment if a case for review is made out, or  in other words, the materials which if would have been before the court the judgment already made would not have been the one but different if placed before the High Court Division then the same decision to advance cause of action is not precluded from reviewing its own judgment."

46. In another celebrated case namely that of Moni Begum and others Vs. Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakha and others, reported in page 154 of 46 DLR (AD) have made the following observation, "In our view the High Court Division, while exercising the jurisdiction relating to a civil matter, is no doubt in seisin of civil proceeding but it has to be borne in mind that this original constitutional jurisdiction of the High Court Division is aimed at securing the speedy and efficacious remedy to an aggrieved person whose legal or constitutional right has been infringed. It is meant to be a summary and swift mode of disposal of disputes and it is not designed to be procedurally intricate and remedially elaborate method of trial of suits of original civil jurisdiction. In fact its procedural simplicity and swiftness marks it out as a remedy recognisable and distinctive constitutional remedy. The petitions are ordinarily disposed of on affidavits, although it is open to the court to take such other evidence in such other manner as it may deem fit following such procedure and making such orders as may appear to it just. The elaborate, detail and technical orders laid down in the Code of Civil Procedure, if literally imported into the writ proceeding through section 141 of the C.P.C will be counterproductive and will defeat the very purpose of speedy remedy of it."

47. We found profoundly helpful guidance from the decision in the case of Khapan Bittahin Co-operative Society Ltd. Vs. Nagendra Mahisya Das, Secretary Nijkurua Matsyajibi Samabaya Samity and other reported in page 502, 45 DLR. In this case their Lordships Fazle Hussain Mohammad Habibur Rahman and Mainur Reza Chowdhury J.J. elucidated the relevant theme of law through the under quoted observation, "The right to claim review of any decision of a court of law, like the right to appeal, is a substantive right and not a mere matter of procedure, and as such, neither of them is available unless it has been conferred by law. Under Article 105 of the Constitution of Bangladesh the Appellate Division of Supreme Court has jurisdiction to review its judgment and order. There is no corresponding provision in the constitution with regard to the High Court Division's jurisdiction to review its decision. However, section 114 of the Code of Civil Procedure confers jurisdiction on the courts of Civil judicature to review judgment pronounced by them, and order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code prescribe grounds on which such review can be claimed apart from the court's limited inherent power of review, this is the only legal position which confers power of review on civil courts, that is, courts of Civil jurisdiction. There appears to be no rule, making the provision of section 114 of the Code inapplicable to the High Court Division in the exercise of its original civil jurisdiction. The court envisages exercise of two kinds of jurisdiction by the High Court Division, namely civil appellate jurisdiction and original civil jurisdiction. Hence, the power of review under section 114 of the Code available to the High Court in the exercise of this jurisdiction. The writ jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution is an original jurisdiction. The question then arises as to whether the provisions of Code of Civil Procedure, other than the provisions expressly excepted, shall apply in the exercise of writ jurisdiction by the High Court under the said article. This question was exhaustively dealt with by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the Case of Hussain Bakhsh Vs. Settlement Commissioner, Rawalpindi reported in 1970 PLD (SC) 1. When the question was whether the High Court had power to review an order made by it in exercise of it's power under Article 98 of the Constitution of Pakistan (1962), the Supreme Court held that apart from the High Court's power to correct errors apparent on the face of the record in exercise of its inherent jurisdiction, the High Court has power under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 to review it's own order made in writ jurisdiction in a civil matter. The proceeding under Article 98 of the Constitution, concerning a civil matter being a civil proceeding relating to the High Court's original civil jurisdiction and section 114 of the Code conferring power of review not having been made inapplicable to the High Court in the exercise of its original civil jurisdiction, the power to review and order made by the High Court in it's writ jurisdiction will be available to it under the said section 114. The Civil Procedure Code regulates civil proceedings. The nature of the proceeding does not necessarily depend on the nature of the jurisdiction of the Court invoked. In order to determine whether a proceeding is a civil proceeding or not, it is necessary to see what are the questions raised and decided in the proceeding. If the proceeding involves the assertion or enforcement of civil right, it is a civil proceeding. The provisions of the Code other than the specially excepted one, shall apply in the exercise of the High Court's jurisdiction in civil matter, whatever may be the nature of that jurisdiction (Sabitri Takurani Vs. Savi 1921 AIR PC 80). In this connection section 141 CPC and the decision in the case of Thakur Prasad Vs Fakirullah, ILR 17 Allahabad 106 and Neerala Tea Estate Vs. Government 41 DLR 90 may be seen. Civil proceeding is a process for recovery of individual right or redress of individual wrong, inclusion, in its proper legal sense, of suits by the crown. Whether a proceeding is civil or not depends on the nature of subject matter of the proceeding and it's object and not on mode adopted or the forum provided for the enforcement of the right. A proceeding which deals with a right of a civil nature does not cease to be so merely because the right is sought to be enforced by having recourse to the writ jurisdiction. Judged from this aspect, it was held by the Supreme Court of Pakistan that a proceeding under Article 98 of the Constitution relating to a Civil matter is a civil proceeding, although the High Court's jurisdiction in such a proceeding is constitutional jurisdiction of an original kind. A civil proceeding in a Court of Civil jurisdiction in governed by the provisions of the Code other than the provisions which are specially excepted 1970 (PLD) SC1.

48. A survey of the ratio of above judgments sway us to the irresistible conclusion that absence of express constitutional provision notwithstanding, this Division is vested with the power to review it's own decision and that the said power stems not only from section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with Order LXVII, rule 1, but is also inherent with this Division's duty to dispense justice.
