According to Dr. Kamal Hossain, as evidence of these forgeries were not available at the time the original writ petition was heard and disposed of by this Division on 22.08.2006, it would now be wholly congruous and cogent for us to review the original judgment in the light of new discoveries, revealing overwhelming forgeries.

51. The review petitioner contends through its pleadings, not controverter, that the previous Vice-Chancellor, Professor Aftab Ahmed, appointed scores of his cronies without any advertisement, without any selection committee and without maintaining any quota system and the same was done in the pretext of the power conferred by section 12 of the National University Act, 1992 and in this way, during his term, the said Vice-Chancellor appointed a total of 1222 persons in violation of various recruitment rules and that as most of this violations were internal in nature, at the time the writ petition no.5125 of 2004 of heard, neither the writ petitioner nor the present petitioner had enough evidence to substantiate the allegations and aspersions. Subsequently, new infallible evidence emerged with invincible shall through immaculate investigation by the National University authority and the University Grants Commission and, criminal cases have been filed and hence the review application.

52. It has been averred by the petitioner, not refuted by the respondents, that basic requirement of prior advertisement, which is indispensable under the provisions of Service (Re-organisation and conditions) Act, 1975, was not adhered to and that several persons were given advance increments making them senior to the previously appointed persons and the same was done for unlawful gain and , that some examples of such illegal appointments were cited in paragraph no.4 of the above mentioned writ petition, where a list of persons who were appointed in exercise of extra-ordinary power under section 12(10) of the National University Act, without following the required procedure. The petitioner further averts that after the conclusion of the appointment process during 17.11.2033 and 04.01.2004 a spurious advertisement was published in the Daily Sangbad on 05.01.2004. So, all the appointments were made through the back stage and hence the same could not be regularised. The petitioner further avers, not refuted, that to finance the burden created through reckless appointment, an additional financial liability of Taka 6 crore had to be shouldered.

53. To consider Dr. Hossain's submission in it's true context we found helpful guidance from the case of Khapan Bittalin co-operative society Ltd. vs. Nagendra Mahisiya Das, Supra. In that case their Lordships Fazle Hussain Muhammad Habibur Rahman and Mainur Reza Chowdhury .J, J. expressed "if fraud is proved, then there is no question of limitation and it would run from the date when fraud was detected." In our view, allegations of fraud having not been refuted, and the same having been proved, the above observation is quite pertinent.

54. A strong chain of authorities suggest that a review petition should succeed on merit if it can be established that the original decision would have otherwise. If subsequently detected evidence were before it.

<u>55. The appellate Division's observation, quoted below, in Sirajuddin Ahmed Vs. A.K.M. Saiful Alam, supra, supports this view; "We are of the view that the High Court Division is very much competent to entertain an application for review and to revise its judgment if a case for review is made out, or, in other words, the materials, which if would have been before the court, the judgment already made would not have been the one but different, in placed before the High Court Division then the said division, to advance cause of action is not precluded from remaining its judgment."</u>

<u>56. In the instant case we are more than satisfied that had the uncontroverted information and the evidence as narrated in the petitioner's pleadings, been before this Division when the writ petition no.5125 of 2004 was adjudicated upon on 22nd August 2006, the judgment and order would have been diametrically different. It is inconceivable that the rule would have been discharged had the petitioner succeeded to substantiate it's claim of irregular and fraudulent appointments by adducing such evidence, as it has been done now. In this respect it is worth mentioning that as the Appellate Division stated in Moni Begum Vs. Rajdhani Unnayan Kartipakha (supra) "the petitions are ordinarily disposed of on affidavits, although it is open to the courts to take such other evidence, in such other manner as it may deem fit, following such procedure and making such order as it may appear just."</u>

57. Some of the high profile decisions where the criteria for successful review petitions have been enunciated, include the decision in the case of Mohammad Amin Khan Vs. Controller Estate Duty 14 DLR SC 276. In that case Justice Kaikaus observed, "While I would prefer not to accept those limitations as if they placed any technical obstruction in the exercise of the review jurisdiction of this Court, I would accept that they would embody the principle on which this court would not, in the exercise of such jurisdiction. It is not because a conclusion is wrong but because something obvious has been overlooked, some important aspect of the matter has not been considered, that a review petition would lie."

58. In Azizur Rahman Vs. Bangladesh CRP No.26-32 of 1993 it was held that discovery of new and important matter of evidence, after due exercise of diligence, a party could not produce at the hearing can be a ground for review judgment, although in this case the review petition was rejected as the court was of the view that the newly discovered material could not have affected the original decision.

59. In Mohindra Vs. District Judge, Delhi AIR 1971 SC 107 the Indian Supreme Court reviewed it's earlier judgment because new materials were placed and the case presented some unusual circumstances.

60. We are of the invariable and unreasonable view that on the basis of the ratio expressed in the above discussed cases, the present review application is bound to succeed. Plentitude of new evidence to substantiate the allegation of fraud, deceit, illegality, impropriety cronyism and corrupt practices, which formed the basis of the original writ petition, namely writ petition no.5125 of 2004, came to light after comprehensive investigation was under taken during the recent period. We reckon, and there is no reason why we should not arrive at that reckoning, that had this evidence and information been before this Division when the said writ petition was disposed of, the judgment would have been quite opposite and the Rule would have been made absolute. In this contest we would also like to add, Lord Denning's immortal proposition, "Fraud unravels everything" (Lazarus Estate Ltd. Vs. Beasley 1956 I QB 702). In the instant case the review petitioner has catalogued fraudulent practices of outrageous proportion and that the said allegations have remained undenied. It is incomprehensible that this Division would have discharged the rule had the evidence and information, as have been adduced before us, were made available earlier.

61. Prof. S.A. De smith in his book Judicial Review of Administrative Action, 4th Edition page 335-336 stated, "the concept of bad faith allure precise definition, but in relation to the exercise of statutory power it may be said to comprise dishonesty (fraud or malice). A power is exercised fraudulently if it's repository intends to achieve an object other than that for which he believes the power to have been conferred. For example, a local authority committee would exercise in bad faith it's power to exclude interested members of the public if it deliberately chose to hold the meeting in a small room. The intention may be to promote another public interest or vitiate interest. A power is exercised maliciously if it's repository is motivated by personal animosity towards those who are directly affected by its exercise."

62. In Dr. Nurul Islam-v-Bangladesh 33DLR (AD) 201, the Appellate Division found the government action, compulsorily retiring the petitioner, as to have been vitiated by malice in law because the said action was taken with a malicious intent.

63. In Protap Singh Vs. Punjab AIR 1964 SC 72 the Supreme Court of India quashed the government action, forcing a civil surgeon to compulsory retirement, on the ground that the said action was taken at the instance of the Chief Minister who wished to wreak personal vengeance on the civil surgeon.

64. In Express Newspaper Ltd. Vs. India AIR 1986 SC 872 government's action, forfeiting the lease of land held by the newspaper, because it was critical about imposition of emergency in 1975, was set aside by the Indian Supreme Court, which held that the decision was prompted by dishonest intention.

65. In O.P Gupta Vs. India AIR 1987 SC 2257 the Supreme Court quashed government decision on malafide ground where departmental proceeding, keeping the petitioner under suspension for 11 years followed by an order of pre-mature retirement, was found to be malafide.

<u>66. In fact the above cited decisions are only few of scores of decisions, supporting the view that a decision arrived at on bad faith, fraud, malice of fact, malice of law or with dishonest intention, cannot withstand the test of validity.</u>

<u>67. Before parting we would like to add that we were not oblivious of the exclusionary provisions, which would defeat a review petition such as that a review petition cannot be equated with the original hearing of the case, that the jurisdiction cannot be utilised for re-hearing of the matter, that review is not allowed on a new ground which was not urged during the hearing of the original matter and that review cannot be equated with revision or appeal.</u>

68. For the reasons recorded above, we remain convinced that none of these nugatory factors can dent the instant application.

69. In all the circumstances, narrated above, the review application is allowed as it ought to be and the instant Rule is made absolute. In consequence the judgment and order passed by this division on 22-08-2006 in writ petition no. 5125 of 2004 is, on review, reversed, and substituted by the order, which shall now read. "The Rule is hereby made absolute without any order as to costs wherefore all the appointments made at the National University during period from 17th November, 2003 to 31st August 2004 are set aside. This follows that all those appointed during that period would cease to remain employed at the said University with immediate effect. The respondents, inclusive of the Secretary, Ministry of Education and the Vice-Chancellor of the National University, are directed to cancel, revoke, terminate rescind the impugned appointments, made during the period from 17th November, 2003 to 31st August 2004, and remove them from the employment of National University without delay".

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 1259 and 1260 of 2004
lawyer:
Md. Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record. ------ For the Petitioner (In both the cases) 
Shamsul Alam, Senior Advocate, instructed by Syed Mahbubur Rahman, Advocate-on-Record.  ------ For Respondent Nos. 1-6 (In both the cases) 
Respondent Nos. 7-39 (In both the cases) ------ Not represented.
parties:
Moulavi Abdul Kader ------ Petitioner (In both the cases)
VS
Mozammel Haque & ors ------ Respondents (In both the cases)
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 27.07.2004 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision Nos. 1414 and 774 of 2002.)
full_judgment:
Amirul Kabir Chowdhury J: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1259 of 2004 has been filed by the plaintiff petitioner seeking leave to appeal against the judgment and order dated 27.07.2004 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1414 of 2002 hearing analogously the Civil Revision No. 774 of 2002 and discharging both the rules.

2. Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1260 of 2004 has been filed by the aforesaid petitioner (the defendant) against the same judgment and order in Civil Revision No. 774 of 2002.

3. The petitioner as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 97 of 1997 praying for partition of the land of Khatian No. 710 stating, inter-alia, that 12 acres of land in C.S. Khatian No. 710 belonged to one Khabir Uddin after whose death his son Mofizul Hoque and two daughters and one wife inherited the property and in view of subsequent transfers Morium Bibi wife of Khabir Uddin inherited 70 decimals of land and that Morium died leaving his son Mofizul to inherits 35 decimals and Bibi Sekantar and Jaynob Banu inherited 17½ decimals each thereby Bibi Sekantar inherited 2.26½  acres of land from her father and 17½ decimals from her mother and while she was in possession of the property, by a deed of gift of 14.03.1973 she transferred 1.78 acres of land to the plaintiff petitioner and through inheritance also he got some land which totaled 2.26½  acres and that the defendants being heirs of Nur Mohammad also inherited portion of the properties and the properties being in ejamli possession there being no partition by metes and bounds the plaintiff petitioner prayed partition of 2.16½   acres in his favour.

4. The suit was contested by the defendant respondents stating, inter-alia, that the claim of the plaintiff on the basis of deed of gift purported to have been executed by Bibi Sekantar is false and in fact the deed was a forged document never acted upon.

5. The learned Assistant Judge decreed the suit by judgment and decree dated 25.04.2000. The defendant preferred Title Appeal No. 67 of 2000 before the learned District Judge, Lakshmipur and the said appeal was heard by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Lakshmipur who by the judgment and decree dated 26.11.2001 set aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial court and allowed shaham of 1.05 decimals of land in favour of the plaintiff petitioner.

6. The plaintiff petitioner being aggrieved moved the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1414 of 2002. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division by the impugned judgment and order discharged the rule.

7. The facts giving rise to Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1260 of 2004 are that the Respondents Mozammel Haque and others filed Title Suit No. 114 of 1997 against the plaintiff petitioner praying to declare the deed of gift dated 14.03.1973 as illegal, void, forged and fraudulent document. The suit was contested by the petitioner filing a written statement. It was averred that Bibi Sekantar, mother of the petitioner gifted the property in his favour voluntarily and that the suit was liable to be dismissed.

8. The learned Assistant Judge heard the suit along with Title suit No. 97 of 1997 and by the same judgment dated 25.04.2000 dismissed the suit (i.e. Other Suit No. 114 of 1992).

9. Being aggrieved the respondent i.e. the defendant of the said suit preferred Title Appeal No. 68 of 2000 and the appeal being heard analogously by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Lakshimpur with the aforesaid Title Appeal No. 67 of 2000, the said appellate court by the same judgment and decree dated 26.11.2001 allowed the appeal, setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial court. The plaintiff being aggrieved moved the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 774 of 2002 and the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division heard the matter analogously and by the impugned judgment and order discharged the rule.

10. Being aggrieved by the judgment and order of the High Court Division this petition has been filed.

11. Mr. Md. Nawab Ali, learned Advocate-on-Record in support of the petition has taken us through the impugned judgment and order and submits, inter-alia, that the High Court Division committed error of law in not holding that the plaintiff petitioner's mother transferred the suit property by the executing and registering the deed of gift and as such interference is called for.

12. He further submits that the trial court being court of first instance considered the evidence and decreed Other Suit No. 97 of 1997 and dismissed Other suit No. 114 of 1997 but the lower appellate court with legally adverting to the findings arrived at by the trial court illegally reversed the same and the High Court Division in its turn committed error in affirming the aforesaid illegal judgment of the lower appellate court.

<u>13. Mr. Shamsul Alam, learned Counsel on the other hand opposes the petition submitting, inter-alia, that the alleged deed of gift is said to have been executed in 1973 but the suit was filed in 1997 and during this long period the plaintiff petitioner did not produce the so called deed of gift anywhere nor disclosed the existence of the said deed at any time and thus the said deed did not see the light of the day and that the lower appellate court being the last court of fact considered the evidence and came to the decision that the deed of gift was not a genuine document and as such decided the case correctly. The High Court Division also, according to the learned Advocate, considered the facts and circumstances and evidence on record and correctly affirmed the judgment of the lower appellate court.</u>

<u>14. We have considered the submissions made by the learned Advocates of the parties. It appears that the High Court Division after considering the facts and circumstances and evidence on record came to the finding that the plaintiff petitioner in support of the deed of gift in his favour failed to produce the scribe or any other attesting witness of the deed.</u>

15. It further appears that one Golam Mostafa was produced who deposed as P.W.2. He deposed that they did not see the woman executing the deed of gift only her hands were seen by them at the time of putting thumb impressions nor any witness saw her. The plaintiff claims that P.W.2 Golam Mostafa attested the thumb impressions of Bibi Sekandar before the Sub-registrar but the said witness disowned the claim and deposed that the signature appearing in the document purported to have been made by him is not that of him and his specimen signatures were taken by the trial court which being compared by the lower appellate court as different from those appearing in the deed as identifier of the LTI of the executant. It appears further that in connection with the suit property there was shalish by the local elite and there also the plaintiff did not produce the deed of gift. In the face of such materials we are of the view that production of the document after 24 years for the first time for the present case smells smear.

16. We have perused the judgment of the lower appellate court and it appears that the lower appellate court considered the evidence meticulously and arrived at correct decision. The lower appellate court being the last court of fact and making the findings on the basis of evidence on record, the High Court Division did not commit any error in affirming the aforesaid judgment of the lower appellate court. There is therefore no error in the said judgment.

17. In this view of the matter both the petitions are dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. Md. Nurul Amin, Advocate ------For the petitioner. 
Mr. Omar Ali Khan, Advocate ------For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Md. Ismail Hossain
Vs.
Mst. Zulfan Ara and Others
full_judgment:
Soumendra Sarker, J: The Rule issued calling upon the Opposite Party No.1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 18.07.2001 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Court, Jhenidah in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 21 of 1998 affirming the judgment and order dated 25.10.1998 passed by the teamed Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Jhenidah in Miscellaneous Case No. 34 of 1997 should not be set aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule in a nutshell can be stated thus, the present opposite party no.1 being pre-emptor filed the original miscellaneous case in the court of learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Jhenaidah contending inter alia that the pre-emptor is a house wife and residing in Dhaka with her husband. Coming to her father's residence situated at Jhenidah the pre-emptor came to learn on 09.02.1997 that the opposite party no. 2 transferred the case land measuring 2½  decimals in favour of the opposite party no.1 on 30.01.1995 A.D. The pre-emptor-opposite party no.1 is a co-sharer by purchase the case joie after purchasing the land appertaining to S.A. Khatian No. 140/1 in plot no, 190 measuring an area of .05 acres of land from the original owner of the land opposite party no. 2 Rejia Khatun and for that reason for getting the land pre-empted due to her necessity after obtaining the certified copy of the case kabla on 15.03.1997 A.D. filed the original case for pre-emption under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. The further case of the pre-emptor-opposite party no.1 is such that she has no other land excepting her purchased 05 decimals of land.

3. Vis-a-vis the case of the pre-emptee-petitioner in brief is such that the case is not maintainable and is barred by law of limitation. The case is also bad for defect of parties & that the pre-emptor-opposite party no.1 is not a co-sharer of the case land. The further case of the pre-emptee is such that he purchased 8½  decimals of land from the opposite party no. 2 on 30.07.1994 at a consideration of Taka 70,000/- (Seventy thousand) and obtained possession from the northern portion of the plot. While the opposite party no. 2 wanted to sale the case land the pre-emptee agreed and accordingly the opposite party no. 2 transferred 2½ decimals of land in favour of the pre-emptee at a consideration of Tk. 20,000/- (twenty thousand). The transfer was held within the knowledge of the pre-emptor-opposite party and her father and as such the original case is hopelessly time barred as it was not filed within the statutory period of limitation. The pre-emptor having full knowledge about the case kabla from the very beginning on false allegation filed the original case which is liable to be dismissed.

4. During trial of the original case both the parties adduced evidence and after hearing arguments from the sides of the respective parties the learned Assistant Judge allowed the miscellaneous case on contest vide judgment and order dated 25.10.1998 A.D.

5. Being aggrieved the pre-emptee preferred an appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No.21 of 1998 in the court of learned District Judge, Jhenidah which was heard and disposed of by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Jhenidah and the learned lower appellate court by the impugned judgment and order dated 18.07.2001 disallowed they appeal affirming the judgment and order passed by the trial court.

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order the pre-emptee-appellant-petitioner has preferred this revisional application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the rule with an interim order of stay.

7. Mr. Md. Nurul Amin the leaned Advocate appeared on behalf of the petitioner while Mr. Omar Ali Khan, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the opposite party.

8. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner during hearing of this revisionl application submits that the learned trial court as well as the appellate court during disposal of the original case and its subsequent appeal committed gross illegality and irregularity. The learned Advocate further submits that despite the pre-emptor-opposite party, no.1 during trial of the original case hopelessly failed to discharge her onus in proving her respective case both the courts below without proper sifting of evidence and appreciation of law decided the merit of the case in favour of the pre-emptor arbitrarily which is perverse in the eye of law. The learned Advocate also submits that from the admission of the pre-emptor it is apparent from the face of the record that after her purchase she mutated her name and paid rent separately and similarly the purchaser pre-emptee after mutation separated the jams and paid rent for his land. Secondly, the pre-emption miscellaneous. case is barred by limitation as the data of registration of case kabla is 19.08.1995 under section 60 of the Registration Act, but the pre-emptor filed the original case on 19.03.1997. In this context; it is the contention of the pre-emptor that she was in the dark about the disputed transfer i.e. case kabla dated 30.01.1995 and for the first time sire came to learn about the said transfer from her father on 09 02.1997. Therefore, the burden of proof is heavily lies upon her that she was not in the know about the transfer prior to that. The learned Advocate on behalf of the petitioner in this regard has drawn the attention of mine on the deposition of the pre-emptor as witness no.1. In her testimony she admits that she knew about the case kabla on 06.02.1998 which is entirely overlooked and misread from the sides of both the courts below in their findings and decision. Beside this the witness no. 2 of the pre-emptor opposite party is a formal witness of the case who has got practically no knowledge about the original case. The witness no. 3 is not an independent competent witness of the case as he happens to be the father of the pre-emptor. Therefore, among all the three witnesses from the side of the pre-emptor-opposite party there is none upon whom the respective case of the pre-emptor can stand or there is no such independent, disinterested competent witness who is dependable and the court can safely believe the contention of the pre-emptor.

9. The learned Advocate also submits that the positive case of the purchaser-pre-emptee-petitioner that after his purchase in the year 1996 there was a survey of the land in presence of the pre-emptor's father. The witness no. 3 of the pre-emptor Md. Ammd Hossain, who is the father of the pre-emptor & the pre-emptor banks upon whom is a lawyer of the court. This important witness not challenged or denied the aforesaid proposition of the pre-emptee in his deposition. Therefore, the very circumstances go to show that the conduct of the witness no. 3 is amounting to admission of the pre-emptee's case. Apart from this; it was another contention of the pre-emptee that a "salish" was held in the month of February, 1996 and in that "salish" many witnesses were present, but none of them was produced from the side of the pre-emptor to establish her case to discard the assertion of the pre-emptee. On the other hand among the witnesses of the pre-emptees the witness no. 3, who is the husband of the vendor-opposite party no. 2 corroborate the case of the pre-emptee-petitioner including the above mentioned Salish. The witness no. 4 for the pre-emptee in his deposition specifically asserts that in the month of March 1996 the service of notice was done in presence of the father of the pre-emptor. This witness no. 4 is one of the co-sharer of the case jote and his statement is not denied or challenged even from the side of the pre-emptor during cross-examination. No denial even is noticed from the side of the pre-emptor. Among the four witnesses from the side of the pre-emptee-appellant-petitioner none of the witnesses was discussed or evaluated or even considered by the trial court as well as the appellate court and the very act of the learned courts below makes it clear that there has been total non-consideration of material evidence from the side of both the courts. Accordingly, the findings and observation is one-sided which is perverse in the eye of law and not sustainable. The learned counsel on behalf of the present petitioner lastly submits that the case is bad for defect of parties as the witness no. 4 for the pre-emptee Abdur Razzak and one Dr. Abdul Malek are the necessary parties in the instant case which is transpired from the cross-examination of the witness no.1 for the pre-emptor-opposite party as the pre-emptor not denied it. In absence of the aforesaid persons it cannot be held that the case is not bad for defect of parties but the courts below arbitrarily held that there is no such defect in the instant case for which the case may fail. It is on record that on 01.06.1998 A.D. the pre-emptor cited three persons as her witnesses, who are the Advocates of the local bar but during trial none of them was examined from her side and there is no explanation as to why those important witnesses were withheld and in this context under section 114(g) of the Evidence Act the presumptive value is such that had they been examined that would not have supported the pre-emptor's case.

10. As against the aforesaid submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party opposing the Rule submits that both the trial court as well as the appellate court during disposal the original cast and its subsequent appeal committed no illegality or irregularity rather in deciding the merit of the case after assessment of evidence and appreciation of law concurrently it was held by the courts below that the pre-emptor-opposite party no.1 is entitled to get relief as prayed for and there is no legal bar in getting pre-emption in the instant case. The learned Advocate further submits that the appellate court being the final court of fact it's decision is immune from interference in the revisional jurisdiction and there is no misreading or non-reading of evidence or non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice by which the impugned judgment and order can be interfered with. The learned Advocate lastly submits that the pre-emptor being a women and resides in Dhaka she was not in the know about the case kabola in time and for the first time while in the occasion of Holly Eid-ul-Fiter she came to Jhenidah she was informed from her father on 09.02.1997 after coming to the residence of her father that the opposite party no.2 transferred the case land without notice to the opposite party no.1. Getting such information she obtained the certified copy of the case kabla on 15.03.1997 and thereafter filed the original case for having pre-emption of the case land.

11. Heard the learned Advocates for both sides, perused the case record, exhibited documents, deposition of the witnesses and all other connected papers.

<u>12. On perusal of the case record it transpires that the case kabla was held on 30.01.1995 A.D. and it's registration was completed under section 60 of the, Registration Act on 19.08.1995 A.D. The original pre-emption Miscellaneous Case was instituted on 19.03.1997 A.D. Therefore, obviously the case is not within the statutory period of limitation. It is the incumbent duty upon the pre-emptor to prove beyond all reasonable doubt by adducing credible tangible evidence that she was not in the know about the transfer prior to the date mentioned by her in her pleading.</u>

<u>13. Secondly, scrutinizing the case record it is apparent that the pre-emptor in support of her case examined three witnesses. The witness no.1 is the pre-emptor herself. The witness no. 2 is a formal witness, who is Nazir, Thana Land Office, Jhenidah Sadar and the last witness no. 3 Md. Amzad Hossain is the father of the pre-emptor Most. Jhulfan Ara.</u>

14. We have come across from the deposition of the witnesses that the pre-emptor in her deposition regarding her date of knowledge states at a stage, “গত ০৬-০২-১৯৯৮ ইং তারিখের পূর্বে আমি নাঃ কবালার বিষয় জানতাম না” In her cross-examination she states in the very beginning that in the month of February, 1994 she went into possession of her land measuring .05 acres and for that portion of land she has mutated her name and she paid rent separately and independently for her portion of land. The witness no. 2 for the pre-emptor being an official of land office, Jhenidah Sadar, brought a mutation case record being No. 51/9-1/95-96. The last witness Md. Amzad Hossein, who is the father of the pre-emptor in his testimony states at a stage that the pre-emptee constructed wall in his land including the case land after his purchase. He also admits that the purchaser of the case land is a co-sharer by purchase in the case jote. He contradicted his daughter regarding mutation of the purchased land of his daughter (P.W.1) and payment of rent separately. On the other hand; the witness no.1 for the pre-emptee is the pre-emptee himself Md. Ismail Hossain, who corroborate his pleading as mentioned in his written objection. The witness no. 2 for the pre-emptee Md. Abdul Motaleb is a deed-writer of Jhenidah Sadar Sub-registry office and as such he is a formal witness of the case. The witness no. 3 Md. Abdul Aziz Mallick is the husband of vendor-opposite party no. 2. This witness asserts in his deposition that he himself told the father of the pre-emptor to purchase the case land prior to the pre-emptee-opposite party no. 1. The last witness Md. Abdur Razzak is a co-sharer of the case jote who states in his deposition that there was a survey in respect of the case land in the month of February, 1996 and at that time the pre-emptor's father was present

<u>15. Consulting the relevant evidence it is evident to note that in respect of the alleged date of knowledge of the pre-emptor in the instant case no such independent, disinterested credible evidence is transpired by which it can be held that the pre-emptor in fact was in the dark about the disputed transfer which was in the year 1995. The witnesses who deposed in favour of the pre-emptor's case are not trustworthy and they obviously contradicted one-another in respect of the positive case of the pre-emptor. Specially; the pre-emptor and her father states contradictory statement before the trial court at the time of giving their deposition which has completely left out from the notice of both the courts below.</u>

16. Having gone through the materials on record, I find that the pre-emptor-opposite party No. 1 though not at all have been able to discharge her onus of proof; even then both the courts below concurrently held that there is no legal embargo in getting pre-emption. It is curious to note that neither the trial court nor the lower appellate court considered the evidence of both the parties in it's true perspective. The witnesses adduced from the side of the pre-emptee-petitioner not at all evaluated by the- courts below in their observation and findings. There has been glaring misreading and non-reading of evidence and non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

17. The arguments advanced from the side of the learned counsel for the petitioner is quite consistent with the case record and I have no way out but to accept and agree with the proposition of the learned Advocate Mr. Md. Nurul Amin from the face of the record. Furthermore; it is evident that the impugned judgment and order was not given after proper assessment of evidence and appreciation of law.

18. Having regard to the findings & discussions referred to above I have every reason to draw such inference that the impugned judgment and order is not a proper judgment of affirmance under the ambit of Order XLI rule 31 and 34 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

19. Despite the lower appellate court is a final court of facts but the law enjoins that the findings of facts arrived at by the appellate court must not suffer from any sort of such illegality or infirmity by dint of which it can be held that there has been misreading or non-reading of evidence and non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the, decision occasioning failure of justice.

20. In view of that I have nothing but hold such a view that inasmuch as the learned lower appellate court in disposing the appeal committed gross illegality and the impugned judgment and order have been passed upon misreading and non-reading of evidence as well as non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision and there has been glaring misconception and misinterpretation of material evidence; the impugned judgment and order is perverse which is contrary to law, evidence and materials on record.

21. In the result, the Rule having much substance is made absolute. The impugned judgment and order-dated 18.07.2001 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Jhenidah in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 21 of 1998 affirming the judgment and order dated 25.10.1998 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Jhenaidah in Miscellaneous Case No. 34 of 1997 is hereby set aside. The original case be also dismissed on contest.

22. The order of stay granted earlier at the time of issuance of the Rule stands vacated.

23. However, there will be no order as to costs.

24. Send down the lower court's record along with the copy of judgment to the learned court below immediately.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1283 of 2004
lawyer:
Sofia Khatun, Advocate-on-Record. ----- For the Petitioners 
Respondents ----- Not represented.
parties:
Hemayet Ali Shaikh and others ----- Petitioners.
VS
Ramesh Chandra Mondal and others ------ Respondents.
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 8th March, 2003 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1977 of 1994).
full_judgment:
Md. Tafazzul Islam J: This petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 8.3.2003 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1977 of 1994 making the Rule absolute upon reversing the judgment and decree dated 24.4.1994 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Bagerhat in Title Appeal No. 212 of 1994 allowing the appeal upon reversing those of dated 18.5.1983 passed by the learned Subordinat Judge (now Joint District Jude), Bagerhat in Title Suit No. 236 of 1981 dismissing the suit.

2. The respondents filed to above suit for declaration of title to the suit land on the averments, inter alia, that 10.33 acres of land out of the land recorded in C.S. Khatian No. 140 and 4.31 acres of land recorded in C.S. Khatian No. 280, originally belonged to 3 full brothers, namely, Judu Nath Mondal, Paban Mondal and Gagon Mondal in equal shares; the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2, the respondent Nos. 1-2 herein, are sons of Gagon Mondal; the plaintiff Nos. 3 and 4, the respondent Nos. 3-4 herein, are grandsons of Gagon Mondal; Paban Mondal died leaving behind a son, Banomali; Judu Nath Mondal died leaving behind a widow Totamoni, a daughter named Ayna moni and defendants Nos. 4-6 sons of Aynamoni; 10.33 acres of land of C.S. Khatian No. 140 was recorded in the name of Totamoni, Gagon Mondal and Banamali in equal share and S.A. Khatian No. 329 was also prepared in their names; 4.31 acres of land recorded in C.S. Khatian No. 280 being acquied with the income of the joint family, the name of Judu Nath Mondal Was wrongly record in the aforesaid C.S. Khatian No. 280 and then during S.A. operation the said land was correctly recorded in the S.A. Khatian No. 116 in the names of Totamoni, Gagon Mondal and Banomali in equal shares; defendants No. 4-6 and Totamoni sold 3.35 acres of land from C.S. Khatian No. 140 and 1.36 acres of land from C.S. Khatian No. 280 to Gagon Mondal by a kabala dated 29.4.1963 and delivered possession thereof to him and after his death the plaintiffs have been possessing the aforesaid land but they could not withdraw the original kabala of the above sale from the concerned Sub-Registrar's office as they lost the ticket; taking advantage of the above situation the defendant Nos. 4-6 created 3 collusive kabalas in favour of defendants No. 1-3, the petitioners herein, and on the basis of those the defendants No. 1-3 on 20.12.1976 threatened to dispossess the plaintiffs from the suit land and hence the suit. The defendant Nos. 1-3, contested the suit by filing a joint written statement contending, inter alia, that the land of C.S. Khatian No. 280 was the self acquired property of Judu Nath Mondal; the kabala dated 29.4.1963 was never acted upon; defendant Nos. 4-6 sold the suit land along with other lands to defendant Nos. 1-3 by three separate kabalas dated 28.10.1976 and delivered possession thereof to them and the defendant Nos. 1-3 are in possession of the suit land and the plaintiffs having no right, title as well as possession in the suit land they were not entitled to get any relief. The learned subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), after hearing, decreed the suit. The defendants then preferred Title Appeal No. 212 of 1984 and the learned Additional District Judge, Bagerhat, after hearing allowed the appeal. The plaintiffs then moved the High Court Division obtained Rule in Civil Revision No. 1977 of 1994. During the pendency of the above Rule the plaintiffs filed an application under Order 6 Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure for amendment of the plaint which was opposed by the defendants. After hearing the High Court Division allowed the said petition for amendment and on the strength of the said amendment made the Rule absolute and thereby decreed the suit of the plaintiffs in amended form.

3. The learned counsel for the petitioners submits that the lower appellate court, the final court of facts, having found that the suit land has not been specified and that the consideration money of the deed dated 29.4.1963 having not been passed, dismissed the suit but the High Court Division made the Rule absolute without curing the defect as to declaration of title of unspecified land and also without adverting to the issue of non-passing of the consideration money and merely stating the above ground has not been raised in the written statement of the defendant Nos. 1-3.

4. As it appears in the prayer portion of the original plaint the plaintiffs sought relief to the effect that ‘‘নালিশী ভূমিতে বাদীগণের স্বত্ব লেখা প্রচার বাবদ ডিক্রী হয়” but after amendment the said relief stood as follows:- "আরজী বর্নিতমতে নালিশী জমিতে বাদী পক্ষের অনুকূলে স্বত্ব সাব্যস্তপূর্বক ৭-১০ নং বিবাদীগণের সহিত এজমালিক দখল কায়েমের ডিক্রী হয়". As it appears, the plaintiff also prayed for allowing them to pay advalorem court fee which was allowed.

<u>5. The High Court Division, as it appears, on consideration of above, held that the prayer for amendment of the plaint sought for is quite in conformity with the plaint case and if the same is allowed that would in no way change the nature and character of the suit; the trial Court give the finding of possession of the suit land in favour of the plaintiffs on consideration of the fact that though D.W.4, Aroz Ali, claimed possession of the suit land through their bargadaras Shamsu and Keramat, but none of them was examined in order to prove the possession of the defendants in the suit land; since D.W.1 deposed that the defendants possessed the suit land through bargadars it was incumbent upon the defendants to examine the bargadars and for this non-examination of the bargadars adverse presumption can very much be drawn against the defendants in view of the provisions of Section 114(g) of the Evidence Act; the lower appellate court did not advert to the finding of the trial court regarding possession; the finding of possession of the trial Court is based on evidence on record; since the plaintiffs are found in possession of the suit land there is no bar to allow the prayer for declaration regarding joint possession of the plaintiff with defendants No.7-10 along with declaration of their title; if the prayer of the plaintiffs for amendment of the plaint is not allowed they will be deprived of their legitimate right of enjoyment of their valuable properties; it is settled principle of law that amendment of the pleading can be allowed at any stage of the proceeding provided that the amendment, if allowed, would not change the nature and character of the suit and that amendment is necessary to effectively decide the real controversies between the parties in the suit; the lower appellate Court dismissed the suit on three grounds i.e. (a) the suit is not maintainable as no consequential relief was prayed for (b) the description of the suit land is vague and (c) the plaintiffs did not acquire any title to the suit land by virtue of their purchase by kabala dated 29.4.63 as consideration money did not pass but the High Court Division found that (1) the suit is maintainable without any consequential relief because the defendants failed to prove their possession in the suit (2) in view of the amendment of the plaint the description of suit land is no longer vague and (3) in the written statement non-passing of the consideration money having not been pleaded, the evidence led by the defendants in his respect is inadmissible in view of the provisions of rule 7 of Order 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

<u>6. We are of the view that the High Court Division on proper consideration of the materials on record and applying the principle of law as applicable arrived at a correct decision and there is no cogent reason to interfere with the said decision.</u>

7. The petition is dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
Moudud Ahmed, Senior Advocate, instructed by Md. Nowab Ali, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Appellants 
Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed Senior Advocate, instructed by Sharifuddin Chaklader Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Respondent
parties:
Dhaka Water Supply & Swearage Authority and other ----- Appellants
Vs.
Matiar Rahman ----- Respondent
case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 12.31.998 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3077 of 1995)
full_judgment:
Mohmmad Gholam Rabbani J :- This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 12.3.98 of a learned Singled Judge of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3077 of 1995 discharging the Rule and thereby upholding the judgment and decree dated 31.1.95 of the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka passed in Title Appeal No. 31 of 1993 dismissing the appeal and affirming those dated 30.11.92 of the 3rd Additional Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka, passed in Title Suit No. 59 of 1992 decreeing the suit.

2. Facts necessary for the disposal of this appeal are stated first below.

3. Respondent Md. Matiar Rahman is an engineer. He joined in the service of the appellant Dhaka Water Supply and Swearage Authority, briefly WASA and at the relevant time he was holding the post of executive engineer on pro-motion in charge of Zone 6 with effect from 14.9.90. Subsequently he was put under suspension consequent to the report of a departmental enquiry committee, but the appointing Authority failed to communicate the charge sheet to the respondent within the stipulated period of thirty days from the date of framing of the charge as required under Rule 46(2) of WASA Employees Service Rules of 1990. Under the Rules the respondent was reinstated to his post and was again put under suspension for the second time respectively by the memo. Nos. 2025 and 2026 both dated 5.11.90.

4. The Charge against the respondent was that he misappropriated goods worth taka twenty eight lac stored in a godown of WASA by issuing a fake indent. The defence of the respondent was that his signature in the indent was forged by his subordinate sub-assistant engineer M. A. Sobhan who admitted it in his written statement to the enquiry committee.

5. The departmental enquiry committee found the respondent guilty to the charge and fixed his liability to the extent of 45% of the value of the said goods. Respondent preferred departmental appeal and the appeal board dismissed his appeal and increased his liability to 60%. Ultimately the respondent was dismissed from the service with effect from 4.4.91.

6. Respondent then filed the above-numbered title suit for declaring the order of his dismissal from service as illegal and for other consequential reliefs. The trial court decreed the suit and the decree was affirmed by the lower Appellate Court and the High Court Division respectively in the above numbered title appeal and civil revision both at the instance of the WASA.

7. Leave was granted at the instance of the appellant WASA to examine following four points as contended by the appellants' learned advocate:-

(i)That the Courts below were wrong to hold the impugned order of dismissal of the respondent from the service as illegal when there was no procedural error or defect in the domestic enquiry rather it was held in strict compliance writ the provisions of WASA Employees Service Rules, 1990.

(ii) That the High Court Division committed an error of law in interfering with the finding of the domestic enquiry committee fixing the liability of the respondent with regard to the value of the misappropriated goods.

(iii) That the High Court Division acted wrongly in finding fault with the authority for not verifying the disputed signature of the respondent in the indent in question vis-a-vis the evidence of the six witnesses before the domestic enquiry committee.

(iv) That the High Court Division was wrong to hold that the effect of Rules 44(5), 44(8) and 46 (2) of the WASA Employees Service Rules of 1990 were mandatory in nature.

8. We have heard the learned advocates for the appellant and the respondent respectively for and against the aforesaid contentions.

9. The contentions of the appellant we the issues framed by the Trial Court. Trial Court noticed that the plaintiff was put under suspension with effect from 20.9.90 vide ext.2 under sub-rule 1 of rule 46 of the WASA Employees Service Rules of 1990 (hereinafter referred to as "the said Rules") and so the WASA was required under sub-rule 2 of rule 46 of the said Rules to serve the date of the order of suspension, but that was not done and consequenjly Ape order of suspension stood cancelled from that date under rule 46(2). Trial Court further noticed that the plaintiff having been reinstated to his post vide memo. no. 2025 dated 5.11.90, the second order of his suspension from service vide memo no. 2026 issued on the same dated on 5.11.90 was illegal and without jurisdiction.

10. Trial Court also noticed that the plaintiff submitted an application objecting to the appointment of Abdul Baki Chowdhury as one of the members of the enquiry committee on the grounds that the said member was junior to him in service and had strained relation-ship with him, but the objection was not taken into consideration.

<u>11. Trial Court further noticed that M.A. Sobhan, the officer who was directly in charge of the godown, was at first found guilty of mis-appropriation and was accordingly punished, the departmental review board exonerated him ignoring the said officer's admission that he forged the signature of the respondent in the  indent and that evidence of the PWs that the  signature in the indent was that of the  dent should not had been treated as legal evidence for not examining the disputed Signature by a hand writing expert. The learned trial Judges obviously had in his mind section 114(g) of the Evidence Act while considering this issue.</u>

12. The lower appellant court as well as the High Court Division considering all the of the case came to the same conclusion as that of the trial Court that there were numbers of illegalities for which both the impugned orders of suspension and dismissal from service must be held to be illegal.

13. In view of our above discussions about the materials on record we come to the same conclusion as that of the Courts below and find no substance in the contentions upon which leave was obtained by the appellant WASA.

14. This anneal is dismissed with costs.

End.

lawyer:
Moudud Ahmed, Senior Advocate instructed by SR Khoshnabish, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Appellants. 
Abdus Salam Khan, Senior Advocated instructed by B Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ------ For Respondent No. 1.
None Represented ------ Respondent No.2.
parties:
Shawkat Hossain (Md) and another ------ Appellants
Vs.
Golam Mohammad and another ------ Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 7-8-2002 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.808 of 1998.)
full_judgment:
Nazmun Ara Sultana J: This Civil Appeal, by leave, at the instance of the defendants, is against the judgment and order dated 7-8-2002 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision. No. 808 of 1998 making the Rule absolute upon setting-aside the judgment and decree dated 26-2-1998 passes by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 374 of 1993 allowing the appeal and thereupon reversing the judgment and decree dated 25-5-1993 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, 5th Additional Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 91 of 1992 decreeing the suit.

2. The respondent No.1, as plaintiff, instituted the above mentioned Title Suit No.91 of 1992 for specific performance of contract against the present appellants. The plaintiff''s case, in short, was that the defendant No. 1 being owner and in possession of the suit property as described in schedule to the plaint, entered into a contract with the plaintiff on 20-11-1986 for sale of the same at a consideration of Taka 50,000 and on receipt Taka 45,000 out of that stipulated consideration as earnest money executed a bainapatra in favour of the plaintiff on the stipulations that he would execute and register the kabala deed in respect of the suit property in favour of the plaintiff within 120 days on receiving the balance consideration of Taka 5,000 from the plaintiff. That on 10-3-1987 the plaintiff requested the defendant No. 1 to execute and register the sale deed as per bainapatra, but he did not do so. The plaintiff then sent a legal notice on 28-8-1987 to the defendant No.1 asking him to execute and register the kabala deed as per the contract but the defendant did not reply. The plaintiff then again sent another legal notice to the defendant on 22-11-1998 but the defendant did not respond to that legal notice also and thus the plaintiff has been compelled to file the suit.

3. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 contested the suit by filling written statement denying the alleged bainanama. Their case is that the defendant No. 1 purchased 0.0168 ajutangsa land from Shahana Bibi by a registered kabala dated 10-4-1984 and subsequently he transferred that land to his wife Rokeya Begum, the defendant No. 2 in lieu of dower money by registered deed dated 11-8-1987. The defendant No. 2 mutated her name in respect of the suit property. That the defendant No.1 never contracted to sell the suit property to the plaintiff never took any earnest money from the plaintiff and never executed any bainapatra in favour of the plaintiff; that the alleged bainapatra is forged. The defendant No.1 in his written statement further contended that he worked as an employee under Railway Department since 1940 and retired in 1977 and during this period, he always signed his name in Bengali and that the so-called signatures in the alleged deed of agreement in English are not of the defendant No.1.

4. In the trial court the plaintiff examined 3 witnesses and produced some documents in order to prove his case. The contesting defendants examined only one witness the defendant No.1 himself. The trial court, on consideration of the evidence adduced by both the parties and other facts and circumstances decreed the suit. The trial court, after comparing the purported signature of the defendant No.1 in the alleged bainapatra with some alleged signatures of the defendant No.1 in exhibit-5 series which are some photocopies of applications to Titas Gas Company and House Building Finance Corporation Office (HBFC), found that the signature appearing in the alleged bainapatra was of the defendant No.1. The trial court opined also that the PW 2 an attesting witness of the alleged bainapatra, proved the execution of the said bainapatra by the defendant No.1.

5. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree of the trial court the defendant No.1 preferred Civil Appeal No. 374 of 1993 which was heard by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka. This appellate court allowed the appeal by setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit for specific performance of contract making observations to the effect that the trial court committed serious error by comparing the disputed signature of the defendant No.1 in the alleged bainapatra with some unadmitted signatures appearing in some photocopies the exhibit-5 series which were not admitted into evidence in accordance with sections 65 and 66 of the Evidence Act. The appellate court found the evidence of PW 2 and PW 3 not satisfactory. The appellate court doubted the genuineness of the alleged bainapatra for the reasons also that the plaintiff could not clarify when and from where the stamp paper of the alleged bainapatra was purchased and that there was no explanation also as to why in spite of payment of almost full consideration money the possession of the land was not delivered.

6. Against the judgment of the appellate court below the plaintiff preferred the above mentioned civil revision before the High Court Division and obtained rule. Ultimately a Single Bench of the High Court Division, after hearing, made that rule absolute upon setting aside the judgment and decree of the appellate court below and restoring those of the trial court. The High Court Division observed that though the defendant No.1 denied the signatures on exhibit-5 series, but ultimately he found it difficult to renounce them. The High Court Division commented to the effect also that the defendant No.1 put his signature in his deposition sheet and in other admitted documents in English but in spite of that he resorted to falsehood by contending that he could not read or write in English with a view to disown his signature in English in the alleged bainapatra and that these were strong circumstantial evidence which tell against his defence case. The revisional court believed both the PW 2 and PW 3 also making comment that the reasons assigned by the appellate court below for not believing these two witnesses were not correct at all.

7. Leave to appeal was granted on the submissions of the learned Advocate for the defendant-leave petitioner to the effect that the exhibit-5 series, the photocopies of the applications filed to Titas Gas Company and House Building Finance Corporation Office collected by the plaintiff-respondent being inadmissible papers, the learned Assistant Judge committed an error of law in comparing the disputed signatures of the defendant No. 1 in the impugned bainapatra the exhibit-1 with the alleged signatures of the defendant No. 1 appearing in this exhibit-5 series as per provision of section 73 of the Evidence Act and that in this circumstance the execution of the alleged bainapatra by the defendant No.1 was not legally proved and that the High Court Division having not considered this aspect committed error of law resulting in error in the decision occasioning failure of justice and that the High Court Division sitting in revisional jurisdiction committed an error of law in construing a portion of the deposition of the PW 2 to nullify the finding of the final court of fact (in respect of same portion) which held the same to be contradictory and such error has affected the decision in that, if the evidence of the sole attesting witness (PW 2) is contradictory, there remained nothing to grant decree to the plaintiff-respondent and in such view of the matter, the findings and decisions of the High Court Division cannot be sustained in law.

8. Mr Moudud Ahmed, the learned Senior Advocate for the defendant-appellants have made submissions to the effect that in this suit for specific performance of contract where the alleged contract (the bainapatra) has been denied by the contesting defendant No. 1 and has also been termed as a forged one and a fraudulent creation of the plaintiff, the court, before passing a decree, ought to have been satisfied by cogent evidence that the defendant No.1 executed this bainapatra and the signatures appearing in this bainapatra is actually of the defendant No.1 . The learned Advocate has argued that in this suit there is no cogent evidence at all to prove that the purported signature of the defendant No.1 appearing in the alleged bainapatra is actually of the defendant No.1. The learned Advocate has submitted that though section 73 of the Evidence Act has empowered the court to compare any disputed signature with any signature admitted or proved to have been of the person who allegedly put the disputed signature, but in the present suit there is no admitted signature of the defendant No.1, that the exhibit-5 series which purportedly bear signatures of the defendant No.1 were photocopies only and as such secondary evidence as per section 63 of the Evidence Act and these were not admitted in evidence as per sections 65 and 66 of the Evidence Act and, as such, the comparison of these signatures with the disputed signature of the defendant No.1 appearing in the alleged bainapatra by the trial court as per section 73 of the Evidence Act has been illegal; that the High Court Division has totally ignored this legal aspect and affirmed the judgment of the trial court without taking into consideration of the inadequacy of legal evidence to prove the execution of the alleged bainapatra by the defendant No. l. Mr Moudud Ahmed has argued also that though one of the attesting witnesses only has deposed in this suit to prove the execution of the alleged bainapata by the defendant No. 1, the other witness, the PW 3, being not the attesting witness or the scribe of the alleged bainapatra the sole evidence of one of the attesting witnesses only the PW 2 cannot be considered sufficient at all to prove the execution "of the alleged bainapatra by the defendant No. 1. The learned Counsel has argued also that in this suit there were so many admitted signatures of the defendant No. 1, even in his deposition sheet also the defendant respondent No.1 put his signature in English, but neither the plaintiff nor the trial court took any initiative to have these admitted signatures examined and compared with the disputed signature of the defendant No.1 in the disputed bainapatra by any hand writing expert; that the trial court even did not compare these admitted signatures of the defendant No.1 with his disputed signature in the impugned bainapatra under section 73 of the Evidence Act. The learned Counsel has argued that the High Court Division did not take into consideration all these facts and circumstances at all in affirming the judgment and decree of the trial court. The learned Counsel has made submission to the effect also that though section 73 of the Evidence Act permits the court to compare the contentious signature with the admitted signature, the safe and best course for the court is to get the disputed signature examined and compared with the admitted signature by hand writing expert. In support of this submission the learned Counsel has referred to a decision of this Division in the case of Tarak Chandra Majhi vs Atahar Ali reported in 8 BLC (AD) 67.

9. Mr Abdus Salam Khan, the learned Senior Advocate for the plaintiff-respondent No.1 has made submissions to the effect that in this suit the plaintiffs has examined two witnesses including one attesting witness of the alleged bainapatra and both these witnesses the PW 2 and PW 3 have deposed before the trial court stating that the defendant No. 1 executed the impugned bainapatra in their presence. The learned Advocate has argued that there is no reason to disbelieve these two plaintiffs'' witnesses and that in the circumstances the trial court did not commit any wrong in finding that the impugned bainapatra was executed by the defendant No. l. The learned Advocate has argued also that though the defendant. No.1 in his written statement has asserted that he always put his signatures in Bengali and he cannot read and write English but during trial it has been proved that the defendant No.1 puts signature in English also and even in the court, in his deposition sheet also, he put his signature in English. The learned Advocate has contended that this conduct of the defendant No.1 very reasonably and strongly supports the falsity of the defence case. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondents has made submissions to the effect also that the court is competent to compare the disputed signature with admitted signature for ascertaining genuineness of the disputed signature and that in this suit the trial court did not commit any wrong in comparing the signature of the defendant No.1 appearing in the alleged bainapatra with the signatures of the defendant No.1 in exhibit-5 series which were admitted in evidence by the trial court without any objection from the defendants.

10. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates of both the sides and gone through the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and those of the appellate court below and the trial court.

11. In this suit for specific performance of contract the only issue to be resolved is whether the defendant No.1 executed the alleged bainapatra the exhibit-1 or in other words whether the signature appearing in the bainapatra the exhibit-1 is of the defendant No. 1. For proving execution of any document the vital witnesses are the attesting witnesses who witnessed the execution of the document by the executant and the scribe of the document. In this suit the plaintiff could not examine the scribe of the disputed bainapatra the exhibit-1. The plaintiff could examine only one of the attesting witnesses of this disputed bainapatra. The plaintiff though examined another witness also the PW 3 who also deposed to the effect that the defendant No. 1 executed this bainapatra in his presence, but there is no satisfactory explanation from the side of the plaintiff as to why he examined this PW 3 instead of the other attesting witnesses of this bainapatra. It appears that the trial court took recourse of section 73 of the Evidence Act to be sure as to whether this bainapatra was executed by the defendant No.1. The trial court examined and compared the disputed signature of the defendant No. 1 appearing in the alleged bainapatra with some alleged signatures of the defendant No.1 appearing in exhibit-5 series. These exhibit-5 series are photocopies of some applications filed to the Titas. Gas Company and House Building Finance Corporation Office. These are secondary evidence which require some procedures to be admitted in evidence. It appears that without following these procedures as prescribed in sections 65 and 66 of the Evidence Act the trial court took these photocopies into evidence and marked these as exhibit in spite of the fact that the defendant No.1 did not admit these signatures to be his own. The defendant No.1, while deposing before court, clearly stated that the signatures appearing in the exhibit-5 series are not his signatures. In course of cross-examination the defendant No.1 stated thus:

"Whether one tenant at that time took my signature to get gas connection-I could not remember".

12. It appears that the High Court Division, putting importance on this very statement of DW 1 made observation to the effect that the defendant No. 1 ultimately found it difficult to renounce these signatures. But we are unable to accept these observations of the High Court Division. The above statement of the defendant No. 1 does not prove at all that he has admitted that the exhibit-5 series were submitted by him and the signatures appearing in these applications are his signatures. So, in these circumstances we approve the findings of the appellate court below that the learned trial judge has committed serious error in comparing the disputed signature of the defendant No. 1 in the alleged, bainapatra with the signatures appearing in exhibit-5 series which were not taken into evidence in accordance with law and which are also not at all admitted by the defendant No. 1.

<u>13. It is true that the plaintiff has examined one of the attesting witnesses of the alleged bainapatra who has deposed to the effect that the defendant No. 1 executed this bainapatra in his presence. Another witness the PW 3, who is neither the scribe nor attesting witness of the alleged bainapatra, also has deposed to the effect that the defendant No. 1 executed this bainapatra in his presence. But in the present facts and circumstances of the case where the plaintiff could not examine the scribe and also the other attesting witnesses of the disputed bainapatra and where there is scope to obtain expert's opinion as to genuineness of the disputed signature of the defendant No. 1 in the alleged bainapatra we do not think that the evidence of PW 2 and PW 3 are sufficient to prove the execution of the alleged bainapatra the exhibit-1 by the defendant No.1. Where other evidence produced before court are sufficient to prove the genuineness of any disputed signature or document the court may not insist for expert's opinion, but where the evidence adduced before court are not sufficient for proving a disputed signature or document the court should obtain expert's opinion. It appears that in this suit there are some admitted signatures of the defendant No.1 in some admitted documents. In the circumstances the best and safe course for the court was to send the impugned bainapatra and some admitted signatures of the defendant No.1 to a hand writing expert and to obtain his opinion as to the genuineness of the disputed signature of the defendant No. 1 in the bainapatra the exhibit-1. In this connection we should refer the decision of this Division in the case of Tarak Chandra Majhi vs Atahar Ali reported in 8 BLC (AD) 67. This Division held in that case "in case of contentious writing, signature, etc., though provision of section 73 of the Evidence Act permits the court to compare the contentious signature with the admitted signature, the safe and best course for the court would be to avoid the practice of comparing the writing or signature etc. and should nor stake its judgment on the opinion formed or view taken upon resorting to risky or, in other words, unsatisfactory and dangerous procedure and the desired course should be to go for microscopic enlargement and expert advice since the science of examination of signature, writing, etc. for determination of similarity has advanced enough and it has reached to the stage of accuracy and certainty as well as expertise skill is also available."</u>

<u>14. Considering the facts and circumstances of this case we are of the opinion that the disputed signature of the defendant No.1 in the alleged bainapatra the exhibit-1 should be examined and compared with some admitted signatures of the defendant No.1 by a hand writing expert and for this purpose the suit should be sent back on remand to the appellate court below.</u>

15. In the circumstances this appeal be allowed in contest without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and also that of the appellate court below are set-aside. The Title Appeal No.374 of 1993 is sent back to the appellate court below. The appellate court will, send the alleged bainapatra along with some admitted signatures of the defendant No.1 to a hand writing expert for his opinion as to the genuineness of the disputed signatures of the defendant No.1 in the alleged bainapatra the exhibit-1 and after receiving the hand writing expert's opinion the appellate court below will dispose of the appeal afresh in accordance with law.

Send copy of this judgment to the appellate court below along with the lower court record, if not already sent back.

End.
