parties:
Atiqullah (Md) ------ Appellant.
Vs.
Government of Peoples Republic of Bangladesh represented by Land Acquisition Collector and ors ------ Respondents.
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 3-3-1998 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos. 2153, 2154 & 2155 of 1993).
full_judgment:
MM Ruhul Amin J: These three appeals by leave have arisen out of the judgment and order dated 3-3-1998 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos. 2153, 2154 and 2155 of 1993, making the Rules absolute against the judgment and award dated 31-8-1992 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) and Arbitrator, Dhaka in Arbitration Revision Miscellaneous No. 14 of 1991 arising out of Arbitration Revision Case No. 1816 of 1990 filed against the Land Acquisition Collector Award in Requisition and Acquisition Case No. 12 of 1987-88.

2. Common questions of facts and law being involved the writ petitions were disposed of by one judgment. So these three appeals were also heard together and are disposed of by this judgment which shall govern all.

3. Short facts are, that the Land Acquisition Collector, Dhaka under the provisions of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 (Ordinance No. II of 1982) hereinafter referred to as the Ordinance, in Land Acquisition Case No. 12 of 1987-88 acquired the case land of the petitioner on 18-3-1989. On 28-3-1989 notifications were issued accordingly and compensation assessment was prepared on 16-10-1991. The petitioner received the award on protest. The petitioner being dissatisfied with the quantum of award filed Arbitration Revision Case No 1836 of 1990 before the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) and Arbitrator, Dhaka who by his judgment and award dated 15-8-1991 in the Arbitration Revision Case dismissed the same and affirmed the award made by the Collector. The petitioner then filed Arbitration Revision Miscellaneous Case No 14 of 1991 under the provisions of Order XLVII, rules 1 & 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for the review of judgment and order dated 15-8-1991. The learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) and Arbitrator allowed the Arbitration. Revision Miscellaneous Case, recalled the judgment and order dated 15-8-1991 and set aside the award dated 18-3-1989 made by the Collector and enhanced the award from Taka 2,12,001 to Taka 5,99,637.63 only as compensation for acquisition. The respondent government being aggrieved by the judgment and order passed in the revision miscellaneous case (review) filed an application under Article 102(2) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh in the High Court Division. The writ petition was contested by the petitioner’s appellants on the ground, inter alia, that the Review Miscellaneous Petition was filed only after obtaining certain valuable documents which could not be produced earlier before the Arbitrator.

4. The High Court Division by its judgment and order dated 31-3-1998 held that section 28 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 provides that any person interested who has not accepted any award made by the Deputy Commissioner within 45 days from the date of service of notice of the award may make an application to the Arbitrator for revision of the award but there is no provision in the Ordinance enabling such a person to file review Miscellaneous Petition under Order XLVII, rules 1 & 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for remedy. Section 34 of the Ordinance provides for the filing of appeal against an award made by the Arbitrator but in the instant case the petitioner without filing appeal under section 34 filed the review petition. The High Court Division did not accept the plea of natural justice as there is no provision in the Ordinance to prefer review application.

5. Leave was granted to consider the submission that the Writ petition filed against the judgment and award dated 31-8-1992 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) and Arbitrator, Dhaka in Arbitration Revision Miscellaneous Case No. 14 of 1991 without exhausting the remedy by way of appeal to the Arbitration Appellate Tribunal under section 34 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 were wholly not maintainable in law and the High Court Division having not adverted to this aspect fell into an error of law and therefore, the impugned judgment and order were wholly illegal and unsustainable in law, that in terms of the provisions of section 32(3) of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 read with section 2(2) and 2(9) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the award made by the Arbitrator under the said Ordinance shall be deemed to be a decree against which a review application under Order XLVII, rules 1 & 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure is maintainable and the application for review having been fled earlier in point of time before the filing of the appeal on the ground, inter alia, on discovery of new and important matter, the court had jurisdiction to deal with the review application; that the court having granted the review and having modified the award before the disposal of the appeal (which was filed after the filing of the review application) the appeal became infructuous and the court did not commit any illegality in allowing the review application and the High Court Division, therefore, committed an error of law in interfering with the award dated 31-8-1992 made by the Arbitrator in Arbitration Revision Miscellaneous Case No 14 of 1991 arising out of Arbitration Revision Case No 1836 of 1990.

6. We have heard Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Senior Counsel for the appellant.

7. The pertinent question for determination in this matter is, whether the learned Joint District Judge and Arbitrator had power to review his judgment earlier passed in view of the fact that in the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 there is no provision for such review.

8. Mr Bhuiyan mainly argued that section 32(3) of the Ordinance provides that every award under the Ordinance shall be in writing signed by the Arbitrator. Every such award shall be deemed to be a decree and the statement of the grounds of every such award a judgment within the meaning of section 2(2) and section 2(9) respectively of the Code of Civil Procedure (V of 1908). Therefore, the right to review is available although there is no express provisions for review in the Ordinance. He further argued that the learned Arbitrator made review of the decree earlier passed by him. So, he correctly did it.

9. In support of his contention, the learned Advocate has cited the case of Adalat Khan Chowdhury & others vs. Province of East Pakistan reported in PLR 1959 Dhaka series 688 and submitted that in that case it was held that the Arbitrator can, at the instance of a party, review his order in accordance with law under Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In that case it was held as follows: The fact remains that the landlord not only suppressed the facts, but also misled the arbitrator in thinking that only the ground floor had been let out in 1938 at a rental of Rs. 100 per month. The fraud was a new and important matter which was not within the knowledge of the Government at the time of arbitration. Further, the contention that they could not detect it at that time with due diligence has also some substance. Hence the allegations made are sufficient to attract the provisions of Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Civil Procedure Code."

10. He next cited the case of Behari Lal and another vs. MM Gobardhan Lal and others reported in AIR 1948 (Allahabad) 353. In that case, it was held that the right to file an appeal is a general right which is not restricted in any way. The right to apply for review of a judgment is restricted under section 114 and Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It should not, therefore, be an appeal subsequently filed which should be rejected as being incompetent in view of a review application having been filed earlier, but it should be the review application which should be rejected on the ground that it is no more competent, an appeal having been filed against the decree sought to be reviewed and the matter being within the purview of the appellate Court which can look into the grounds on which the review application is presented.

11. He then cited the case of Jwala Prasad vs Jwala Bank Ltd reported in AIR 1961 Allahabad 381 and submitted that in that case, it was held, by virtue of section 117, section 114, CPC applies to proceedings taken by the High Court in the exercise of its appellate jurisdiction. Thus, the High Court may (subject to the conditions and limitations to be found in Order XLVII of the Code of Civil Procedure) review its judgment in all cases except where an appeal from a decree or order founded upon that judgment is allowed under the Code and has been preferred. Where, therefore, no appeal has been preferred, a decision given by the High Court in a special appeal is open to review. A special appeal is the name given by the Rules of the Allahabad High Court to an appeal which lies from judgment of one Judge of the High Court in the circumstances mentioned in C1.10 of the Letters Patent.

12. He next cited the case of Abul Basher Chowdhury vs Mehar Khatun reported in 35 DLR 6 and submitted that under Order XLVII, rule 1 a review may be granted only under specific circumstances to meet certain specific situations and not for re-opening the order or decree on any pretext.

13. He then cited the case of Hussain Bakhsh, vs. Settlement Commissioner and another reported in 21 DLR (SC) 456. In that case, it was held that the High Court in its writ jurisdiction is competent to review its own decision under clause (b) of section 114 of the Code. It was further held that the right to claim review of any decision of a court of law, like the right to appeal, is a substantive right and not a mere matter of procedure.

14. He next cited the case of Begun Lutfunnessa vs Nazimuddin Ahmed and others reported in 40 DLR 232. In that case, it was held that, award given by an Arbitrator shall be deemed to be a decree and the statement of the grounds of such award to be a judgment within the meaning of section 2(2) and section 2(9) of the Code of Code of Civil Procedure respectively. The Arbitrator shall have all the powers of a civil Court under section 36 of the Ordinance No. 2 of 1982. In that case, it was further held that Arbitrator is a persona designate, a functionary designated not by name but as one of a class and as the Arbitrator is not a Court at all within the meaning of the Code of Civil Procedure there can be no question of his being sub-ordinate to the High Court Division. Hence, no contempt proceedings can be drawn against the opposite parties. In that case, it was further held that the Arbitrator does not exercise a judicial function in course of inquiry or investigation into the amount of compensation although he is expected to act within judicial norms. It was further held that in view of the deeming provision in section 32(3) of the Ordinance the award of the Arbitrator is appealable as a decree and also executable as a decree. But the status of the Arbitrator has not undergone any change thereby. He is not elevated by virtue of the deeming clause in sub-section (3) of section 32 of the Ordinance to the position of a Civil Court.

15. He lastly cited the case of Khaled Akbar vs. The Government of Bangladesh and others reported in 42 DLR 66. In that case it was held that Member of the Arbitration Appellate Tribunal is a court and his decision is amenable to the revision jurisdiction of High Court Division. In the above cited cases accepting the case reported 42 DLR 66 all the cases were civil proceedings governed by the Code of Civil Procedure.

16. Section 36 of the Ordinance provides that the Arbitrator, while holding any enquiry or proceeding under this Act, shall have the same powers as are vested in a civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure (V of 1908) for the purpose as enumerated in the section itself that is for the following purpose:

(a) summoning and enforcing the attendance of any person and examining him on oath;

(b) compelling the production of any document or record;

(c) reception of evidence on affidavit;

(d) issuing commission for examination of witnesses;

(e) requisitioning any public record from any court or office.

17. The Arbitrator is a creature of statute (Ordinance II of 1982) and under section 36 of the Ordinance he has been vested with some limited powers of the Civil Court while holding any enquiry or proceeding as stated above.

<u>18. Therefore, from our above discussion it is clear that the Arbitrator is a Civil Court for a limited purpose as enumerated in section 36 of the Ordinance and by no stretch of imagination it can be said that the Arbitrator is a Civil Court for all purposes, although in section 32(3) it has been provided that every award passed by the Arbitrator shall be deemed to be a decree and the statement of the grounds of every such award a judgment within the meaning of section 2(2) and section 2(9) respectively of the Code of Civil Procedure (V of 1908).</u>

<u>19. It is needless to mention that section 114 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides for substantive right of review by the aggrieved party and Order XLVII, CPC provides for the procedure. The mere fact that in section 32(3) of the Ordinance it has been said that the award shall be deemed to be a decree and the statement of the grounds of such award a judgment within meaning of section 2(2) and section 2(9) respectively of the Code of Civil Procedure it will not confer any substantive right of review on the petitioner in the absence of any specific provisions for review in the Ordinance. Therefore, the submission of Mr. Bhuiyan that only because the award passed by the arbitrator shall be deemed to be a decree, the right of review is available to the petitioner cannot be accepted.</u>

<u>20. Since there is provision for appeal under section 34 of the Ordinance and the appellants without filing appeal preferred review application before the Arbitrator, the review application is not maintainable.</u>

21. Mr. Bhuiyan lastly submitted with reference to judgment passed by the Arbitrator in Review Arbitration Miscellaneous Case 16 of 1991 that the Arbitrator in the judgment held that land acquired in the same LA case in respect of the same and other adjoining mouzas the compensation money was assessed at a higher rate and the petitioner was entitled to that rate. In this view of the matter, the Arbitrator reviewed the earlier judgment and fixed the amount of award at Taka 6,38,797.63. Mr. Bhuiyan submitted that the reasons assigned by the Arbitrator for enhancing the rate of compensation money are quite legal and based on the facts on record. He accordingly, submitted that under Article 104 of the Constitution, this court has power to issue such directions, orders, decrees or writs as may be necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it, including orders for the purpose of securing the attendance of any person or the discovery or production of any document.

22. He further submitted that after getting favorable order in the review case, the petitioner allowed the arbitration revision appeal No 16 (which filed by him subsequent to the filing of the review case) to be dismissed for non-prosecution and, as such, he is now left with no remedy. We find substance in this submission of Mr Bhuiyan.

<u>23. In view of the discussion made above, these appeals are dismissed with modification without any order as to costs.</u>

<u>To do complete justice in the matter under Article 104 of the Constitution, the respondent No. I is directed to pay within 60 days Taka 6,38,797.63 to the appellant.</u>

End.

lawyer:
Rajik-al-Jalil, Deputy Attorney-General, instructed by Zainul Abedin, Advocate-on-Record—For the Appellant. 
Abdul Matin Khasru, Senior Advocate, instructed by Sufia Khatiun, Advocate-on-Record—For Respondent No.1. 
Md. Taufiq Hossain, Advocate-on-Record—Respondent No.2.
parties:
Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Housing and Public Works, Bangladesh Secretariat, Dhaka------ Appellant
VS
ATM Mannan and another------ Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 23-8-2006 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.5426 of 2004).
full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain J: This appeal by the writ-respondent as the appellant following leave is directed against the judgment and order dated 23-8-2006 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 5426 of 2004 making the Rule absolute with a direction to exclude the property from the 'Kha' list of abandoned buildings.

2. The facts leading to this appeal are precised below:—

The respondents as the writ petitioners filed Writ Petition No. 5426 of 2004 against the enlistment of the property with building and premises measuring 18 kathas and 10 chhataks in Plot No. 330-D, Block-C of Plan No. 613/58 Road No. 28 (Old) Dhanmondi Residential Area, Dhaka in the 'Kha' list of the abandoned buildings published in the Bangladesh Gazette dated 23-9-1986 at page 9764(15) at serial No.7 and prayed for direction to release the said property from the list.

3. The case of the respondents was that the property in question originally belonged to Syed Ali Hasan who obtained the same by way of lease for a period of 99 years, commencing on 15th December, 1961 from the erstwhile Government of East Pakistan by a registered of lease deed dated 16-12-1961. After that Syed Ali Hasan constructed a one-storied building on the case property and continued in possession thereof. While in peaceful possession of the case property, he made an oral gift of the said property to his wife, Mrs. Farhat Hasan on 2-8-1968 and delivered possession thereof to her in presence of witnesses. In support the said oral gift Syed Ali Hasan affirmed an affidavit before the Court of Magistrate, First Class, Dhaka. While in possession of the said property, Mrs. Farhat Hasan mutated her name in respect of the same in the government records and also in the register of the City Corporation. She paid all taxes including the municipal tax. Subsequently while in peaceful possession of the property, Mrs. Farhat Hasan being in urgent need of money decided to sell the property. The writ petitioners proposed to purchase the property for a consideration of Tk. 20,00,000 and the Mrs. Farhat Hasan agreed to sell. Accordingly, she executed a bainapatra dated 16-2-1986 in favour of the writ petitioners on receipt of Tk.10 lakh and delivered possession of the same and also handed over the relevant papers to the writ petitioners. Subsequently, said Mrs. Farhat Hasan received another amount of Tk. 5,00,000 on 28-1-1992 and lastly on 14-6-1997 an amount of Tk. 4,50,000 from the writ petitioners. But on 25-1-1998, the writ petitioners requested her to execute and register the deed of sale on receipt of balance consideration amounting to Tk. 50,000 but she refused to execute the same on demanding an additional amount of Tk. 20,00,000 as the price of the case property increased by leaps and bounds. The writ petitioners filed Other Class Suit No.42 of 1998 before the Third Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Dhaka for specific performance of contract impleading Mrs. Farhat Hasan as defendant No.1. The Government of Bangladesh and the Ministry of Housing and Public Works were made defendant Nos.2 and 3 respectively. The suit was subsequently transferred to the Third Court of Sub-ordinate Judge (Arbitration), Dhaka and renumbered as Other Class Suit No. 01 of 2000. The said suit was decreed ex-parte by the judgment and order dated 24-7-2000 and Mrs. Farhat Hasan was directed to execute and register necessary deed of sale within 30 days. Since Mrs. Farhat failed to do so, the Court executed and registered the deed of sale dated 28-9-2000 in favour of the writ petitioners.

4. The further case of the writ petitioners is that they have been in possession of the case property and have paid taxes to the Government regularly. After that, they filed an application to the Secretary, Ministry of Housing and Public Works on 15-7-2001 for mutating their names in respect of the case property. But the Ministry refused to do so and informed the writ petitioners by the letter dated 10-12-2001 that the said property was listed as an abandoned property under the category of 'Kha' list at serial No. 7. On query the writ petitioners also came to know of the said fact. The writ petitioners filed two separate applications both under section 12 of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 to the concerned authority of the Ministry of Housing and Public Works on 29-8-2002 and 24-3-2003 respectively for exclusion of the case property from the list of the abandoned property but to no avail. After that, the writ petitioners prepared an application under section 7 of the Ordinance, 1985 to file before the First Court of Settlement, Segun Bagicha, Dhaka for exclusion of the case property from the list of abandoned property. But that application was not entertained as the aforesaid Court of Settlement could not carry on its business for lack of constitution.

5. The vendor of the writ petitioners had always been in exclusive and peaceful possession of the case property till 16-2-1986 and had been managing the same in person. The vendor also executed bainapatra in favour of writ the petitioners and delivered possession thereof to them as part performance of the contract. There was no allegation that she was not a citizen of Bangladesh or she was the national of any country, which was at war with Bangladesh at any time after 25th March, 1971. As such, the very inclusion of the case property in the Kha list of abandoned buildings is ex-facie void for want of jurisdiction and is violative of the Article 42 of the Constitution.

6. The writ-petitioners further submitted that no notice was served upon them or their vendor for surrendering or taking over possession of the case property as abandoned by the concerned authority which was mandatory requirement of Article 7 of the PO 16 of 1972 or section 5(1)(b) of the Ordinance No. LIV of 1985. Thus the very inclusion of the case property in the list of abandoned buildings is violative of the aforesaid provisions of law and, as such, the same has been done without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the enlistment of the disputed house in the 'Kha' list of abandoned buildings, the writ-petitioners filed Writ Petition No. 5426 of 2004 before the High Court Division and obtained Rule Nisi.

8. The writ-respondent No.1, Government of Bangladesh, the Ministry of Housing and Public Works appeared and contested the rule by filling affidavit-in-opposition denying all the materials statements made in the writ petition. The case of the Government, in short, is that Mrs. Farhat Hasan was a Non-Bengali and she left the country just after independence or prior thereto. It was further contended that since the writ petitioners failed to submit any papers before the Court that their vendor was present in Bangladesh on 2-8-1986, 28-1-1992 and lastly on 14-6-1997 when the writ petitioners allegedly claimed that she received Tk. 4,50,000. Since Mrs. Farhat Hasan left Bangladesh before independence and her property was liable to be treated as abandoned property. Hence the Government lawfully included the said property in the 'Kha' list of abandoned buildings and, as such, the Rule was liable to be discharged.

9. After hearing the parties, the High Court Division by the judgment and order dated 23-8-2006 made the Rule absolute directing respondent No. 1 to exclude the said property from the 'Kah' list within 3 (three) months from the date of receipt of the judgment.

10. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with judgment and order dated 23-8-2006 passed by the High Court Division, the writ respondent as leave-petitioner filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1561 of 2006 and obtained leave on 25-3-2008 resulting in Civil Appeal No. 99 of 2008.

<u>11. Mr. Rajik-al-Jalil, learned Deputy Attorney-General, appearing on behalf of the appellant, submits that the suit of the writ petitioners for specific performance of contract was barred under section 6 of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 (in short Ordinance of 1985)and that even the Government is not bound by a decree passed in a suit for specific performance of contract in view of the principle enunciated by this Division in the Case of CQMH Md. Ayub Ali vs Bangladesh, 47 DLR (AD) 71. He further submits that the onus is on the respondents to prove that the building was not an abandoned property and that the Government has no obligation either to deny the fact alleged by the claimant or to disclose the basis of treating the property as abandoned property merely because the same was disputed by the claimant and, as such, the impugned judgment should be set-aside. He lastly submits that the original owner left the country during the war of liberation leaving the disputed building uncared for and that the disputed building has become abandoned property by operation of law and that the High Court Division without looking into this broad fact made the Rule absolute and, as such, the impugned judgment should be set-aside.</u>

12. Mr. Abdul Matin Khasru, learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of respondent No. 1, on the other hand, submits that the writ petitioners entered into an agreement to purchase the disputed building for a consideration of Tk. 20,00,000 and accordingly, a bainapatra was executed and registered on 16-2-1986 and that subsequently by filing Other Class Suit No. 42 of 1998 in the Third Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Dhaka for specific performance of contract the writ petitioners obtained a decree and, as such, the listing of the disputed property in the 'Kha' list of the abandoned buildings was illegal and without jurisdiction. He further submits that the no notice as required under the Ordinance of 1985 was served before enlisting the disputed building in the 'Kha' list of the abandoned buildings and, as such, the enlistment of the disputed building in the 'Kha' list is ex-facie illegal and without jurisdiction and, as such, no interference is called for. In support of his contention, the learned Advocate relies upon the case of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works vs Helal Uddin, 4 MLR (AD)140.

13. We have considered the submissions of the learned Deputy Attorney-General for the appellant and the learned Advocate for respondent No.1, perused the impugned judgment and the papers incorporated in the paper-book.

14. Before addressing the conflicting submissions of the learned Deputy Attorney-General for the appellant and the learned Advocate for respondent No. 1, it is necessary to go through the submissions on which leave was granted as under:—

I. The respondents failed to prove by submitting any paper to show that their predecessor Mrs. Farhat Hasan was present in Bangladesh on 2-8-1986, 28-1-1992 and lastly on 14-6-1997 when the respondents allegedly claimed that she received Tk. 4 lakh and 50 thousand, Mrs. Farhat Hasan in fact should be taken to have left Bangladesh before Bijoy Dibos and her property was liable to be treated as abandoned property, the enlistment was legal and lawful the High Court Division overlooking the facts of the case properly committed error in directing to exclude the property from 'Kha' list.

II. The respondents on 11-3-1998 filed Title Suit No. 42 of 1998 for specific performance of contract against the said Mrs. Farhat Hasan and they got possession on 16-2-1986. Such occupation cannot give one the right to continue to stay in the property. The property in question has been published in the gazette dated 23-9-1986 showing inclusion in the `Kha' list of the abandoned property rightly as per section 5(1)(b) of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985, the judgment of the High Court Division is thus liable to be set-aside.

III. The SRO No. 365-L/86 published in Bangladesh Gazette dated 23-9-1986 itself shows that the authority published the list of the building of which notice for delivery of possession or taking possession have been served, the contention that notice had not been served in respect of the property in question is not a valid contention or the same cannot be used as rebuttable presumption about the existences of the original owners and, as such, the High Court Division erred in law in directing the authority to release the property.

IV. The High Court Division passed the judgment on the basis of the respondent's averment that they obtained ex-parte decree but overlooked that the earlier suit for specific performance of contract was barred under section 6(a) of the Ordinance 54 of 1985 and the respondents also failed to get remedy before the court of settlement as per section 7 of the said Ordinance.

15. Admittedly, the disputed property originally belonged to Syed Ali Hasan who obtained the same by a registered deed of lease dated 16-2-1961 for a period of 99 years. Soon after, Syed Ali Hasan constructed a one-storied building on the case property and had been in possession thereof. He was stated to have made an oral gift of the disputed property to his wife, Mrs. Farhat Hasan on 2-8-1968 and was stated to have delivered possession thereof to her. In support of the oral gift Syed Hasan Ali was stated to have affirmed an affidavit before the Court of Magistrate, First Class, Dhaka. Mrs. Farhat Hasan mutated her name in respect of the disputed property in the Government-record and also in the register of the City Corporation and paid municipality tax and other taxes regularly to the Government. Mrs. Farhat Hasan was stated to have entered into an agreement with the writ-petitioner to sell the disputed property for a consideration of Tk. 20,00,000 on 16-2-1986. The writ-petitioners stated to have paid the entire money except an amount of Tk. 50,000. When Mrs. Farhat Hasan refused to execute and register the deed of sale, the writ-petitioner filed Other Class Suit No.42 of 1998 before the Third Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Dhaka, impleading Mrs. Farhat Hasan as defendant No.1, the Government of Bangladesh and the Ministry of Housing and Public Works as defendant Nos. 2 and 3 respectively. The suit was transferred to the Third Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Dhaka and renumbered as Other Class Suit No. 01 of 2000. On 24-7-2000, the suit was decreed ex-parte and Mrs. Farhat Hasan was directed to execute and register necessary deed of sale within 30 days. She having failed to do so the Court executed and registered the deed of sale on 28-9-2000 in favour of the writ-petitioners.

16. The writ-petitioners stated to have entered into a contract to purchase the disputed building on 16-2-1968. Admittedly, they filed Other Class Suit No. 42 of 1998 before the Third Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Dhaka, renumbered as Other Class Suit No.01 of 2000 for specific performance of contract. Such a suit in 1998 is barred according to the provisions of section 6 of the Ordinance,1985 which is quoted below :-

6. No suit to lie in respect of certain buildings.—Save as otherwise provided in this Ordinance, no suit or other legal proceedings shall lie before any court for.....

(a) specific performance of contract in respect of any building the possession of which has been taken by the Government as abandoned property under the President's Order or in respect of which notice for taking possession by the Government as abandoned property under that Order has been issued, or

(b) a declaration that a building is not an abandoned property and has not been vested in the Government under the President's Order or the right or interest of any person in any building has not been affected by the provisions of that Order, or

17. Having considered Clause (a) of section 6 of the Ordinance, 1985, in particular, it appears that a suit for specific performance of contract in 1998 was barred and the ex-parte decree obtained in that suit is of no avail to the writ-petitioners.

18. Even the Government is not bound by a decree passed in a suit for specific performance of contract. This view has been taken by this Division in the case of CQMH Md. Ayub Ali (ibid) in which it has been held that the decree in a suit for specific performance of contract will show that it was only decided the controversy between the vendor and the vendee and the vendor was directed to execute the necessary document in favour of the vendee. It has further been held that such a decree is not the one which is contemplated in proviso (a) and, as such, the existence of such a decree can not be pleaded as a bar for inclusion of the building in the list. In the case in hand, the suit was filed after the Ordinance of 1985 came into being. Therefore, the decree passed in the suit for specific performance of contract on 24-7-2000 has got no legal effect.

19. Admittedly, the disputed property was enlisted in the 'Kha' list of abandoned buildings by a gazette notification dated 23-9-1986. It is pertinent to quote a portion of the notice as under :—

“ নং এস, আর  ও ৩৬৫-এল/৮৬-১৯৮৫ সনের পরিত্যক্ত ইমারত (সম্পুরক বিধান) অধ্যাদেশ (১৯৮৫ সনের ৫৪নং অধ্যাধেশ এর ৫(১)(খ) ধারা অনুযায়ী এবং অত্র মন্ত্রণালয়ের বিজ্ঞপ্তি নং এস,আর, ও ১৪২-এল/৮৬/শাখা/৯/১ এম-৭২/৮৫/৪১৭, তারিখ ২৮শে এপ্রিল, ১৯৮৬ বাতিলক্রমে সরকার ১৯৭২ সনের বাংলাদেশ পরিত্যক্ত সম্পত্তি (নিয়ন্ত্রন, ব্যবস্থাপনা ও হস্তান্তর) আদেশ (১৯৭২ সনের রাষ্ট্রপতির ১৬নং আদেশ)-এর অধীনে যে সমস্ত ইমরাতের দখল হস্তান্তর করায় বা দখল নেওয়ার জন্য নোটিশ জারী করা হইয়াছে সে সমস্ত ইমারতের একটি তালিকা এতদসংগে প্রকাশ করিতেছেন।”

20. From the aforesaid quotation, it appears that the notice, in fact, was served according to the provision of the Ordinance,1985 for handing over or taking over the disputed building. According to section 114(e) of the Evidence Act, it is to be presumed that judicial and official acts have been regularly performed.

<u>21. It has been now well settled by different pronouncements of this Division that the onus is on the claimant of the building to prove that the building is not an abandoned property and that the Government has no obligation either to deny the facts alleged by the claimant or to disclose the basis of treating the property as abandoned property merely because the same is disputed by the claimant. In this connection, reliance may be made on the case of Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works vs Md. Abdul Jalil, 48 DLR (AD)10, in which, this Division held as under :—</u>

<u>"The onus, therefore, is squarely on the claimant of the building to prove that the building is not an abandoned property. The Government has no obligation either to deny the facts alleged by the claimant or to disclose the basis of treating the property as abandoned property merely because the same is disputed by the claimant."</u>

22. Mr. Abdul Matin Khasru, learned Senior Advocate for respondent No.1 has cited the case of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works and others (ibid) in which it has been held that prior service of notice for enlistment of the building as abandoned property is a condition precedent and when no notice was served the so-called enlistment was not valid and, as such, the writ-petitioners were not required to go to the Court of Settlement.

23. The case referred to above is different from the case in hand. From the Gazette notification dated 23-9-1986 (Exhibit-G to the writ petition) it appears that notice as required by law was, in fact, issued.

24. In the light of the findings made before, we find that the High Court Division was not justified in making the Rule absolute.

Accordingly, the appeal is allowed and the impugned judgment is set-aside. There is no order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Khondker Mahbuddin Ahmed with Kamaluddin Ahmed, Advocates ----- for appellant
Ahmed Sobhan with Nizamuddin Haider, Advocates ----- for respondent 1
parties:
Shafi Khan
Vs.
Mannujan Hossain & Others
full_judgment:
Md. Altaf Hossain, J:- This application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against the judgment and order passed by the Subordinate Judge, Khulna on 18.9.76 in Miscellaneous Case No. 291 of 1974 of his court allowing an application for pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. The facts of the case are as follows:

The Non-Agricultural holding  to which the case land appertains belonged to deceased opposite party No. 2 Al-Haj Abdul Bari Khan. The petitioner Mst. Munujan Hossain was a co-sharer in the holding by purchase. The deceased O.P. No. 2 Al-Haj Abdul Bari Khan by kabala dated 28.5.74 sold the case land to O.P. No. 1 Md. Atosh Khan who was a stranger for Tk. 30,000/-. No notice of transfer was served upon the petitioner. The petitioner who owns only 25 bight of land is entitled to pre-empt the case land. She filed this application for preemption on making the statutory deposit. The O. P. No. 2 having died during the pendency of the case, his heirs were substituted of whom O.P. No. 2 (ka) filed objection. Both the written objections are practically identical. The OPs contended that the Misc. Case was barred by limitation, was bad for defect of, parties, and was not maintainable. Their substantial case, however, was that Al-Haj Abdul Bari Khan who owned the property executed the kabala under pre-emption in favour of O.P. No. 1 who was his nephew but no consideration money was paid and as a result no possession of the land was delivered to O.P. No. 1. The kabala under pre-emption was not acted upon. The O.P. No. 1 failed to pay the consideration, when deceased O.P. No. 2 filed Title Suit No. 334/74 for a declaration that kabala under pre-emption was not acted upon. Subsequently the O.P. No. 1 executed and registered a deed of kabala on 31.10.74 reconvening the land to Al-Haj Abdul Bari Khan. Thereafter, Al-Haj Abdul Bari Khan withdrew the Title Suit. The petitioner had filed this case for pre-emption after the second kabala and as such he had no cause of action for getting pre-emption, O.P. No. 1 having no subsisting interest at the time of filing of the case. At the time of hearing, the Oars did not press their objection on the grounds of limitation and defect of parties. They rather came up with a case that the application for pre-emption was pre-mature. The petitioner examined 2 witnesses on her side. P.W. 1 Delwar Hossain is the husband of the petitioner and claimed to depose for her. P.W. 2 Shaikh Altaf Hossain is a neighbour. The O.Ps. examined 3 witness is on their side. O.P.W. No. 1, Md. Shafi Khan is the O.P. No. 2 K (a) himself. O.P.W. No. 2 is the O.P. No. 1. These two O.Ps. contested the case. O.P.W. No. 3 Abdul Ghani is a person who used to live in the case land itself. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the cases of the respective parties and the evidence on record both oral and documentary, came to the conclusion that the Misc. case was not premature and that Title Suit No. 334/74 filed by O.P. No. 2 and the second kabala executed by O.P. No. 1 in favour of O.P. No. 2 were fraudulent and collusive. He also found that the kabala under pre-emption was acted upon, consideration passed thereon and O.P. No. 1 was put into possession. He held that by the alleged reconveyance, even if genuine, the petitioner's right of pre-emption could not be defeated in the absence of any contract for reconveyance. On the above findings, the learned Subordinate Judge allowed the petitioner's application for pre-emption. Being aggrieved, the O.P. No. 2 (ka) Shafi Khan has filed this appeal.

2. It appears from the evidence on record, the kabala under pre-emption was executed on 28.5.74, presented for registration on 17.6.74 and entered in the volume with the endorsement Registered on 12.4.76. The Misc. Case was filed on 1.11.74. It is now settled law that before registration is completed by entering the document in the volume with the endorsement 'Registered' as required under section 60 of the Registration Act, no cause of action for pre-emption can arise. In that view of the matter the learned Subordinate Judge's finding that the application for pre-emption was not premature cannot be sustained this however, by itself, does not affect the result of the case. It has been held by Appellate Division in Abdur Rahman ® Abdul Rahman v. Maklis Ali and another (1) that if the document is registered while the pre-emption application is still pending the defect of prematurity is fully cured and the application for pre-emption is not liable to be thrown out on that ground. In the instant case, the admitted position is that the document was registered during the pendency of the pre-emption application. This point of, prematurity is, therefore, of no consequence in this case.

3. The next point that requires consideration is whether the kabala under pre-emption was acted upon. The only oral evidence on the point comes from the mouth of O. P. W. No. 2 Md. Ayesh Khan, the purchaser. O.P. W. No. 1 Md. Shaft Khan was not present at' the time of transaction. He says that he was informed by his father about the transaction by letter but that letter is alleged to be missing and has not been produced. The only evidence that remains is the recital of the kabala under pre-emption itself. Ext. 'A' is that kabala which was executed by Al-Haj Abdul Bari who is since dead. In this document Abdul Bari Khan has stated that he has received the consideration amount of Tk. 30,000/-. This statement of deceased Abdul Bad Khan is relevant under section 32 (2) of the Evidence Act and in the instant case constitutes the best and the most reliable evidence. The evidence of the 0. P. W No. 2 Md. Ayesh Khan cannot baggier any importance because it has become evident that he was Sailing in the same boat with Abdul Bad Khan and is none but a nephew of Abdul Bad Khan. It is clear that Abdul Bari Khan and Md. Ayesh Khan were in collusion. Apart from it, it appears from the evidence of P. W. 2 Shaikh Altaf Hossein who is a red. Government employee and a close neighbor that O.P. No. 1 Md. Ayesit Khan constructed a decal but and a Kutcher latrine in the case-land O.P. No. 3 an own; witness of the O.Ps., when cross-examined, stated that he did not know if O.P. No. 1 constructed the latrine, and as such could not deny the construction of the latrine by O.P. No. 1. It is clear that the purchaser O.P. No. 1 was put into possession after his purchase under the kabala under pre-emption. There cannot be any manner of doubt that the kabala under preemption was acted upon consideration thereunder passed and the purchaser O.P. No. 1 was put into possession. Even without this finding this case must, however, succeed. It has came out from the mouth of O.P. No. 1 (O.P.W. No. 2) Md. Ayesh Khan himself that it was stipulated that he would pay consideration in in-stamens but he failed. Sale as defined in the. Transfer of property Act is a transfer of ownership in exchange for a price paid or promised or part-paid and the case of 'the O.P. No. 2 (Ka) and deposed in his favour it has appeared that the transfer was made on his promise of patient of the consideration in in-stamens, a transfer by sale has been completed giving rise to a pre-emptible right to the petitioner who was admittedly a co-sharer by purchase. Here we would also like to say a few words about the nature and Character of the second kabala, Ext. B executed by Md. Ayesh Khan in favour of Abdul Bari Khan. The learned Subordinate Sage on consideration of the evidence on record and the circumstances of the case has come to the conclusion that the suit and the second kabala were results of collusion be, tween the 02s for defeating the petitioner's right of pre-emption. It has appeared in evidence that the Title Suit was filed on 29.7.74 after the petitioner took certified copy of the kabla under pre-emption. The second kabala was executed on 31.10.74. It was registered at Satkhita and presented for registration at 2-30 P.M. on the same date. The stamps were purchased on 30.10.74 from the Khulna Treasury and the income Tax clearance certificate was obtained on 31.10.74 that is, on the date of presentation of the kabala for registration.

4. The learned Subordinate Judge has noticed the remarkable promptness with which the Income Tax clearance certificate was taken at Khulna and the kabala was registered at Satkhira, and has considered the relationship between the O.Ps and has come to the conclusion that the second kabala was created collusively and fraudulently with a view to defeat petitioner's claim for pre-emption.

5. We find no reason to take a different view and hold and find agreeing with the learned Subordinate Judge that the second kabala is a result of collusion and fraud between the O.Ps. created to defeat and frustrate the petitioner's right of pre-emption and is totally vitiated By this kabala the interest of O. P. No. 1 has not stood retransferred to deceased O.P. No. 2, and cannot defeat petitioner's claim for preemption On this score, if such retransfer could in law be at all a good ground for defeating a right of pre-emption. We would, however, hold in this case for reasons following that even if the second kabala was a genuine document, the right or pre-emption of the petitioner could not be defeated.

6. Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the appellant has contended that the land transferred under the kabala under pre-emption was reconveyed to Al-Haj Abdul Bari Khan the original owner before the pre-emption application was filed as such the petitioner had no longer any cause of action for pre-emption. The learned Advocate has placed before us two case laws Yakub Khan and another v. Amjad Ali Khan and another (1) and Upendra Chandra v. Janab Ali (2) both decided by a single Bench of this Court. In the first case between the dates of filing of the application for pre-emption, and its final disposal the vendor filed a suit for specific performance of contract against the transferee on the ground that at the time of the transfer of the holding the transferee stipulated to recovery the property to the vendor and on that agreement obtained an ex-parte decree against the transferee this being the situation, the court held that the pre-emption application could not be granted.

7. In the second case, on 1.8.69 a co-sharer applied for pre-emption in respect of the land sold. The vendor thereupon produced a reoonveyance deed executed on 26.7-69 selling the same land back to him on the basis of an oral agreement which was however registered on 5-8-69. The court held that the application for pre-emption must fail as the land had already been reconveyed to the original vendor. In both the reported cases, there was a contract of reconveyance between the original owner and the purchaser and it was observed that the pre-emptor could not have better title then the pre-emptee had and that the pre-emptor was bound by the contract for re-conveyance. In the instant case before us, there was no such contract of reconveyance.

8. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed has, however, argued that these reported cases are also authorities for the view that if the land under pre-emption is retransferred to the original owner before the filing of a pre-emption application there was no further scope for pre-emption. We are afraid that there is nothing in the reported cases which even suggest such a view.

9. Mr. Ahmed Sobhan, learned Advocate for the respondent has placed the cases of Girija Nath Kundu v. Ahamadali Sardar and others (1) and Shaikh Lokeman Ali v. Abdul Motalib and another (2) In Girija Nath Kundus case it was held that as soon as a transfer of a share in a holding is effected, a right to pre-emption immediately accrues to the co-sharer tenants and any subsequent transferee of the property must take it subject to that right. If at any time after an application for pre-emption has been made, the property is again transferred, such subsequent transferee may be made a party to the penning pre-emption proceeding and pre-emption allowed against him also. In. Shaikh Lokman Ali's case it was held that as soon as a trans- for of a share in an occupancy holding is made, a right to pre-emption immediately accrues to the co-sharer tenants and any sub-sequent transferee of the holding takes it subject to that right, whether the transfer is made before or after an application for pre-emption is made.

<u>10. The above 2 cases are authorities for the proposition that as soon as a transfer is made a right to pre-emption immediately accrues to the co-sharer tenants and any sub-sequent transferee of the holding must take it subject to that right. On principle we do not find any difference between a case where the subsequent transferee is a third party and a case where he is the original owner. The fact that the original owner, even after the transfer has retained a share in the holding is of no consequence and cannot give rise to a different legal position, as suggested by Mr. Khondker Mahbuddin Ahmed. A right of pre-emption vests on a co-sharer tenant under the statute and unless there in anything in the statute itself to divest him of that right under circumstances that have been alleged in the instant case, that is to say, if before the pre-emption application is filed, the purchaser has transferred the land back to the seller who had retained a share in the holding after the purchase, the co-sharer tenant is not and cannot be divested of that right. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed could not show anything for taking a view otherwise. The case-law reported in 19 D.LR. (SC) 136 (Abdul Wadud v. Ms. Zamrut) on which the learned Advocate has sought reliance is not on this, point and has no manner of application to the facts and circumstances of the case.</u>

11. Having considered the facts and circumstances and evidence of the case and the legal question involved we hold that the learned Subordinate Judge has rightly allowed the application for pre-emption and no reason to interfere. In the result the appeal is dismissed, and parties are made to bear their own costs.

End.

caseno: Civil Revision No. 4787 of 2003 and Civil Revision No. 547 of 2005.
lawyer:
Md. Jahangir Alam, AAG-For the Petitioner 
Abdul Kalam Chowdhury-For Opposite Parties
parties:
Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) ----- Plaintiff-Petitioner 
Vs
Abdur Rab and others ----- Defendant-Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
Shahidul Islam J: The Rule in Civil Revision No. 4787 of 2003 and the Rule issued in Civil Revision No. 547 of 2005 having arisen out of the selfsame property and the parties being common and the fate of both the cases being based upon common issues and similar facts and the laws involved for decision of the rules being common, those are taken up together for disposal by a single judgment, although the rules were heard separately.

2. In Civil Revision No. 4787 of 2003 the fact relevant for disposal of the rule are that the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Noakhali (Now Feni) in the capacity as in charge of Vested and Non-residents Property instituted Title Suit No. 6 of 1981 / 390 of 1974 in the Court of learned sub-ordinate Judge, Noakhali for declaration that the order of attachment dated 23-7-1973 made in Money Exaction Case No 10 of 1973 and the auction held there under dated 27-9-1973 and the said auction having had confirmed on 30-11-1973 to be illegal, collusive, void and not binding upon the plaintiffs contending, inter alia, that the suit land appertaining to mouza Raipur, Police Station Feni, Khatian No. 271, Plot No. 3078 measuring 4 decimals of land with a 2-storied building constructed therein belonged to Monoranjan Banik who left the then East Pakistan for India, after 1960 and accordingly the said property was declared as Enemy Property vide Case No. 1032 of 1967-68. Possession of the same was taken over by a Magistrate and that was leased out with one Nur Mohammad but the lessee failed to renew the lease period and thereafter the Civil Defence Committee being represented by Krishna Dhar Banik prayed for taking lease of the property but failed to pay rent. That property was being possessed by Feni Bastra Hawker Samabaya Samity and that Samity prayed for taking lease. At that stage it came to the notice of the plaintiff that the property was sold in auction as stated above. The attachment as made in Execution Case was held against law of Enemy Property and, as such, the plaintiff came forward for a declaration as stated above.

3. The defendant No. 6 contested the suit by filing written statement denying the plaintiffs case and contending, inter alia, that Money Suit being No. 29 of 1982 and 22 of 1964 were instituted against Monoranjan, the actual owner of the property. Those two suits were decreed in full by the High Court Division in Second Appeal. Thereafter the decrees were put to execution and the suit property including building were attached and were duly sold in auction and that auction was lawfully made and was confirmed. The decree holder while was in the process of getting possession through Court, the Feni Hawker's Samabaya Samity trespassed into the suit building and the executing officer could not hand over possession in favour of the auction purchaser and at that stage the suit was filed.

4. The fact relevant for disposal of Civil Revision No. 547 of 2005 were that in Title Suit No. 6 of 1981 the Feni Bastara Hawker Samabaya Samity was made defendant No. 4 who contested the suit by filing written statement supporting the plaintiff's case and seeking for a lease of the suit building.

5. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge framed the following issues:—

a) Is the property scheduled to the plaint is a Enemy Property?

b) Whether the auction held in Money Execution Case No. 10 of 1973 was illegal?

c) Is the plaintiff entitled to a decree as prayed for?

6. The plaintiff examined the concerned VP Tahshilder as PW 1 and another Mofizur Rahman, stationery Shop owner of the Banik Samity was examined as PW2 and they were cross-examined. The defendant No. 6 examined himself as DWI and one Ganu Miah was examined as DW2. The order dated 16-4-1968 recorded in EPSC No 1032 of 1967-68 was marked as Exhibit-2. The said order is not available on record. Other documents were marked as Exhibit-2(a), 3, 4, 1, 5 and 6. The defendants' documents were marked as Exhibit-A series, B series, C, D, E, F, G and H.

7. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge by the judgment and decree dated 29-1-1982 dismissed the suit.

8. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and decree the plaintiff preferred Title Appeal No. 184 of 1985. That appeal was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, Feni who by the impugned judgment and decree dated 14-7-2003 dismissed the appeal.

9. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and decree the Additional Deputy Commissioner, (Revenue) being in Charge of Vested and Non-Residents Property preferred Civil Revision No. 4787 of 2003 and the Feni Bastara Hawkers Samabaya Samity being represented by its President Mofizul Haque Khan preferred Civil Revision No. 547 of 2005. This Court upon receipt of the applications issued the instant Rules.

10. Mr. Md. Jahangir Alam, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appeared for the plaintiff petitioner in Civil Revision No. 4787 of 2003 and Mr. AKM Enayetullah Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appeared for the petitioner in Civil Revision No. 547 of 2005. Mr. Abdul Kalam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appears in both the Rules for the opposite parties.

11. Main argument for the petitioners of the rules have been advanced by the learned Assistant Attorney General Mr. Md. Jahangir Alam who taking me through the impugned judgment and decree submitted that transfer of Enemy Property by private sale or auction sale in execution of a decree is illegal. He submitted that the law of Enemy Property (section 8) prohibited any transfer of Enemy Property and, as such, the attachment made in 1973 was illegal and the sale took place in execution of Money Decree was void and, as such, the Courts below committed an error of law resulting an error in the decision occasioning a Failure of justice and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree are liable to be set side and the Rules are liable to be made absolute. He lastly submitted for sending the suit back on remand.

12. Mr. AKM Enayetullah, the learned Advocate adopted the submissions made by the learned Assistant Attorney General.

13. Mr. Abul Kalam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate at the very outset raised the question of locus standi of the plaintiff of the original suit in filing the suit. Mr. Chowdhury submitted that after the repeal of Act No. I of 1969 by promulgation of PO No. 29 of 1972 the office of Assistant Custodian and Deputy Custodian was abolished. He submitted that the property which was declared as Enemy was vested with the Government and, as such, the plaintiff of the suit had no locus standi to institute the suit challenging the execution proceedings as well as the auction sale held in Money Execution Case No. 10 of 1973. Thereafter he submitted that the Money suit was instituted in 1962 and the suit was ultimately decreed in full by the High Court Division in Second Appeal No. 842 of 1964 and, as such, the decree in execution was made in a suit prior to the promulgation of Defence of Pakistan Ordinance and Rules and, as such, the legality and validity of the execution proceedings as well as attachment cannot be challenged by the Assistant custodian who had no authority to institute the suit. He submitted that the plaintiffs totally failed to prove the fact that Monoranjan left the country for India during the life time of Enemy Property Act and, as such, the Courts below were quite justified in dismissing the suit. He further submitted that the notices of Money Execution Case No. 10 of 1973 was duly and lawfully served upon Monoranjan and, as such, under section 114(e) of the Evidence Act there carries a presumption that the claim of vesting with the enemy property was baseless and, as such, the Courts below did not commit any illegality in dismissing the suit. With these submissions Mr. Chowdhury prayed for discharge of the rules.

14. From the submission as raised by Mr. Abul Kalam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the opposite parties, I need to decide the following points for determination in disposing of the Rules:—

a) Whether the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Feni, in the capacity as in Charge of Vested and Non-Resident Property had any locus standi to file the Title Suit No. 390 of 1974 before the learned Subordinate Judge claiming the property in suit to be vested property and challenging the legality and validity of the order of attachment dated 23-7-1973 as well as the auction held vide. Money Execution Case No. 10 of 1973 on 27-9-1973?

b) Whether the suit property as scheduled to the plaint was immune from auction sale in execution of a decree?

c) Whether the impugned judgment and decree are sustainable in law?

15. Let us take us the point No. (a) Whether the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Noakhali in the capacity as Assistant Custodian of Enemy Properties had any locus standi to institute the Title Suit No. 390 of 1974 before the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, claiming the property in suit to be vested property and challenging the legality and validity of the order of attachment dated 23-7-1973 as well as the auction sale held vide Money Execution Case No. 10 of 1973 on 27-9-1973?

16. To answer this question let us look to the legal history of the law of enemy property and its subsequent position. On the outbreak of the war between Pakistan an India on the 6th September 1965 the President of erstwhile Pakistan issued a Proclamation of Emergency under clause (1) of Article 30 of the Constitution of Pakistan, 1962 and on that very day he promulgated the Defence of Pakistan Ordinance (Ordinance No. XXIII of 1965) in exercise of the power under clause (4) of Article 30 read with clause (2) of Article 131 of the said Constitution to meet the emergency and to provide for special measures to ensure the security, the public safety and interest and the defence of Pakistan and for the trial of certain offences. Section 3(1) of the Ordinance authorized the Central Government to frame Rules thereunder. Accordingly, the Defence of Pakistan Rules was framed. Rule 182 of the rules provided, inter alia, for appointment of the Custodian, Deputy Custodians and Assistant Custodians of Enemy Property and the vesting of Enemy Properties in the Custodian.

17. Following an appointment of the Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property, the Governor of East Pakistan under the authority delegated to him by the Central Government issued in exercise of the powers conferred by clause (b) of the sub rule (1) of Rule 182 of the said Rules a notification being No. 1199 Genl. Dated 3rd December, 1965 which was published in the Dhaka Gazette Extraordinary on the 4"' December, 1965. In pursuance of the notification all lands and buildings which were Enemy Property within the meaning of sub-rule (4) of the rule 169 of the Rules and which were not connected with enemy firm as defined in sub-rule (2) of that Rule were vested in the Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) with effect from the date of that order.

18. The Proclamation of Emergency was, however, revoked on the 16th February, 1969 resulting in the repeal of the Defence of Pakistan Ordinance and the Rules framed there under but the provisions of the Defence of Pakistan Rules relating to the control of trading with enemy and the control of enemy firm and the administration of the property belonging to the enemies were made to continue by the Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provision) Ordinance, 1969 (Ordinance No. 1 of 1969).

19. Bangladesh emerged as a Sovereign Independent State on the 26th March, 1971 and under the Laws Continuance Enforcement Order all laws which were in force in the territory now comprised in Bangladesh were continued subject to Proclamation of Independence and to such consequential changes as may be necessary as a result of the creation of the new state of Bangladesh, on the 26th March 1972 the President of Bangladesh promulgated the President's Order No. 29 of 1972 vesting all properties and assets which were vested in the Government of Pakistan or were vested in or managed by any Board constituted by or under any law or in the former Government of East Pakistan in the Government of Bangladesh on and from 26th day of March 1972. The clause (1) of Article 2 of this Order has been amended by the Bangladesh (Vesting of Property and Assets) (Amendment) Order, 1972 being President's Order No. 134 of 1972. By virtue of the said amendment the properties and assets which were vested in any officer appointed by the Government of Pakistan including the Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property (Lands and Building) were also vested in the Government of Bangladesh with effect from that date.

20. The aforesaid Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provision), 1969 (Ordinance No. 1 of 1969) was repealed by the Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provisions) (Repeal Act. 1974 and under clause (1) of sub-section 1 of section 3 thereof all enemy properties which were vested in the Custodian of Enemy Property appointed under the provisions of Defence of Pakistan Rules were again vested in the Government. On that day another Act titled the Vested and Non-Resident Property (Administration) Act, 1974 was made providing, inter alia, for administration of such properties through committees to be constituted by the Government. On 27th November, 1976 this Act was replaced by the Vested and Non-Resident Property (Administration) Repeal Ordinance, 1976 (Ordinance XCII of 1976). Under another Ordinance called the Enemy property (Continuance of Emergency Provisions) (Repeal) (Amendment) Ordinance 1976, Ordinance No. XCIII made on that day, the Government was authorised to administer, control, manage and dispose of the property by itself or by such authority as the Government may direct.

<u>21. With this background I now proceed to consider the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner. That in view of Article 2(1) of the President's Order No. 29 of 1972 as amended by President's Order No. 134 of 1972 and in view of Section 3(1)(a) of Act XLV of 1974 mutatis mutandis all enemy properties which were vested in the Deputy Custodian, Enemy Property (lands and buildings) under the provisions of the Defence of Pakistan Rules have been vested in the Government with effect from the 26th March, 1971 and it is, therefore, the Government which alone was competent to maintain the suit in respect of the disputed property, and as the present suit having had not been brought by the Government the same is not maintainable in law. Accordingly, I answer this question negatively against the plaintiff petitioner and the defendant No. 4, (the petitioner of Civil Revision No. 547 of 2005) holding that the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) had no locus standi to file the suit in the capacity of Assistant custodian of Enemy Properties, Noakhali.</u>

22. Let us take up the point No. (b) Whether the suit property as scheduled to the plaint was immune from auction sale in execution of a decree?

23. The Money Suit No. 29 of 1962 were instituted against Monoranjan Banik and that suit was decreed in full in Second Appeal No. 842 of 1964. That decree was passed by this Court 21-7-1972, and the decree was put to execution by filing Money Execution Case No. 10 of 1973. Since the Money Execution Case was filed after 1 year of the decree, a notice was issued against Monoranjan. The service of summons is very much available in the record. That has been marked as Exhibit-D. It appears that the executing Court accepted the service of summons against Monoranjan as good service. The Enemy Property Act has come into being on and from 6-9-1965 the rule 182 was published in the gazette extraordinary. The suit was instituted long before the commencement of the said Defence of Pakistan Rules. There is no document available on record to show that Monoranjan left this country for India during the life time of the Defence of Pakistan Ordinance, although some papers were filed before the trial Court showing declaration of property as enemy property but the plaintiff being the Custodian had to prove the fact by adducing legal evidence that the property was declared as Enemy Property lawfully. Both the Courts below concurrently held that the property was not declared as enemy property. The plaintiff petitioner has totally failed to bring out any case of misreading of evidence, non reading of evidence and non-consideration of evidence in the application for revision This Court sitting in revision is not authorize by law to interfere with the concurrent finding of facts unless any case of misreading of evidence, non-reading of evidence and non-consideration of evidence are brought out.

24. In view of the above, I find that the decision taken by the Courts below are supported by the evidence on record. Accordingly this point is answered holding that, the property was not immune from auction sale.

25. Let us take up the point No. (c) Whether the impugned judgment and decree are sustainable in law?

26. From the discussions as made above, I find that, the Courts below have not committed an error of law resulting an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in passing the impugned judgment and decree.

27. Herein I need to make a comment upon the locus standi of defendant No. 4, the petitioner of Civil Revision No. 547 of 2005. Upon perusal of the judgments of the Courts below as well as the evidence on record I find that the defendant No. 4, Feni Bastara Hawker Samabaya Samity had no legal right to file Civil Revision nor there accrued any right to its favour to institute any legal proceeding. It has been made a party by the plaintiff for the reasons best known to him. He is neither a necessary party nor a proper party in the suit and, as such, I do not find any merit in the Rule issued in Civil Revision No. 547 of 2005. The Courts below have not committed an error of law resulting error in the decision, occasioning failure of justice.

28. So far the prayer for remand is concerned as made by the learned Assistant Attorney General, I need to answer that-the question of remand cannot be automatically made by a revisional court. For getting an order of remand the petitioner had to show that unless the remand is made there will be occasioning failure of justice. Already I have seen that the office of Assistant Custodian and Deputy Custodian has been abolished before the filing of the instant suit and, as such, an order of remand cannot be made for affording Opportunity to the plaintiff to amend the plaint. Accordingly the prayer for remand is rejected.

29. In the result, the Rules issued in Civil Revision No. 4787 of 2003 and Civil Revision No. 547 of 2005 are discharged, however, without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree dated 14-7-2003 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Feni in Title Appeal No. 184 of 1985 dismissing the appeal and affirming those dated 29-1-1982 passed by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, Feni in Title Suit No. 6 of 1981 dismissing the suit are affirmed. The order of status quo granted by this Court stands vacated. The executing Court is directed to proceed on with the Money Execution Case No. 10 of 1973, now pending before the learned Assistant Judge, Feni.

The office is directed to send down the lower Court records.

End.
