parties:
Makku Mian and Others
Vs.
Ali Hossain Buiyan and Others and Bangladesh and Other
Vs.
Ali Hossain Bhuiyan and Others
full_judgment:
Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J. Civil Appeal No. 39 of 1981 by special leave is directed against the judgment and decree dated 29th April, 1980 passed by the High Court Division in appeal from appellate Decree No. 962 of 1969. Defendant is the appellant.

2. Civil Appeal No. 44 of 1983 by special leave is directed against the judgment of the High Court Division in Second Appeal no. 962 of 1969 and the Government of Bangladesh is the appellant.

3. These two appeals arise out of the same judgment of the High Court Division and leave was granted to consider the question of interpretation of section 87(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and whether the High Court Division was correct in holding that the plaintiffs are owners of the riparian land by purchase from the original riparian owner and the suit lands being accreted to their land, they are entitled to get the suit lands as they have stepped into the shoes of the original riparian owners.

4. The respondents brought the suit for a declaration that the settlement of land described in the 4th Schedule of the plaint made by the Government with the defendants was illegal. The plaintiffs claim the land as accretion to their adjoining land.

5. Both the trial court and the lower appellate Court below rejected the plaintiff's claim that it was an accretion the plaintiffs land and the view was taken that it was government khas land formed out of the river bed due to loop cutting by WAPDA and on such finding suit was dismissed.

6. The High Court Division, however, in Second Appeal reversed the findings of facts and decreed the suit holding that the suit land was an accretion to the plaintiffs adjoining land.

7. The Leave was granted for considering the correctness of the decision of the High Court Division.

8. In C.A. No 44 of 1983 the Government preferred the appeal against the same judgment and the contention was that the riparian owner of the accreted suit land having not been recognised or declared as a malik by any competent authority or court, the suit has abated under sub-section 3 of Section 87 of the Act.

9. Facts may be stated briefly: Plaintiffs case was that the land described in Schedule 1 of the plaint comprises a portion of bed of the river Dakatia. The river gradually silted up the land of schedule No. 1 of the plaint and thus this land was accretion to the adjoining upper land of the raiyati including the plaintiffs who have been in possession of the entire second schedule lands by growing boro crops for more than 12 years. His contention is that under section 87 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the second schedule are to be considered as accession and increment to the plaintiffs raiyati land. On the advice of the local Tahsildar, plaintiffs filed a petition to defendant No. 2 for assessment of rent for the second schedule land in the Settlement Case No. 69 of 1962-63 but the defendant No. 2 assessed the rent for 2'00 acres of land at an annual rent to Tk. 12/50 paisa out of 5.00 acres of land of the second schedule though the plaintiffs are in possession of the entire second schedule land measuring 5'00 acres. These 2'00 acre of land has been shown in the 3rd schedule. The local Tahsildar in collusion with the defendants started Settlement case No. 12 of 1964-65 for assessment of rent of the remaining land of second schedule which have been shown in the 4th schedule of the plaint in the name of second party defendant quite illegally and without jurisdiction. Plaintiffs case was that the defendant had no land near the 4th Schedule and never possessed 4th Schedule or any part of it. Plaintiffs filed an objection against the settlement to the second party defendant on the ground that it was their accreted land and it cannot be settled with second party defendant. The matter was however, decided exparte and the Additional Deputy Commissioner passed the order of assessment in the name of second party defendant with regard to the settlement and ordered for assessment of rent in the name of second party defendant. This was challenged by the plaintiffs.

10. Defendants contested the suit and the admitted position was that the suit land comprises a portion of the bed of river Dakatia but they denied that the suit land accreted to the adjoining upper land by gradual deposit of silt nor the plaintiffs even possessed the land for 20/22 years or for any time. Further contention was that the river Dakatia was never a public navigable river and so the land cannot be claimed by accretion by the owner of the adjoining upper land. It was contended that the suit land formed by loop cutting by the defendant No. 1 in 1959 when the course of the river was diverted but the suit land remained under several cubit feet of water during all the seasons of the year and the land was never culturable. The gist of the defendants' case was that the settlement was made in accordance with rules with the defendants and they are in actual possession of the 4th Schedule land.

11. Both the Courts below came to the conclusion that the river Dakatia became a lake as a result of the loop cutting by the WAPDA since 1959 and the river started silting up gradually and it became fit for cultivation. Ext A(1) to A(3) admittedly proved about the loop cutting and the gradual development of the bed of the river into dried land. The plaintiffs themselves prayed for settlement of the land which shows that the plaintiffs were not in possession for the last 20/22 years as claimed. It was found that the land belonged to the Government and the plaintiffs themselves admitted the ownership when they took 2 acres of land for settlement after proper salami. In this view of the matter it was concluded that the plaintiffs could not claim that’s land either under section 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or under the provision of section 4 of the Bengal Alluvion and Dilluvion Regulation (XI of 1825). In this view of the matter the trial court and the appellate court below dismissed the suit.

12. The High Court Division considered section 87 and its amendment by P.O. 137 of 1972. It was noticed that Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was operative in the District on and from 10th May, 1963. The disputed land reformed after the loop cutting in 1959 and the plaintiffs purchased the disputed land prior to 10th of May, 1963 and it was concluded that the plaintiffs are entitled to the benefit of section 87 before amendment. In this view of the matter the order of assessment of rent in the name of defendants by the Additional Deputy Commissioner in Settlement Case No. 12 of 1964-65 regarding the 4th Schedule and of the plaint was declared as illegal and without jurisdiction and the suit was accordingly decreed.

13. As stated above both the defendants and the Government filed above named appeals against the said judgment and both the appeals will be disposed of by this judgment as common question of law arose out of the proceeding.

14. Section 87 may be considered: This section has undergone a change since the date of enactment. In 1951 the position was that any land by gradual accession will be considered as increment to the holding subject to sub-section (2). That sub-section imposed a limitation that it will not be increment if it exceeds the limit laid down in section 90 of the Act. But the proviso says that this will not apply in the case of large-scale co-operative fanning or mechanical cultivation or for cultivation of the tea or sugarcane. Sub-section (3) gives guidance to the Revenue Officer as to how to deal with excess land and provided the manner of vesting.

15. Thereafter in 1967 by Ordinance VIII of 1967 a second proviso was added which said that sub-section (1) or (2) shall not apply to cases of gradual accession caused by any artificial or mechanical process due to development work by Government or by WAPDA or Agricultural Development Corporation. It may be noted in passing that the suit was instituted in 1963 and admittedly the loop cutting was made by WAPDA in this case sometime in 1958. Ordinance VIII of 1967 did not give any retrospective effect to the section and its proviso.

16. Next the Ordinance XII of 1971 amended the section and sub-section (2) and the two proviso were deleted and a new sub-section (2) was substituted which provided that if it exceeds 15 standard bighas then it will not be considered as an increment and a proviso was added stating that it will not he increment if caused by WAPDA or by artificial or mechanical processes. Sub-section (3) concerning the excess land was preserved e.g. excess land vests in the Government and explanation was added as to the meaning of river or sea and gradual accession.

<u>17. Then in 1972 by P.O. 72 the entire section 87 was recast and it said that no such land shall be considered as increment but shall vest absolutely in Government. Again, by P.O. 137 of 1972 the position was altered and it provided that the existing provision shall be renumbered as sub-section (1) and two new sub-sections were added, namely, subsection (2) which says that sub-section (1) shall apply to all lands before or after 28.6.72 but shall not apply to any land so gained if the right of a malik to hold as increment was finally recognised or declared before the promulgation of P.O. 137 of 1972 i.e. 4.11.72 and sub-section (3) which says that all suits concerning such land shall abate and no such claim can be entertained by Court. The above analysis of the evolution of section 87 shows that in 1965 when the suit was filed such gradual accession was considered as in increment to the holding subject to the limitation that it shall not exceed the limit mentioned in section 90 and which again will not apply in the case of a large scale, co-operative farming etc. When the suit was filed in 1963 E.P. Ordinance No. VIII of 1967 was not on Statute book nor had its any retrospective effect. Therefore the gradual accession or artificial or mechanical process due to development work by WAPDA would not deprive the plaintiff from increment to his holding. The Bengal Regulation XI of 1825 (The Bengal Alluvion and Diluvion Regulation, 1825) noticed that in consequence of the frequent changes which take place in the channel of the principal rivers and the shifting of the sands which lie in the beds of those rivers, chars or small islands are after thrown up by alluvion in the midst of the stream, or near one of the banks and large portion of land are carried away by an encroachment of the river on one side, whilst accessions of lands are at the same time or in subsequent years, by dereliction of the frequent source of contention and affray. The Governor-General in Council promulgated rule "for the general information of individuals as well as for the guidance of Courts of Judicature" and provided when) the land gained by gradual accession from the recess of a river or of the sea "shall be considered a increment to the tenure of the person to whose land or estate, it is thus annexed" and the 4th proviso says that the chars or small and shallow river belong to the proprietor of the indivisibles on the record and the 5th proviso provides that in cases which are no specifically provided for by the rules contained in this Regulation, the Courts of justice in deciding upon such claims and disputes, "shall be guided by the best evidence they may be able to obtain or established by local usage, if there be any applicable to the case, or if not, by general principles of equity and justice." This shows from the very beginning of the Nineteenth century, it was noticed "law and custom of the country had established rule applicable to such cases" and rules were framed under Regulation 11 of 1825 recognizing such increment "to the tenure of the person to whose land or estate it is thus annexed."</u>

18. The plaintiffs case was that he purchase the adjoining land of the original riparian raiyat during the year in 1960-63. The disputed land was reformed after the loop cutting in 1959. The suit was filed in the district of Comilla on 26.10.65. Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act became operative from 10th May, 1963. In this view of the matter the High Court Division correctly observed that the suit land as gained by accession to their adjoining land and the plaintiffs are entitled to a benefit of section 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act prior to the amendment.

19. An argument was built up by the defendant as to the retrospective operation of the P.O. 72 dated 28.6.72 and P.O. 137. This point is covered by our decision in the case of Abdul Mannan and others Vs. Kulada Ranjan Mowali and others reported in 31 D.L.R (AD) 195. In that decision this court considered the full scope of section 87 read with P.O. 72 and 137 of 1972 and it was observed:

For the considerations discussed in connection with the interpretation of section 87 of the Act, we are of the opinion that the provisions of sub-sections (2) and (3) of section 87 of the Act cannot be given any retrospective effect beyond the date of coming into force of Part V of the Act in the area in which diluviated land is situated.

It was explained that the retrospectively of the provision of sub-section (2) of section 87 of the Act cannot therefore be pushed beyond the date of the commencement of Part V of the Act in the area where the accretion in question had taken place and it was further observed:

It is only such accretion as took place after the coming into force of Part V of the Act, to which sub-section (1) read with sub-section (2) of section 87 may apply.

This decision clearly gives the complete answer raised by the defendant appellant and in the given case accretion took place after 1958 and the plaintiff purchased this adjoining land between 1960-63 and Part V came into operation on 10.5.63. Therefore the irresistible conclusion is that the plaintiffs suit is also not hit by the abetment clause nor his right are disturbed by the operation of sub-section (2) because the provision of that sub-section is to be understood prospectively. It is not necessary to detail the reason which have been given in the case of Abdul Mannan and others Vs. Kulada Ranjan Mowali and others exhaustively and that decision fully covers the facts and circumstances of the present case.

20. In the result, therefore, both the appeals are dismissed and the decision of the High Court Division is affirmed. There will be no order as to casts.

End.

case_source: From the judgment and order dated 6.3.91 passed by the High Court Division Dhaka in Writ Petition No. 13 of 1991
full_judgment:
M.H. Rahman, J: This appeal by special leave is directed against the High court division's judgment and order dated 6th March, 1991 passed in writ petition No. 13 of 1991.

2. In that writ petition the appellant challenged the detention of her husband. Abdul Kader Siddique, by an order dated 13th January, 1991, under Section 3(I) (a) of the Special Powers Act, 1974. Her case, in brief, is that for recognition of his contributions in the liberation war the detenu was awarded the second highest gallantry award, Bir Uttam, not awarded to any civilian so far. After the assassination of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman on 15th August, 1975, he left the country and stayed in India. The detenu came back to Bangladesh on 16th December, 1990, and contested to in the parliamentary election. He was arrested in the early morning of 17th January, 1991, from the WAPDA Rest House, Jhenaidah, where he was spending the night before his intended journey to Mujibnagar. When he asked for the reason of his arrest the police officer vaguely hinted at some order of conviction, not known to the detenu. The detenu then wanted to see the warrant of arrest. When the police officer failed to show any warrant the detenu refused to accompany him. Then the impugned order of detention was shown to the detenu where it was alleged that it was necessary to arrest the detenu for public safety and public order. It was asserted that the detenu was not in Bangladesh for quite a long time, and on his return to Bangladesh he did not do any act that can be called prejudicial to the interest of public safety or public order. No ground of detention was served on the detenu till the filing of the writ petition. It was contended that the impugned order was violative of fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 27,28,31, 32 and 33 of the Constitution.

3. In their affidavit-in-opposition the respondents did not controvert the statements made in the writ petition. Their case is that as the order of detention under the Special Powers Act had already been withdrawn the writ petition had become infructuous and that the detenu is now in custody as a convict, serving out a sentence of seven years rigorous imprisonment upon conviction by Special Martial Law Court No. 1 in Tangail P.S. Case No. 15(4) 76 and G.R. No. 385(2)76 under M.L.R. No. 11/9 of the Marital Law Regulations, 1975. The Government filed two memoranda, marked as Annexures 1 & 2 to the Affidavit-in-Opposition. Annexure 1 is an order dated 9th February, 1991, of the Deputy Secretary (Security) of the Ministry of Home Affairs, copy of which was forwarded to the Jail authorities and other functionaries, showing that the detention order had already been rescinded and the detenu would be deemed to serving his sentence as a convict. It was mentioned in Annexure I that the District Magistrate, Jessore, had already taken steps for executing the warrant of commitment issued by the District Magistrate, Tangail. Annexure 2 is a letter dated 31st January, 1991, of the Deputy Inspector General of Prisons, Khulna Division, addressed to the Ministry of Law and Justice, stating that he received the order of detention dated 13th January, 1991, from the Home Ministry for detaining Abdul Kader Siddiqui for 120 days and then on 22nd January, 1991, he received the warrant of commitment dated 19th January, 1991, of the Additional District Magistrate, in brief ADM, in connection with an order of conviction dated 24th July, 1978, passed by the Special Marital Law Court No. 1 and that the order of detention had already been rescinded by an order dated 29th March, 1991, of the Home Ministry and the prisoner is in jail custody serving as a convict.

4. The appellant in her affidavit-in-reply contended that the detention having continued, the writ petition had not become infructuous. Though the detenu is alleged to have been convicted, no judgment and order of conviction of the detenu nor the warrant of the Court (under Section 383 read with Section 389 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) which passed the sentence was produced in court to show that there was any valid basis for detention of the detenu. The appellant reiterated her statements made in the petition as to the manner of the arrest of the detenu. The appellant reiterated her statements made in the petition as to the manner of the arrest of the detenu, and asserted that she was not aware of any Marital Law Case against the detenu or of any conviction in any such case, and that she belived that there was no such case. On an information slip filed by the father of the detenu with the officer-in-charge of the Record Room of Tangail to know what were the papers and documents in support of the entry in the General Register in respect of G.R. Case No. 385(2)76, an information was supplied to the effect that it was not known on what basis the entry was made in the General Register and that there was no valid document in support of the entry.

5. At the time of the hearing the respondents produced, without any affidavit, before the High Court Division, a copy of a warrant of commitment, issued by the ADM. Tangail, address to the Superintendent of Jessore Central Jail.

6. The High Court Division discharged the Rule after finding wrongly that the detenu did not deny the order of conviction; that Annexures-1 and 2 and the warrant of commitment, as public documents, cannot be presumed that those are not correct; that had there been no trial, there would not have arisen any reason for the detenu's father to take information in 1986 from the Police court, though not the custodian of the record, to show that there was no basis for the conviction; that the judgment passed by the Martial Law Court is protected under paragraph 18 in the Fourth Schedule, inserted there by the Constitution (Fifth Amendment) act, 1979, (Act 1 of 1979), and it is still in force under Section 6(a) of the General Clauses Act, 1897, made applicable to the said Proclamations and the marital Law Regulations and Marital Law Orders promulgated during the marital Law period; that under the law the Sessions Judge was to issue the warrant in this case, but the issuance of the warrant by the ADM, Tangail, is a mere irregularity, and this kind of irregularity though not covered under Section 530 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, "will not affect the sentence or its undergoing as it is no where mentioned in the Code of Criminal Procedure or any other law that if any irregular custody warrant is issued by a District Magistrate or Additional District Magistrate instead of Sessions Judge it will be fatal and the convict cannot be kept in custody for undergoing imprisonment."

7. Before we consider the contentions of the respective parties, let us refer to some relevant provisions of the Chief Marital Law Administrator's Proclamation dated 7th April, 1979. By that Proclamation the Marital Law, declared on the 15th August, 1975, was withdrawn and the Third Proclamations of the 20th August, 1975 and 8th November, 1975, and the Third Proclamation of the 29th November, 1976, together with all other Proclamations and orders amending or supplementing them were revoked. For the instant case let us refer to the following saving provisions:

"(b) all Martial Law Regulations and Martial Law Orders made in pursuance of the proclamations. And in force <u>IMMEDIATE</u>ly before the 7th April 1979 the commencing day, shall stand repealed on the commencing day:

(c) every case pending <u>IMMEDIATE</u>ly before the commencing day before a Special Martial Law Court or a Summary Martial Law Court or a Special Martial Law Tribunal constituted under the said Martial Law Regulations shall, on the commencing day, stand transferred to the Criminal Court which would have jurisdiction to try the offence constituted by the facts of the case under the ordinary law and shall be tried by such Criminal Court in accordance with the procedure applicable to the trial of such case under the ordinary law;

………		…………..			……………….

(e) the proceedings of very case tried and disposed of at any time before the commencing day by a Special Martial Law Court or a Special Martial Law Tribunal shall, after the commencing day, be reviewed by the Government, hereinafter referred by the Government, hereinafter referred to as the reviewing authority, as if the said Martial Law Regulations and Marital Law Orders had not been repealed;

(f) the proceedings of very case tried and disposed of at any time before the commencing day by a Summary Martial Law Court shall, after the commencing day, be reviewed by the sessions Judge, hereinafter referred to as the reviewing authority, as if the said Martial Law Regulations and Martial Law Orders had not been repealed;

…………			………….				……..

(j) every sentence of death or transportation for life passed in any case at any time before the commencing day by a Special Martial Law Court or a Special Martial Law Tribunal shall, after the commencing day, be put into execution on the order of the Government under the warrant of the Sessions Judge of the area in which the person under sentence may be found, as if the sentence were passed by him;

(k) every sentence of imprisonment or whipping passed in any case at any time before the commencing day by a Special Martial Law Court or a Special Martial Law Tribunal shall after the commencing day, be put into execution under the warrant of the sessions Judge of the area in which the person under sentence may be found, as if the sentence were passed by him;

(l) every sentence of imprisonment or whipping passed in any case at any time before the commencing day by a Special Martial Law Court shall, after the commencing day, be put into execution under the warrant of the District Magistrate of the area in which the persons under sentence may be found, as if the sentence were passed by him;

(m) every sentence of fine or confiscation of property passed in any case at any time before the commencing day by a Special Martial Law Court or a Summary Martial Law Court or as Special Martial Law Tribunal shall, after the commencing day, be put into exaction under the warrant of the District Magistrate of the area in which the person under sentence ordinarily resides, as if it were a sentence of fine or confiscation of property passed by him;

8. The appellant challenged all the findings of the High Court Division. It is submitted that as the judgment and order of conviction and sentence were not produced for the scrutiny of the court, the High Court Division ought to have held that there was no basis for the conviction; that the warrant of commitment was issued without lawful authority and executed in an unlawful manner, the respondents ought to have been directed to release the detenu.

<u>9. It is further contended that in absence of the order of conviction it could not be ascertained whether it reached finality in review under Paragraph 4(2) of Martial Law Regulations No.1 of 1975 or by the Government after the withdrawal of Martial Law under clause 4 of the Proclamation. The respondents have challenged this new plea, neither raised before the High Court Division nor in the petition for special leave to appeal, nor any leave was granted on that point. A question of fact or a mixed question of fact and law ought to be raised in the High Court Division, the Court of first instance, for a proceeding under Article 102 of the Constitution. An appellant should not ordinarily be allowed to convert this division into a Court of first instance, otherwise the respondents may ask on the ground of surprise for opportunity to controvert the new facts and the proceeding may unnecessarily prolong and, more important, this Division will be deprived of the valued opinion of the High Court Division on the newly disputed point. In this case respondents' failure to produce the conviction will be necessary for examining the sufficiency of the return.</u>

10. The learned counsel for the appellant also challenged the martial Law Regulations and their validation by the Fifth Amendment, and submitted that, at the worst, the Fifth Amendment could only validate a past and closed transaction and not a case like the instant one where the sentence is yet to be executed. After a brief cannonade against the Fifth Amendment the learned counsel dug in and stayed close to the proclamation and directed his missiles against the warrant of commitment and the respondents' failure to produce the order of conviction in court.

<u>11. The respondent's main contention is that the writ who as it appears on the papers of the return is kept in custody in execution of a legal sentence. Reliance is placed on In re: Bonomaly Gupta, DLR 1917 Ca1.723 (723), Janardhan Reddy & others V. The State of Hyderabad & others AIR1995 (SC) 217 and Col. Rr. B. Ramachandra Rao V. The State of Orissa and others, AIR 1971 (SC) 2197. In all these cases the existence of conviction or sentence was not challenged In spite of the Safe's failure to produce some relevant papers in justification of the custody in AIR 1971 (SC) 2197, the Supreme Court refused to grant a writ of habeas corpus because it was the common case of both sides that the petitioner was undergoing trial in three criminal cases.</u>

<u>12. It is contended that in a case of preventive detention the onus is on the detaining authority to satisfy the Court that the detention is in order, but where a prisoner is in custody on the basis of an order of conviction, the onus of the respondent is discharged as soon as the return shows that there is an order of conviction justifying the custody. <u>‘The question whether the provision in a statute are directory or imperative has frequently arisen in the country, but it has been said that no general rule can be laid down and that in every case the object of the statute must be looked at... 26. The history of this provision of our Constitution may be traced back to 1773, when under be Regulating Act,. 1773, the Supreme Court was established at Fort William in the Presidency Town of Calcutta by a Royal Carter and each of the Justices of that Court was given power to issue the English writ of habeas corpus like the Court of King's Bench in England within the local limits of the Court. Two other Supreme Courts were established in tow other Presidency Towns in Madras and Bombay in 1800 and 1823 respectively. By the High Courts Act of 1861 the three Supreme Courts were abolished and they were replace by the High Courts and they continued to exercise the power of issue of prerogative writs within the limits of their original jurisdiction but not upon mofussil Courts or Tribunals or to persons outside the limits of three Presidency towns.

<u>27. Norman J. in Ammer Khan (1870) 6 Beng. L.R 459 held to the effect that the Supreme Court in India had power to issue the common law writ of habeas corpus into the mufassil an that power was inherited by the High Courts also. By Section 81 the Criminal Procedure Code (Act X of 1872) the Presidency High Courts were given the right to issue Wirt of habeas corpus in the case of detention of European British subject both within and outside their original jurisdiction, but by section 82 of that Act the power to issue the writ of habeas corpus beyond the Presidency Towns was taken away. Section 148 of the High Court Criminal Procedure Act (X of 1875) gave the Presidency High Courts power issue directions in the nature of habeas corpus on certain conditions. The above two Acts of 172 and 1875 were repealed by the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1882. Section 491 of the new Act Made provision for issuing directions in the nature of habeas corpus, but the power was to be exercised within the limits of the ordinary original civil jurisdiction of the High Court. The Criminal Procedure Code of 1882 was repealed by the Code of 1898 but the latter reproduced section 491 of the earlier Code. The Criminal Law Amendment Act of 1923 amended section 491 of the Code of 1898and conferred the power to issue the writ of habeas corpus on each of the superior courts of the various provinces within their Appellate Criminal Jurisdiction. In C.P. Mathen V. District Magistrate. Trivandrum AIR 1939 (PC) 213 it was held that in consequence of the laws passed on the authority given under the High Court Act of 1861 "the Legislature had taken away the power to issue the prerogative writ of habeas corpus in matters contemplated by section 491 Cr.P.C." Section 491 laws providing for preventive detention.</u>

28. In 1954 adding section 233A to the Government of India Act, 1935, which remained the Constitution of Pakistan until 1935, the High Courts were given powers to issue some writs including that of habeas corpus, By Article 170 of Constitution of 1956 those powers were continued. Notwithstanding the abrogation of that Constitution on 7th October, 1958, the power of the High Court to issue the writs including that of habeas corpus continued under the laws (Continuance in Force) Order, 1958, except that no writ could be issued against the Chief Administrator of Martial Law, or the Deputy Chief Administrator of Martial Law or any person exercising powers or jurisdiction under the authority of either. The Constitution of 1962 came into operation on the 8th June, 1962. By virtue of sub-clause (b) (i) of clause (2) of Article 98 thereof the High Court empowered on the application of any person to make an order "direction that a person in custody in the province be brought before the High Court so that the Curt may satisfy itself that he is not being held in custody without lawful authority or in an abrogation that Constitution of 1962 on 25th March, 1969, all Courts were allowed to continue and exercise all their powers and jurisdiction which they would have exercised had the Constitution not been abrogated under Article 5 of the Proclamation of Martial Law.

After the Proclamation of Independence of Bangladesh on the 10th day of April 1971, by the Laws Continuance Enforcement Order of that date, it was provided that all laws that were in force in Bangladesh on the 25th March, 1971, were to continue to be in force with such consequential changes as may be necessary on account of the creation of the Independent State, On 11th January, 1972, under the Provisional Constitution of Bangladesh Order 1972, the High Court of Bangladesh was set up. From the 17th January 1972, till 16th day of December , 1972, when the present Constitution came into force, the High Court's power to issue writ of habeas corpus remained suspended by virtue of the High Court of Bangladesh Order 1972 (P.O. No. 5 of 1972) as amended by P.O No. 91 of 1972.Under Article 102 of the Constitution of Bangladesh the High Court Division is given the power to make a direction in the nature of habeas corpus in terms similar to those in Article 98 of the Constitution of 1962. In spite of the is not very heartening history of the writ of habeas corpus, the sapling that was brought in 1773 from a different clime and a different country has survived. The writ of habeas corpus has grown into a solid tree in Bangladesh and it has withstood quite a few nasty non-western. Despite a series of set backs in constitutionalism and frequent suspension of fundamental rights since 1947 (or because of that ?), the Superior Courts in our country have successfully evolved a revise system for protecting the blessings of liberty that have been enshrined in Articles 31 and 32 for our Constitution.

<u>31. <u>32. In Abdul Hannan's case H. Rahman J, observed:</u>

<u>"It is true that in a general sense such a writ may issue to test the validity of any detention whether by the Executive or by a private person or by any other authority exercising judicial or quasi-judicial powers, but it appease to us that in such proceedings the answer to the writ is usually considered to be sufficient if a valid commitment order is produced by the detaining authority and, where a person has been convicted by a Criminal court, ex facie the is such a valid order for the detention of the person concerned. Therefore, in cases where this writ is taken out to challenge the validity of a conviction by a Criminal Court, its scope is somewhat restricted and it may be said that is such cases the Court will only interfere by a writ of this nature, if it clearly appears to it on the record itself or on the face of the commitment order that the act for which the person concerned is committed is no crime or if it is a crime, he has been committed for it by a person who has no jurisdiction so to commit him or if the sentence imposed upon him is in excess of that prescribed by law" (283)</u>

<u>"A definite meaning had, therefore, to be given to each to them ... In my view the words "in an unlawful manner" in sub-clause (b) of Article 98 (2) have been used deliberately to give meaning and content to the solemn declaration under Article 2 of the Constitution itself that it is the inalienable right of very citizen to be treated in accordance with law and only in accordance with aw. To my mind therefore, in determining as to how and in what circumstances a detention would be detention in an unlawful manner one would inevitably have first to see whether the action is in accordance with law, if not, then it is action in an unlawful manner. Law is here not confined to statute law alone but is used in its generic sense as connoting all that is treated as law in this country including even the judicial principles laid down from time to time by the Superior Courts. It means according to the accepted form of legal process and postulates a strict performance of all the functions and duties laid down by law. It may well be, as has been surfeited in some quarters, that in this sense it is as comprehensive as the American "due process" clause in a new garb. <u>38. In view of the wider jurisdictional approach this Court has taken in the aforementioned cases the decisions of foreign jurisdictions may not be always helpful to us. We may, however, benefit from some well know earlier decisions for their persuasive value and assurance.</u>

<u>39. The Bushell's Case (1670) Vaughan 135, is probably the earliest case of the broadest review power a Court claimed in a habeas corpus mater. Finding the return insufficient, Vaughan C.J discharged a juryman committed for contempt of Court by the London Court of sessions with the following observation:</u>

<u>"The Court hath no knowledge by this return, whether the evidence given were full and manifest, or doubtful, lame ,and dark, or indeed evidence at all material to the issue, because it in not returned what evidence in particular, and as it was delivered, was give. For, it is not exposed to a man's judgment. But here the evidence given to the jury is not exposed al all to the court, but the judgment of the Court of Sessions upon that evidence is only exposed to us who tell us it was full and manifest. But our judgment ought to be grounded upon our own inferences and understanding, and not upon theirs." (Vaughan 135 at 137).</u>

<u>40. What would suffice as a sufficient cause cannot be defined with precision and it will vary the from case to case, In its jurisdictional approach the Court may enquire into the sufficiency of the return. In repelling a view that at common law habeas corpus was available only to inquire into the jurisdiction, in a narrow sense, of the Committing Court, Brennan J. in Fay V. Noia 372 US 391, relied on the Bushell's case and quoted the following: "[When a man is brought by habeas Corpus to the Court, that he was against Law imprisoned and detained  he shall never be by the Act of the Court remanded to his unlawful imprisonment, for then the Court should do an 'act of injustice in imprisoning' him, de novo, against Law, whereas the great Charter is, Qucid nullsu libet homo imprisnetur nisi per legem terrace. This is the present case, and this was the case upon all the Presidents (precedents) produced and many more that might be produced, where upon Habeas Corpus, may have been discharged.... "This appears plainly by many old Books, if the reason of them be rightly taken. For insufficient causes are as no causes returned seems unworthy of a Court." Vaughan, at 156 124 Eng Rep, at 1016 9 Howell's State Trials, at 1023.</u>

41. Let us now examine the sufficiency of the respondents' return. It is true that a presumption is attached to Annexure-1 and 2, the respondents' two official papers, that they were regularly made, but in no sense they can prove the conviction challenged in this ease. Court Division without any affirmed statement by the ADM or any other person competent to affirm on his behalf as to the manner of its issuance. With regard to the post-trial papers, the Magistrate's General Registrar of cases cognizable by the police and the Registrar of cases committed to sessions show some nothings as to the conviction but there is no back-up affirmed statement as to the custody and genuineness of the papers Minutes before we announced the decision on 18th August, 1991, the day fixed for that, the respondents produced before us he registrar of Warrant of imprisonment, and a copy of an application dated 19th January, 1991, of the Officer-in-Charge of Tangail Police Station before the District Magistrate for the issuance of the warrant. Without the order of conviction at hand the respondents are scouring for paper till he last minute and trying to stage Shakespeare's Hamlet without the Prince 01 Denmark.

<u>43. Defect in a warrant for committal may be ignored when it is issued by the sentencing court itself or where it is issued by a subordinate court after the sentence is passed or affirmed by the appellate court or the records disclose no infirmity in the order of conviction. But where the order of conviction is not made available to the court, with no explanation or excuse for not doing so, a lot of question would then remain unanswered.</u>

<u>44. In the King V. Governor of Lewes Prison ex-parte Doyle [1917] 2 K.B. 254 (269). Viscount Reading C.J. observed:</u>

<u>Even though we had come to the conclusion that the warrant of commitment was had on the face of it, as this is a case of commitment after conviction we arc again not only entitled but bound to look at the conviction in order to see whether there is more than a mere technical defect in the commitment. Upon behalf to the applicant is has been strenuously contended that we are dealing with been strenuously contended that we are dealing with the liberty of the subject, but we are also administering law and justice, and we have to see whether or not there is any ground for alleging that the applicant has not been properly convicted and committed. Rex V. Hawkins, Fortes cue, 272. Vol. II 1971 and Rex V. Taylor 7 Dow & Ry. 622 are authorities which abundantly support the proposition that in considering the validity of the committal, the conviction must be looked. It is clear that the court in Rex V. Taylor though that they ought to look at the conviction, and if they came to the conclusion that there was a defect in the commitment but none in the conviction they would not grant a writ of habeas corpus."</u>

45. In this case the best evidence, the order of conviction and sentence or its certified copy, has not been produced. No explanation has been given for this. No case is also made out for the production of papers that have been produced at different stages as secondary evidence. It is no knowing whether the case record, the judgment and order of conviction of sentence are misplaced, lost or spirited away.

<u>46. It is idle to speculate whether on the basis of the papers that are filed before us the Sessions Judge could have issued the warrant or he would have asked for the records of the case and the judgment to see whether it reached finality on review or whether the sentence is still executable not being already remitted under section 401 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The fact remains that the order of conviction was not before the ADM, otherwise it could have been produced before the High Court or before this Court.</u>

47. Had the ADM read relevant law, law could he issue the warrant? He would not have issued the warrant because he had clearly no jurisdiction in the matter. He could have issued it if he decided to act without applying his mind at all. In this case the ADM has exactly done that. This is an instance, if one is needed at all, for the justification of separation of judiciary from the executive. Due to exigencies of situations an executive officer may act expeditiously and take expedient measures. This matter exemplifies that the judicial work is too serious a matter to be left safely in the hands of executive officers who, in spite of their best of intentions, because of their involvement in multifarious works, may not have time to apply their mind properly. If the ADM acted, at the behest of the administrating, as alleged by the appellant, then no fault can be found for that. The administration is entitled to get the sentence against the detenu executed in accordance with law. But from the uncontroversial statements of the appellant is the writ petition it appears the order of detention was used as stopgap arrangement for taking the detenu into custody; and after the filing of the appellant writ petition that order was rescinded on 09.0.91 and the warrant of commitment was issued by the ADM to prevent the prisoner to come out of the jail, in case the respondents are asked by the Court to release him forthwith. The issuance of the warrant by the ADM was dehors the Proclamation dated 7th April, 1979. And it was malafide because the ADM had no reasonable ground for believing that the Proclamation justified him in what he did.

48. It will not be inappropriate to view this matter as if a fugitive from justice is challenging his conviction after a lapse of time by a joyride on a writ proceeding. The detenu went on exile after the assassination of President Sheikh Mujibur Rahman in August, 1975. He is alleged to have been tried in absentia along with his brother for alleged misappropriation of moneys of a Co-operative Society by the Special Martial Law Court in 1978. When an accused is tried in absentia, not an ordinary norm, though now sanctioned by law in our country, the functionaries in charge of the administration of justice should take care to maintain and preserve the records till the convict is apprehended and the sentence is executed in accordance with law.

<u>49. From the above, the respondents' return appears insufficient even for the preliminary scrutiny of the High Court Division, not to speak of a broader review whether the court that had passed the conviction was properly constituted and it had the appropriate jurisdiction, and that court followed the relevant procedure, and that the order was not passed malafide. In view of the bad commitment order, not issued by a proper authority, and the respondent; authority, and the respondent's return, being both insufficient and unsatisfactory, I hold that the appellant's husband is being held custody without lawful authority and in an unlawful manner. The judgment of the High Court Division is set aside, the appeal is allowed. No cost. Let the appellant's husband, Abdul Kader Siddiqui, be release forthwith if not wanted in connection with any other matter.</u>

A.T.M Afzal, J: It is not may purpose to add to the erudition of may learned brother M.H. Rahman, J.; even so, J wish to add few lines in order to highlight the requirement of a proper warrant of commitment for the custody of a person alleged to be convicted on a criminal trial, the' absence of which has been decisive in this ease.

51. Admittedly the detention order dated 13.1.91 passed under section 3(1)(a) of the Special Powers Act, 1974, under which the detenu was arrested on 17.1.91, was revoked on 9.2.91 and the respondent Government in its affidavit-in-opposition dated 20.2.91 disclosed that the detenu was being held in Jail. Custody to serve out his sentence of 7(seven) Years rigorous imprisonment upon conviction in Tangail P.S case No. 15(4)76 and G.R Case No. 385(2)76 under Regulation 11/9 MLR/75. The learned Additional Attorney-General Produced the warrant o commitment 'dated 19.1.91 issued by the Additional District Magistrate, Tangail, and addressed to the Superintendent, Jessore Jail, before the High Court Division as also before us (included in the additional paper Book) which shows that the detenu was convicted by the Special Martial Law Court No. 1, Gana Bhaban , <u>Dhaka</u>, on 24.7.78 under the aforesaid Regulations and sentence of to R.I. for 7 years and a fine of Tk.3 (three) lacs, in default, to R.I for 3(three) years more. Therefore, the basis of the custody of the detenu now was this warrant of commitment which speaks: of and is evidence of an order of conviction, against the detenu. The High Court Division found that it cannot be said that the detenu is being held in custody without lawful authority and in reaching this conclusion it reasoned thus.

52. In the instant case the sentence was passed by the Special Martial Law Court and so under the law the Sessions Judge was to issue the warrant but the Additional District Magistrate, Tangail, instead of Sessions Judge, issued the same. It is, therefore, an irregularity no doubt but it will not affect the sentence or its undergoing as it is now-here mentioned in the Code of Criminal Procedure or any other law that if any irregular custody warrant is issued by a District Magistrate or Additional district Magistrate instead of a Sessions Judge, it will be fatal and the convict cannot be kept in custody for undergoing imprisonment.

53. It must be said with respect that the High Court Division fell in grave error in construing the "regularity" of the warrant of commitment on the basis of the "code of Criminal Procedure or any other law" while exercising, jurisdiction under Article 102 of the constitution which by Sub-Article (2) (b) (i) provides that the High Court Division on the application of any person may make an order-

"(i) Directing that a person in custody be brought before it so that it may satisfy itself that he is not being held in custody without lawful authority or in an unlawful manner."

The inquiry, therefore, in a case as in the present should be directed to see whether to person is being held in custody without lawful authority or in an unlawful manner. Now what is meant by the phraseology, "without lawful authority" and "in an unlawful manner" (same as occurring is Article98 (2)(b)(i) of the Constitution of 1962) has been acidly explained by Hamoodur Rahman, J. in the celebrated decision, Government of West Pakistan Vs. Begum Agha Shorish Kashmiri 21 D.L.R (SC) 1. In dealing with a case of custody, be it punitive, the exposition of law as made in that case should always be taken as an effulgent guide. The relevant portion of the decision reads thus:

"It is agreed that within "lawful authority" will be comprised a questions of virus of the statue itself as also of the person or persons action under the statute, i.e., there must be a competent law authorizing the detention and the officer issuing such an order must have been lawfully vested with the power.....

In my view the words "in an unlawful Manner: is sub-clause (b) of Article 98(2) have been used deliberately to give meaning and content to the solemn declaration under Article 2 of the Constitution itself that it is the inalienable right of very citizen to be treated in accordance with law and only in accordance with law (which corresponds to Article 31 of our resent Constitution). To my mind, therefore, in determining as to how and in what circumstances a detention would be detention in an unlawful manner, one would inevitable have first to see whether the action is in accordance with law, if not, then it is action in to statute law alone but is used in its genetic sense as connoting all that is treated as judicial principles laid down frame time to time by the superior court.."

54. What is the law in the present case which has authorized the custody of the detenu? Is the officer issuing the custody warrant lawfully vested with the power? Has the warrant been issued in according with law? These are the questions which must be answered for determining whether the detenu was being held or not without lawful authority or in an unlawful manner.

55. The general law as to execution of sentence passed in a trial is to be found in Chapter XXVIII of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898. Section 383 provides that when the accused is sentenced to transportation or imprisonment or the court passing the sentence shall forthwith forward a warrant to the Jail in which he is, or is to be confined... Section 389 provides that every warrant for the execution of any sentence may be issued either by the Judge or Magistrate who passed the sentence or by his successor in office. In execution of a sentence, emphasis has been given to the court which passes the sentence and for obvious reasons, because the records of the case are in that court which provide the basis for execution and further the executed warrant, makes the said record complete, section 400 CrlPC provides thus:

400.-When a sentence has been fully executed, the officer executing it shall return the warrant to the Court from which is issued, with an endorsement under his hand certifying the manner in which the sentence executed.

The General Rules and Circular Orders of the High Court (Criminal) Vol.1 in Chapter III under the heading "Records" provide that Records of Courts of Season shall consist of two files, to be styled and marked respectively, File A and File B. File A shall contain the following papers which shall be arranged in the following order:-

1.	…………………………………………………………………………………………..

2.	…………………………………………………………………………………………

18. Warrant returned after execution by the Jail authorities. Similar provision is there in respect of Magistrate's Records.

56. As to preservation and destruction of records it is provided, inter alia, in the said Rules and Orders, that the record of any case in which the sentence has not expired and the record of any case in which any of the accused or parties proceeded against has not been apprehended shall not be liable to destruction.

57. In a case, therefore where, the warrant of commitment is issued by the court which passed the sentence, the said warrant will be ordinarily treated as a sufficient return is a proceeding of the nature of habeas corpus. It is in this sense that an a long line of cases relating to the habeas corpus writs, it has been held that when the return states that the party who is alleged to be unlawfully detained, is detained in execution of sentence on indictment on a criminal charge, the return cannot be controverter. As to whether Jurisdiction of the curt passing the sentence can be gone into it has been held in AIR (38)1951 S.C 217, Janardhan Reddy Vs. State of Hyderabad, that the trend of decisions seems to be in favour of the view that if it should appear on the face to the return that a person is in detention in execution of a sentence on indictment on a criminal charge, that would be a sufficient answer to an application for a writ of habeas corpus. In the case of B.R Rao Vs. State of Orissa, AIR 1971 (SC)197, the principle is reiterated that such writ (of habeas corpus) is not granted where a person is committed to Jail custody by a competent court by an order which prima facie does not appear to be without jurisdiction or wholly illegal. These decisions were referred to and relied upon by the learned Additional Attorney General in support of his contention that in the face of the warrant of commitment showing that the detenu was serving a sentence on conviction , there remains nothing for further inquiry. He also referred to an old case, Bonomally Gupta, ILR 1917 (Vol. 54 ) Calcutta 723, where Chaudhuri, J, sitting in a Special Bench observed that it is well established that a writ of habeas corpus in not granted to persons convicted or in execution under legal process, including persons, in execution of a legal sentence after conviction on indictment in the usual course.

<u>58. It is not necessary to well upon the scope of enquiry under Article 102 of the Constitution and that under the old prerogative writ of habeas corpus upon which the Indian decisions are base. The law declared in 21 D.L.R (SC) (Supra) is followed in this country which says that by the words used in Article in 98 (present Article 102) the Constitution makers advisedly left it to the High Court to review the actions of the detailing authority, untrammeled by the formalities or technicalities of either section 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure or the old prerogative writ of habeas corpus not only with regard to the issues of the law or the officer concerned but also enjoined upon them to satisfy themselves that the detention is not in any manner contrary to law. Although this decision was given in a case of preventive detention, but the principles are applicable in the case of custody by a public authority in any manner. The appellant's argument, inter alia, was that in order to justify the custody of the appellant the respondents must produce the judgment of the Martial Law Court so that the High Court Division can satisfy itself as to the jurisdiction of that court recording the conviction. In my opinion, the respondents must, at least, satisfy the court that the warrant of commitment was validly issued by a proper authority. It will be seen that in the Indian decisions cited by the learned Additional Attorney General, no question was raised as in the present case as to the warrant of commitment upon which the persons concerned were in custody. That instrument is peon to a variety of criticisms in this case which will be examined now.</u>

59. The detenu was allegedly convicted by a Special Martial Law Court on 24.7.78 in absentia under the martial Law Regulations 1975 (Regulations No.1 of 1975). The said Regulations, by Regulation No.8 therein, made the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure applicable to the proceedings of Martial Law Courts and Tribunals. Therefore, it was for the Special Martial Law Court connected which ought to have issued the warrant of commitment for the custody of the detenu. That Martial Law Court ceased to exist with the repeal of all Martial law regulations by the Proclamation of the 7th April, 1979, by which Martial law itself (declared on the 15th August, 1975) stood withdrawn. All Proclamations, Martial Law Regulations etc. have been ratified and confirmed by the Constitution (Fifth Amendment) Act, 1979 (Act No.1 of 1979). The Proclamation of the 7th April, 1979 provided, inter alia, that:

k) every sentence of imprisonment or whipping passed in any case at any time before the commencing day by Special Martial Law Court or a Special Martial Law Tribunal shall, after the commencing day, be put into execution under the warrant of the sessions Judge of the area in which the person under sentence may be found, as if the sentence was passed by him;

i) every sentence of imprisonment or whipping passed in any case at any time before the commencing day by a Summary Martial Law Court shall, after the commencing day, be put into execution under the warrant of the District Magistrate of the area in which the person under sentence may be found as if the sentence were passed him;
