61. In the present case the trial was held in <u>Dhaka</u> and so the records of the case ought to be in the Record Room of the District and Sessions Judge, <u>Dhaka</u>. Admittedly, the detenu returned to Bangladesh on 16th December, 1990, and was found in the area of the Sessions Judge, <u>Dhaka</u>. Therefore, in terms of para (K) of the Proclamation to the 7th April, 1979, the warrant of commitment should have been issued by the Sessions Judge, <u>Dhaka</u>. In the scheme to the general law to the land as indicated above as also in keeping with the special provisions made prior to and in the proclamation to the 7th April 1979, the Court in possession of the records of the Martial Law Court and in whose Jurisdiction the accused is found is the only authority which can validly issue the warrant of commitment. The same, however, having been issued but the Additional District Magistrate, Tangail, it must be said that it was not from the proper authority and further the action was not taken in accordance with law. The learned Additional Attorney-General argued that the warrant issued by the Additional District Magistrate may be irregular but cannot be said to be without jurisdiction. He submitted that the requirement of the Sessions Judge issuing the warrant is only directory and not mandatory and, therefore, the warrant in the present case cannot be said to be wholly invalid.

62. I feel no hesitation in rejecting the submission to the learned Additional Attorney-General in view of the clear legal provisions as referred to above. When the law says that A shall do a particular thing, it confers a power on A, and if B does it, it will be without lawful authority unless saved by the law itself. But for the provisions made in the proclamation referred to above, the sentence passed by the Martial Law it was a special enactment making special provisions relating to execution of sentence passed by defunct Martial Law Courts and Tribunals. It must be followed strictly and the rule to be applied in such as case is what the Privy Council said in the case of Nazir Ahmed Vs. King Emperor; Air 1936 P.C. 253 that where a power is given to do ascertain thing is a certain way the thing to do ascertain thing in a certain way the thing must be done in that way or not at all. The rational for investing the Sessions Judge with the power to issue warrant is not far to seek; the records of the Special Martial Law Courts have been consigned to his court and the alone can order execution of any sentence on the basis of the said records.

<u>63. It is not understood what prevented the Government from getting the necessary warrant issued form the Sessions Judge concerned if there was really an order of conviction passed against the detenu as alleged. The detenu was already in custody under the Special Powers Act and so there was enough time to get a proper warrant from the proper person. Instead of doing the right thing in right way, the Government merely substituted its own order authorizing detention by another order of commitment passed by one of its inferior officers, That officer had neither the authority nor the necessary records of the case before him. The issuance of the warrant, therefore, to say the least, does not seem to be above board. The allegation made by the appellant that it was a mere command performance by the said officer cannot be ignored altogether. In any view of the matter, the fact remains that the detenu has not been treated in accordance with law which, the constitution says, is his inalienable right. The sum total of the argument of the learned Additional Attorney General has been that there might not have been an absolutely correct warrant of commitment, but then, what does it matter for a person who has to suffer imprisonment upon conviction by a court anyway. The answer is that a warrant form the Sessions Judge was the minimum which the Government was required to produce by way of return to the Rule Nisi for the satisfaction of the Court that there was in fact an order of conviction against the detenu, That having not been done, it cannot be said that the detenu is being held with lawful authority and in lawful authority and in a lawful manner.</u>

Mustafa Kamal, J: I find very little to add to the exhaustive and lucid exposition of the issues by my learned brothers M.H. Rahman and A.T.M Afzal, JJ. Except to say a few words by way of projecting my own way of looking at the issues

65. My own view is the basic issue in this case in how the legacy of Martial Law can survive when the Constitution is revived.

66. The detenu Abdul Kader Siddique was not convicted and sentenced by any ordinary Court of law under any ordinary criminal offence. He was allegedly convicted and sentenced by a Special Martial Law Court under Regulation No. 11/9 of the Martial Law regulation, 1975 (regulation No.1 of 1975).

67. After proclamation of Martial Law on the 15th August, 1975, several types of Martial Law Courts were constituted by the aforesaid Martial Law Regulation, 1975, promulgated on 22.8.75.

68. A Special Martial Law Court was to consist of a Chairman and two other Members and a summary Martial Law Court was to consist of only one member. The Chairman of a Special Martial Law Court was to be appointed from among the sessions Judges or Officers of the Defence Services or Bangladesh or Rifles not below the rank of lieutenant Colonel or equivalent, and of the two the Members of such Court, one was to he appointed form Assistant Sessions Judges or officers of the defence Services or Bangladesh Rifles not below the rank of Major or equivalent and the other from among Magistrates to the Class.

69. The Member of a Summary Martial Law Court was to the appointed from among Magistrates of the first class or officers of the Defense Services not below the rank of Major or equivalent.

70. The Martial Law regulations 1975, therefore, it prescribed, recognized and maintained a perceptible difference in the status composition and powers of the Special Martial Law Courts and the Summary Martial Law Cowls, All Martial Law Courts. Special or Summary, could try any offence punishable under other law, but whereas a Special Martial Law Court could pass any sentence authorized by the authorized by the Marital Law Regulation or Order for the punishment of the offence tried by it, a Summary Martial Law Court could not pass a sentence of death, transportation or imprisonment for a tern exceeding 5 years.

71. Proclamation of Martial Law, creation of Martial Law offences and trial thereof by Martial Law Courts are not provided in the Constitution of Bangladesh. These are extra-constitutional measures outside of the scheme of our Constitution. As such, when Martial law it becomes necessary for Martial Law Authorities (a) to revoke the A Martial Law Proclamations, (b) to repeal all Martial Law Regulations and Orders with provisions consequential and incidental there to and (c) to make provisions in the Constitution itself for ratification and confirmation of its tenure and actions. This periodic exercise is a habitual feature of our short but eventful constitutional history. Martial Law goes but its actions are ratified and the remnants of martial law are grafted into the constitutional system.

72. Therefore, the Proclamation of Martial Law, Martial Law offences and Martial Law Courts die a natural Law offences and Martial Law Courts die a natural death when the Martial Law is revoked, but its legacies and fallouts continue to the extent and in the manner expressly provided by the saving clauses repealing Martial law regulations and orders.

73. It is in this light that I view the Proclamation, dated 7th April, 1979, revoking the Proclamations of the 20th August, 1975, 8m November, 1975 and 29th November, 1976 and repealing al Martial Law Regulations and orders and making provisions consequential and incidental there to, Cause (k) of the said Proclamation provides that every sentence of imprisonment or whipping passed in any case at any time before the commencing day (i.e. 8 P. Mon the 6th April, 1979) by a Special Martial Law Court shall, after the commencing day, by put into execution under the warrant of the Sessions Judge of the area in which the person under sentence will be found, as if the sentence were passed by him.

74. My learned brother A.T.M. Afzal. J. has diligently unearthed a copy of the instructions from the office of the Chief Marital Law Administrator dated 28th March, i.e. barely 10 days before the revocation of Marital Law, directing that the records of Special Marital law Court shall be kept in the record room of the District and Sessions Judge of the area where the trial was held. This direction was given not without any reason, because Special Marital law Courts were presided over either by a Sessions Judge or by an officer of the Defence. Services or Bangladesh Rifles not below the rank of Lieutenant Colonel or equivalent. The hollowness of the submission of the learned Additional Attorney-General that the requirement of a warrant of commitment from the Sessions Judge is a mere directory provision is obvious from the scheme of operation of the Marital Law Courts and of their demise.

75. Similarly, unexecuted sentence of imprisonment or whipping passed by a Summary Martial Law Court (which was presided over by either Magistrates of the Class or Officers of the Defence Services not blow the rank of Major or equivalent) could be put into execution under the warrant of the District Magistrate of the area in which the person under sentence may be found, as if the sentence were passed by him. For the same reason the records of Summary Martial Law Courts were consigned to the record room of the District Magistrate of the area where the trial was held.

<u>76. Proclamation of the 7th April, 1979, was both a repealing and saving legislation. Unexecuted sentences of Special Martial Law Court Can be executed only in the manner and by the authority prescribed in the saving clauses. The question of these clauses being directory or mandatory does not arise at all. The remains of Martial Law are either saved by following the saving clauses in full or they are not saved at all. The regular Constitution of the country will admit of a Martial Law hangover only by the express words of the saving clauses. The detenu was allegedly convicted and sentenced by a Special Martial Law Court. The sentence remained unexecuted for 14 years. If the sentence is to be e3xceuted now, it can only be exe3cuted by the authority and in the manner prescribed by the saving clauses and by no other authority and in no other manner whosoever.</u>

77. The saving clauses (k) and (I) of the Proclamation dated 7th April, 1979, also provide that the unexecuted sentence may be put into execution under the warrant of the Sessions Judge or of the District Magistrate as the case may be "as if the sentence were passed by him." These words are not without significance. Section 400 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is as follows:-

"400. Return of warrant on execution of sentence.-When a sentence has been fully executed, the officer executing it shall return the warrant to the Court form which is issued, with an endorsement under his hand certifying the manner in which the sentence has been executed."

78. If the detenu was kept in custody on receipt of a warrant of commitment from Sessions Judge of the area in which he was found, then the sentence would have been regarded as a sentence passed by the Sessions Judge and when the sentence would be fully executed, the warrant would be returned to the Court from which it was issued with an endorsement under the hand of the executing officer certifying the manner in which the sentence had been executed. A warrant of commitment issued by an Additional District Magistrate does not make the sentence as if it was passed by the Sessions Judge of the area in which the person under sentence was found. By a legal fiction the sentence is to be converted from a sentence passed by a Special Martial Law Court to a sentence passed by the Sessions Judge and this exercise in legal fiction is necessary for purposes of return of warrant of execution of sentence.

<u>79. Also, under section 401 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the Government may suspend the execution of a sentence or remit the whole or any part of the punishment to which an accused has been sentenced. Whenever an application is made to the Government for the suspension or remission of a sentence, the Government may require the presiding Judge of the Court before or by which the conviction was heard or confirm to state his opinion as to whether the application should be granted or refused, together with his reasons for such opinion and also to forward with the statement of the opinion a certified copy of the record trial or of such record thereof as exist. By resorting to a legal fiction, making the unexecuted sentence passed by a Special Martial Law Court as a sentence passed by a Sessions Judge and by consigning records of Special Martial Law Courts to the record room of the Session Judge, the door has been kept open for exercise by the government of its power of suspension and remission of sentence. The warrant of commitment must, therefore, be issued by the Sessions Judge, so as to make the sentence as if it were passed by him.</u>

80. The warrant of commitment issued by the Additional District Magistrate was still-born and was doomed to perish from the start.

Latifur Rahman, J: While agreeing with the judgment of by brother M.H. Rahman, J.I want to add a few words of my own in support of his judgment.

82. The facts of the case having been elaborately dealt with in the main judgment, I need not repeat the same, In Writ Petition No.136 of 1991, which is in the nature of habeas corpus petition, the initial detention of the detenu Mr. Abdul Kader Siddique was challenged calling in question his detention under Section 3(1)(a) of the Special Powers Act. During the tendency of the said writ petition, the government revoked the said order of detention and by filling an affidavit-in-opposition submitted that the detenu is kept in custody by virtue of warrant of commitment on a sentence of imprisonment issued by the Additional District Magistrates, Tangail, to serve the sentence of 7 years' imprisonment in a case in which the detenu was found guilty under Regulation No.11/9 of Martial Law Regulation 1975, by the Special Martial Law Court No. 1, <u>Dhaka</u>, on 27.4.78. The Government submitted that the detenu is detained in custody to seven out his sentence as awarded by the Special Martial Law Court.

83. The primary question for consideration in this appeal before us is, whether the detenu is being held in custody in an unlawful manner or without lawful authority. Mr. Amirul Islam, learned Counsel appearing for the detenu, has made various arguments on the constitutionality of the 5th Amendment and with regard to the legality of the sentence as passed by Special Martial Law Court on 24.7.78. We have heard the learned counsel at length on various aspects both on law and fact. I consider it unnecessary to decide the constitutional point raised in the proceeding and that narrows the matter down to the only question whether the detenu is held in custody in an unlawful manner or without lawful authority as contemplated under Article 102(1)(b)(i) of the Constitution.

84. At the outset I must say, that the challenge to the legality of the sentence as passed by the Special Martial Law Court and as argued by the learned Counsel cannot be accepted. The judgment and order as passed in the Special Martial Law Court No. 1, <u>Dhaka</u> on 27.4.78 could not be traced out till today. But some documents have been filed before us in the Additional Paper Book, such as, the F.I.R., charge-sheet, Gazette Notification while trying the detenu in absentia, extracts from the Magistrate's General Register of case cognizable by police, Register of cases committed to sessions and warrant of commitment of sentence of imprisonment signed by Additional District Magistrate, Tangail on 19.1.91. All these documents filed before us in the Additional paper Book unmistakably show that there was a trial and ultimately judgment was delivered on 24.7.78. Thus, I for myself do not like to go into the question of the legality of the sentence of the Special Martial Law Court when only the judgment is not available after long lapse of 13/14 years and when Special Martial Law Court is evidently not a Court of Record.

85. In this proceeding, primarily we are to see whether the liberty of a citizen has been rightly curtailed in a lawful manner and with lawful authority under the constitutional mandate.

86. The Martial Law which was imposed on the 15th August, 1975 was withdrawn h) the Proclamation of 7th April. 1979, and the said proclamation of withdrawal revoked and repealed all Martial Law Regulations and Martial Law Orders and the said proclamation made provision consequential and incidental thereto with regard to pending cases, review, execution of various sentences and investigation of offences. The said proclamation of withdrawal in sub-paragraph ‘K’ reads as follows:-

"(K)". every sentence of imprisonment or whipping passed in any case at any time before the commencing day by a Special Martial Law Court or a Special Martial Law Tribunal Shall, after the commencing day, be put into execution under the warrant of the Sessions Judge of the area in which the person under sentence may be found, as if the sentence were passed by him."

87. Thus, the law provides that the execution of the sentence in Special Martial Law Court be put into execution under the warrant of the Sessions Judge of the area in which the person under sentence may be found. In the present case the warrant of commitment of sentence was not passed by the Sessions Judge within whose area the detenu was found as contemplated under the proclamation of 7th April, 1979. Under the proclamation of withdrawal, it is the Sessions Judge who is alone lawfully competent to issue the warrant of commitment in the present case.

88. Article 102(1)(b)(i) of the Constitution imposes an obligation on the High Court Division to "satisfy self that the detenu is not being held in custody without lawful authority and in an unlawful manner." Article 98 of the Constitution of 1962 has also been worded in the above terms. Hameodoor Rahman. J. in the case of West Pakistan Vs. Begum Agha Abdul Karim Kashmiri, reported in 21 D.L.R. I., while interpreting Article 98 of the Constitution has very clearly spelt out the meaning of these two expressions "without lawful authority" and "in an unlawful manner," wherein his Lordship observed as follows:

"They all agreed that the expressions "without lawful authority" and "in an unlawful manner" occurring in sub-clause (b) were not merely tautologous. A definite meaning had, therefore, to be given to each of them. The Constitution, it appears, cast a heavy responsibility upon the Court to satisfy itself with regard to both these two matters. The question, therefore, arises as to what are these matters. It is agreed that within lawful authority will be comprised all questions of vires of the statute itself as also of the person or persons acting under the statute, i.e., there must be a competent law authorizing the detention and the officer issuing such an order must have been lawfully vested with power."

89. In that decision the words "in an unlawful manner" has also been very clearly explained in paragraph 21 as an act not in accordance with law, (act with a) malafide or colourable action, actions taken upon no ground at all or without proper application of mind of the detaining authority. In the yardstick of the observations made by his Lordship in that decision, in can be argued that the detenu is not being held in custody in an unlawful manner but his detention is undoubtedly without lawful authority.

90. According to learned Additional Attorney General, the custody warrant passed by Additional District Magistrate, Tangail, is only an irregular one and not an illegal and unlawful order. Had the order been prima facie appeared to have been passed with a person having lawful authority, then, of course, the argument of the learned Additional Attorney-General could have been accepted. Herein, I find that the detenu is in Custody by virtue of an order of commitment of sentence of imprisonment not imposed by a competent and lawful authority. It is needless to say that the petition was in the nature of habeas corpus, where the illegal custody of the detenu was under challenge.,' he liberty of a citizen being curtailed without lawful authority, the Hrgh Court Division was called upon to satisfy itself that the detenu is not being held in custody without any lawful authority. Hence, the submission of the learned Additional Attorney General that the order is an irregular one only and not an illegal order, as it does not affect the sentence or of the detention of detenu is untenable in law. I may further point out that proclamation of 7th April, 1979, is not only protected and made part of the Constitution, but I find that this proclamation in sub-paragraph 'o' reads as follows:-

"(o) The President may, for the purpose of removing any difficulty that may arise in giving effect to any provision of this Proclamation, make by order, such provisions as he deems necessary or expedient and every such order shall have effect notwithstanding anything contained in the Constitution or in any other law for the time being in force."

<u>91. Thus, it appears that for the purpose of giving effect to any provision of this proclamation, the President was given the power to pass necessary order to remove any difficulty to give effect to any provision of that proclamation notwithstanding anything contained in the Constitution or in any other law for the time being in force. It is patently clear that after the withdrawal of Martial Law, the proclamation contemplate that when civil Government will be established and the country will be governed in accordance with the Constitution and law, if in a given case any difficulty arises, the President can alone resolve that difficulty. Subsequently, this proclamation on the commencing day was ratified and embodied in the constitution by amendment. Hence, I hold that the Additional District Magistrate, Tangail, could not have issued the order of commitment in custody at all.</u>

<u>In the case reported in AIR.1936 (Calcutta) 149, a person was convicted and sentenced by a Special Magistrate passing sentence of fine under provision of section 23 of Ordinance Xl of 1931. That special Ordinance came to an end in 1932 and the sentence remained unexecuted it was contended on behalf of the crown that the ordinary Magistrate after the expiry of the special Ordinance was the successor-in office as per section 389 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Judges of the Calcutta High Court held that the sentence having been passed by the special Magistrate under a special ordinance and that ordnance having expired, the Sub divisional Magistrate could not be held to the a successor in office of that Special Criminal Court within the meaning of section 389 of the Code and the warrant of sentence was quashed. In the present case, the executing authority is mentioned in subparagraph 'IC of the proclamation of withdrawal of 7th April, 1979 and consequently the order of the Additional District Magistrate. Tangail is wholly illegal and without jurisdiction as he had no lawful authority to pass the order of warrant of commitment in custody. Hence, the order of detention is without any lawful authority, and on that score alone the detention of the detenu is liable to be set aside.</u>

End.

full_judgment:
Syed JR Mudassir Husain CJ: I have gone through the judgments proposed to be delivered by learned brother, Amirul Kabir Chowdhury, the author Judge and additional judgments written by my brother Md Ruhul Amin, my brother MM Ruhul Amin and my brother Md Tafazzul Islam.

<u>2. Having concurred with their judgments, I would like to add only few words stating to the effect that preparation of Electoral Roll is one of the positive steps for democratic process which will ensure the right of franchise of the people and also help stability of our democratic institutions.</u>

<u>3. Now as per our judgments, the Election Commission will prepare the electoral roll with utmost expedition.</u>

<u>Md Ruhul Amin J: I have gone through the judgment of brother Amirul Kabir Chowdhury and the addition made to the same by brother Md Tafazzul Islam. I agree with the reasons and the conclusion arrived at as to result of the appeal on modification of the judgment under appeal, but would like to add few lines in support of the judgment.</u>

5. The moot point in the appeal was whether keeping in view the next parliamentary election or, in other words, for the ensuing parliamentary election the Election Commission would prepare a fresh voter-list without having any regard to the existing voter list or the Election Commission would prepare the voter list taking into consideration of the existing voter list or, in other words, Election Commission upon additions, deletions and modifications of the existing voter list will prepare the voter list for the purpose of holding the ensuing parliamentary election. In the instant case the Election Commission (the Commission) in its meeting held on August 6, 2005 took the decision to prepare the voter list as the Commission felt necessity of preparing the voter list "সম্পূর্ণ ক্রটিমুক্ত".

6. The provision of Article 119 of the Constitution has assigned to the Commission, amongst others, the function of preparation of electoral roll for holding election of Member of Parliament. In sub-Article 2 of Article 122 of the Constitution and in section 7(1) of The Electoral Rolls Ordinance, 1982 (Ordinance No. LXI of 1982), (the Ordinance), the qualifications of a person for being enrolled on electoral roll for the electoral area or constituency have been given.

7. Section 5 of the Ordinance provides for preparation of electoral roll for the purpose of election to different elective bodies upon registration of the voters and in section 7 of the Ordinance manner has been laid down for the preparation and publication of the electoral roll. Sub-section 6 of section 7 of the Ordinance provides for maintaining the final electoral roll (published under section 7(4) of the Ordinance) in the manner prescribed and the electoral roll so maintained shall be available for public inspection and that copy of said electoral roll would be available to a person when applies therefor on payment of prescribed fees. Sub-section 7 of section 7 of the Ordinance provides for cancellation of an electoral roll of any electoral area or constituency or draft thereof by the Commission on account of any gross error or any irregularity in or in the preparation of an electoral roll and thereupon for preparation of the electoral roll for that electoral area or constituency "afresh".

8. It was the contention of the respondent Nos.1 and 2 in Civil Appeal No. 54 of 2006 and the respondent No. 1 in Civil Appeal No. 55 of 2006 that the Commission is not authorised to prepare a fresh voter list upon ignoring the existing voter list. As against that, it was the contention of the appellant in the respective appeals that in view of the provision of sub-section 7 of section 7 of the Ordinance there is no embargo on the power of the commission to prepare a fresh voter list and in the preparation of fresh voter list the Commission is not by the law required to take notice of the existing voter list. It is the contention of the respondents that there should be continuity of the voter list and as against that, it is the contention of the appellant that the concept of continuity of voter list as contended by the respondents is quite foreign to the law providing procedure for preparation of voter list.

9. The appellant in support of his contention that there is no embargo on the authority of the Commission for preparing a fresh voter list relied on the provision of section 7(7) of the Ordinance. The provision of sub-section 7 of section 7 is as follows:

"(7) If the Commission, on account of any gross error or irregularity in or in the preparation of an electoral roll for any electoral area or constituency or draft thereof, considers it necessary so to do, it may by order direct that such roll or draft shall stand cancelled and that an electoral roll for that electoral area or constituency be prepared afresh".

10. It may be mentioned that sub-section 6 of section 7 of the Ordinance provides for maintaining of electoral roll. The provision thereof is as follows:

"(6) An electoral roll shall be maintained in the prescribed manner and shall be kept open for public inspection; and copies of such roll shall be supplied to any person applying therefor on payment of such fee as may be prescribed".

<u>11. From the provision of sub-section 7 of section 7 of the Ordinance it is seen that the Commission is authorised to prepare a fresh an electoral roll of an electoral area or constituency where there has been gross error or irregularity "in or in the preparation" of said electoral roll. As seen from the provision of sub-section 6 of section 7 of the Ordinance that under the said provision an electoral roll is to be maintained when the same is prepared following the procedure prescribed in sub-sections 1 to 4, and finally published, of section 7. On reading the provision of sub-section 7 of section 7 of the Ordinance my view is that the said provision does in no way authorise the Commission to prepare a fresh voter list for all electoral areas or constituencies upon scrapping already existing voter list since there is provision for amendment, correction and revision of voter list in sections 10 and 11 of the Ordinance and there is provision for deletion of names from the electoral roll in section 13 of the Ordinance. From the provisions of sections 10, 11 and 13 of the Ordinance it is seen that there is no scope for the Commission while it goes for preparation of fresh voter list with the lapse of time between the parliament election held earlier and the period fixed for finalisation of the voter list for holding election of the next parliament. In my view, when the Commission takes step for preparation of a fresh voter list it will delete from the existing voter list names of the persons who have acquired any disqualification for being enrolled as a voter and will add on following the provision of sections 7, 8 and 9 of the Ordinance and the rules 4-18 of the Rules framed under the Ordinance the names of the persons who have acquired qualification for being listed as voter between the period that passed from the date of preparation of the last voter list and till the date of finalisation of the voter list to be published finally as per provision of section 7(4) of the Ordinance. If we look to the rules prepared under the Rule making power as provided in the Ordinance we find Rule 19 relates to a fresh electoral roll which will be prepared for an electoral area or constituency as per provision of sub-section 7 of section 7 of the Ordinance and Rule 20 provides for amendment and correction of the electoral roll and Rule 2 provides for revision of electoral roll. The provision of sub-section 6 of section 7, 10 and 11 of the Ordinance and the Rules 20 and 21 of The Electoral Rolls Rules, 1982, (The Rules) clearly show that continuity of the electoral roll is to be maintained or, in other words, whenever step would be taken for preparation of a fresh voter list the Commission should prepare such list taking into consideration the existing voter list or, in other words, the fresh voter list would be a list already in existence with additions, deletions and modifications. To be more clear and specific in view of the provisions as mentioned hereinbefore, in my view, the fresh voter list which would be prepared by the Commission should contain the names of the voters already in the existing list, if one has not acquired disqualification for being listed as a voter, as well as the names of the persons who in between the period while the existing list was prepared and the time fixed for being listed as a voter have acquired the qualification, as are in Article 122(2) of the Constitution and in section 7(1) of the Ordinance. Sections 10 and 11 of the Ordinance provides for amendment and correction as well as revision respectively of electoral roll. When these provisions are read with the provision as in section 7(6), section 7(7) of the Ordinance as well as Rules 20 and 21 of the Rules it is seen there is contemplation of maintaining existing list with necessary additions, deletions and modifications or upon revision. It has been submitted on behalf of the appellant that the provisions in sections 7, 10 and 11 are independent and there is no scope for reading the same taking them together and there is no scope to take the view that the law in the Ordinance and the Rules provide for continuity of the voter list or, in other words, maintaining of the electoral roll and preparation of a fresh electoral roll taking into consideration of the electoral roll so maintained. In my view the submission so made is of no merit because of the provision of sections 10, 11 and 7(6) and 7(7) as well as Rules 20 and 21 of the Rules. It may be mentioned the Commission in its meeting held on August 6, 2005 did not take decision for cancellation of the existing roll for the reasons as in sub-section 7 of section 7 of the Ordinance. It is seen from the minutes of the meeting of the Commission held on August 6, 2005 that the Commission felt necessity of preparing a fresh voter list free from mistake. In that state of the matter it cannot be said that the Commission took decision to scrap the existing voter list or to discontinue the existing voter list. Provision of sections 10 and 11 read with Rule 20 and 21 provides for correction of the existing voter list by addition, deletion and modification.</u>

<u>12. It was submitted on behalf of the appellant that in the past voter lists were prepared in the manner similar to instant manner, but no exception was taken in any respect and there was no claim for continuity of the existing voter list. The submission so made, in my view, lacks substance since an act done in violation of the law or in disregard of the Rule would not be clothed with legality only because, of lapse of time or for not taking exception to the act so done in disregard of the law and the Rules, rather when challenge is made to the act done in disregard of the law and the Rules then the authority which is competent to put the person or the body acting in violation of law and the Rules on the right track is quite competent to make direction to the person of the body that acted or is acting upon violation of the law and the Rules to do or perform its function or act in due compliance of the law and the Rules.</u>

<u>13. The provision in section 7(7) of the Ordinance providing for preparation of an electoral roll 'afresh' by the Commission is limited to particular or specific electoral area or constituency in the state of the matters as are therein and not beyond that or, in other words, the said provision does not authorise the Commission to prepare a fresh electoral roll scrapping/obliterating the existing electoral roll. The Commission in its meeting held on August 6, 2005 felt necessity of preparing "সম্পূর্ণ ক্রটিমুক্ত". electoral roll. In my view, for achieving that purpose the Commission is not required to obliterate the existing voter list or to consign the same to cold-storage and then replace the existing voter list by a fresh voter list. Device for preparing "সম্পূর্ণ ক্রটিমুক্ত". voter list without scrapping existing voter list is very much in the Ordinance (sections 10 and 11) and the Rules (Rules 20 and 21) framed under the Ordinance. The continuity of voter list or, in other words, non-scrapping of existing voter list is also seen from the provision of section 11A of the Ordinance and the Rules 22, 23 and 26. In fine, I am of the view, the Ordinance and the Rules framed under the Ordinance postulate continuation of existing electoral roll with necessary additions, deletions, revision, modifications, corrections and amendments.</u>

<u>14. I am of the view whenever the Commission will take step for preparation of electoral roll, the same will perform the said function upon taking into consideration the list maintained under section 7(6) of the Ordinance in the light of the provisions of sections 10 and 11 of the Ordinance as well as Rules 20 and 21 of the Rules and not by scrapping or obliterating the existing list.</u>

MM Ruhul Amin J: I have gone through the judgment proposed to be delivered by my learned brother Amirul Kabir Chowdhury, J and the reasonings added by my learned brother Md Tafazzul Islam, J and I have nothing more to add.

Md Tafazzul Islam J: I have read the proposed judgment of my brother Amirul Kabir Chowdhury. I concur with the decision dismissing the appeals with some modification. However I want to add the following:

<u>17. Electoral Rolls Ordinance 1982 provides for preparation of electoral rolls for the purpose of elections to different elective bodies and Electoral Rolls. Rules 1982 provides details in this regard. Ordinance 1982 as well as Rules 1982 more or less envisage 5 stages i.e. (1) preparation of the draft electoral roll, (2) after making addition or modification or correction in the draft electoral roll publication of the final electoral roll (3) maintenance of the final electoral roll in the prescribed manner and keeping it open for public inspection. (4) addition, modification and correction of the final electoral roll (5) revision of the existing electoral roll and preparation of subsequent electoral roll after revision.</u>

18. At the first stage in terms of the provision of section 7(1) read with rules 3, 4 and 5, a draft electoral roll has to be prepared after complying with the requirements, as laid down.

19. At the second stage in terms of section 7(2) read with rules 6-8 a draft electoral roll shall be published inviting claims and objections and in terms of section 7(3) read with rules 7 to 10 the registration officer shall, on the basis of any decision or on the basis of claims and objection, make addition, modification or correction in the electoral roll and in terms of section 7(4) read with rules 7-17 requirements as provided therein are to be complied with before publication of the final electoral roll and in terms of section 7(5) read with rule 18 final electoral roll is to be published.

20. At the third stage in terms of section 7(6) read with rule 28 final electoral roll has to be maintained in the prescribed manner and also be kept open for public inspection and copies thereof are to be supplied on payment of fees.

21. In the fourth stage in terms of section 10 and section 15 read with rule 20 amendments and corrections may be made in the electoral roll on complying the provision as contained therein and in terms of section 15, the Election Commission may at any time include or exclude a person from the electoral roll and also correct any entry in the electoral roll.

22. At the fifth stage in terms of section 11 read with rule 21, unless otherwise directed by the Election Commission, before each election to an elected body, the electoral roll shall be revised and, if directed by the Election Commission, the electoral roll shall also be revised in any year.

<u>23. As it appears, the provisions of section 7(7) providing preparation of electoral roll afresh applies only to a particular electoral area or constituency, for gross error or irregularity in the preparation of electoral roll of that area or constituency but the facts of the present appeals are different inasmuch as order has been passed for preparation of the electoral roll afresh for the whole country.</u>

<u>24. As it appears, sub-Rule (1) of Rule 21, which deals with revision of electoral roll, specifically provides that for the purpose of revision of the electoral roll for any electoral area, the electoral roll of the electoral area for the time being in force shall, with such additions, deletions and modifications as may be necessary, be published as draft electoral roll in the manner provided in rule 6 and thereupon the provisions of rules 7 to 18 shall apply in relation to every such roll as they apply to the first preparation of an electoral roll for an electoral area.</u>

<u>25. Further, the words "first preparation of an electoral roll for an electoral area," indicates that only such first preparation is the preparation of the electoral roll afresh and there is no other scope for preparing electoral roll afresh. After revision only a revised electoral roll is published.</u>

<u>26. Accordingly, before the 9th Parliamentary election it is the existing electoral roll, i.e. the electoral roll of 2000, with some addition, deletions and modification as may be necessary, which is to be published as draft electoral roll and since the electoral roll 2000 will be the basis for preparing the draft electoral roll, the same has a continuity.</u>

<u>27. It also appears that sub-rule 1 of rule 21 refers to rules 7-18 which contain the procedure for inclusion, deletion and correction and Rule 14 provides for issuance of notice in the case of correction of an entry and Rule 15 also provides for service of such notice either personally or by post.</u>

<u>28. So, the decision of High Court Division, with the observations/directions as contained in paragraphs III and IV of the judgment and order does not call for any interference.</u>

Amirul Kabir Chowdhury J: Civil Appeal No. 54 of 2006 arises out of Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 88 of 2006 at the instance of the Election Commission represented by the Chairman (Chief Election Commissioner), the appellant, against the judgment and order dated the 4th January, 2006 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 9157 of 2005.

30. Civil Appeal No. 55 of 2006 arises out of Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 166 of 2006 at the instance of aforesaid appellant against self-same judgment and order dated the 4th January 2006 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 9180 of 2005.

31. Both the writ petitions were disposed of by the same order. As the two appeals arose out of common fact and involve common question of law the same are disposed of by this single judgment.

32. In Writ Petition No. 9157 of 2005 giving rise to Civil Appeal No. 54 of 2006, Alhaj Advocate Mohammad Rahmat Ali MP and others as writ petitioners prayed to:

"Issue a Rule Nisi calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why (i) the impugned decision to prepare a fresh electoral roll taken by the respondent No. 2, without consent of two of the three commissioners of the respondent No. 1 and (ii) the impugned appointment given by the respondent No. 3 to about 2,40,000 enumerators, 70,000 supervisors, 6235 assistant registration officers and 83 registration officers in pursuance of the impugned decision shall not be declared to have been taken without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and unconstitutional and void as being repugnant to Articles 27, 31, 39 and 118 of the Constitution.

Pending, hearing of the Rule, stay operation of the impugned decision of preparation of fresh electoral roll and the impugned action of the respondent No. 3 that is the purported appointment of 2,40,000 enumerators, 70,000 supervisors, 6235 assistant registration officers and 83 registration officers.

33. In Writ Petition No. 9180 of 2005 leading to Civil Appeal No. 55 of 2006 Mr M A Jalil MP moved the High Court Division for almost, similar reliefs adding thereto some other prayers challenging appointment of Upazilla Election Officers appointed by the Government through Public Service Commission, etc.

34. The aforesaid writ petitions were taken up by the High Court Division for hearing. In the midst of hearing, the Election Commission, the present appellant, was also heard through his learned Advocate. An Affidavit-of-Compliance was filed by the Election Commission the appellant.

35. The decision to prepare fresh electoral roll and appointment of Enumerators, Supervisors, Registration Officers and Assistant Registration Officers was challenged in both the writ petitions. The writ petitioners stated that they felt aggrieved as a result of the decision of the Chief Election Commissioner ignoring objections of two other members of the Election Commission in the matter of taking decision as to preparation of fresh Electoral Roll instead of updated voter list and it was averred that the Commission meant the Chief Election Commissioner and other members of the Election Commission and, as such, the decision taken by the Chief Election Commissioner alone was illegal and the actions taken by the Chief Election Commissioner in the name of Election Commission are liable to be declared as without lawful authority.

36. In the Affidavit-of-Compliance the Election Commission asserted that the decision was taken by the Commission in its meeting dated 6th August 2005 for a new voter list and for appointment of Registration Officers and Enumerators, etc. and pursuant to the said decision the Commission moved the Government for budgetary provision for expenses and considering the requirement of Enumerators, Supervisors, Registration Officers and Assistant Registration Officers the Election Commission took steps for their appointment and printed necessary forms for preparation of fresh voter list and spent about Taka 6 crore in the process and it has also been asserted that while the file was again put up by the Secretary to Election Commissioner Mr AK Mohammad Ali, he wrote a note of dissent to the said proposal for appointment of officials and there was no such note of dissent of Mr MM Munsef Ali, the other Election Commissioner and it was averred that under the provisions of Electoral Rolls Ordinance 1982 and the Electoral Rolls Rules 1982 new Electoral Rolls were prepared for general election held in 1983, 1990, 1992, 1995, 1996 and 2000.

37. The High Court Division after hearing the parties disposed of the writ petitions as under:

"In view of what has been discussed above let us sum up our findings and observations as under:

(i)	It is held that the decision for preparation of Electoral Roll taken in the meeting on 6th August, 2005 was not unilateral decision of the Chief Election Commissioner rather it was a decision of the Commission for the preparation of the Electoral Roll and appointment of the Registration Officers etc.

(ii) The Election Commission of Bangladesh is a composite body and it must function enhanced. That is, it must function institutionally and not individually. In case of difference of opinion all decisions must be taken by majority opinion. The Chief Election Commissioner is on par with other Commissioners on all matters except that the Chief Election Commissioner is the Chairman of the Commission under Article 118(2) and can exercise his sole discretion under Article 123(4) of the Constitution.

(iii)	The Commission should prepare Electoral Roll taking the existing Roll maintained under section 7(6) of the Ordinance as a major basis. If there is a computerized database the Commission should make the best use of it and, if not, a computerized Electoral Roll with database should always be maintained to avoid future controversy, cost and labour

(iv) The persons whose names are already in the existing electoral roll cannot be dropped from that roll unless they are dead or have been declared to be of unsound mind or ceased to be residents or ceased to be deemed to be residents of that area or the constituency.

(v)	The Chief Election Commissioner should immediately call a meeting of the Commission and the Commission should decide and take all appropriate steps to implement the decision of the Commission taken on 6th of August, 2005 in its meeting for preparation of Electoral Roll in the light of this judgment."

38. The appellants calling in question the legality of Directive Nos. III and IV preferred the appeals.

39. Leave was granted to consider the submissions made on behalf of the appellants-petitioners that in view of the provisions of section 7 to 11 of the Electoral Rolls Ordinance 1982 and Rule 4 of the Electoral Rolls Rules 1982, the observation made in the judgment that "the preparation of the voter list would be made taking the existing voter list as major basis" is erroneous and contrary to law and that section 7 of the Ordinance, 1982 having not provided that the existing voter list "shall be major basis" for preparation of a fresh voter list, the observation made by the High Court Division in paragraph III of the summing-up portion of the judgment is erroneous and liable to be set aside.

40. Leave was granted also to consider the submission that the observation made in paragraph IV of the summing-up portion of the judgment to the effect that "the persons whose names are already in the existing electoral roll cannot be dropped from that roll unless they are dead or have been declared to be of unsound mind or ceased to be resident or ceased to be deemed to be resident of that area or the constituency" is erroneous and inconsistent with the provision of law, inasmuch as, in that case, the process of enumeration of voters by door-to-door visit to ascertain who are fit to be entered in the electoral roll according to Article 122 of the Constitution and section 7(1) of the Electoral Roll Ordinance. 1982 and the Rules become meaningless and that continuation of an electoral roll in pursuance of the provision of section 7(6) of the Ordinance 1982 till the same becomes obsolete on the publication of a fresh voters list as per section 7(5), is necessary for holding bye-election to parliamentary constituencies between two general elections and also for holding elections to different elective bodies like the Corporations, Pourashavas and Union Parishads but section 7(6) cannot be construed or declared to be "basis" for preparation of a fresh voters list.

41. Mr Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Counsel appearing for the appellant in both the appeals, has taken us through the materials on record including the impugned judgment.

42. Challenging the legality of the findings and observations/directives given by the High Court Division in paragraphs III and IV of its judgment Mr Ahmed refers to the minutes of the meeting dated 6-8-2005, (Annexure-I), of Uhe Election Commission, hereinafter referred to as the Commission and the relevant portion of the said minutes are as follows:

স্বাধীনতার পর উপরোল্লিখিত আইন ও বিধি/অনুরুপ আইিন ও বিধি (Bangladesh Electoral Rolls Order, 1972 Bangladesh Electoral Rolls Rules, 1972 Electoral Rolls Ordinance, 1976 ও Electoral Rolls, 1976) অনুসারে ১৯৭৩ সনে, ১৯৮৩ সনে ১৯৯০ সনের ১৯৯৫ সনে সারাদেশে ভোটার তালিকা প্রণয়ন করা হয়েছিল। তাছাড়া ১৯৯২ সনে শুধুমাত্র পৌর এলাকার ভোটার তালিকা প্রণয়ন করা হয়েছিল। সর্বশেষ ২০০০ সনে বিদ্যমান  ভোটার তালিকা প্রণয়ন করা হয়েছে। অর্থাৎ জাতীয় সংসদের সাধারণ নির্বাচনের পূর্বে নতুন করে ভোটার তালিক প্রণয়ন করা হয়েছে।

(vide paragraph 2(I) of Annexure-I at page 109 of Paper Book)

43. Referring to paragraph 2(2) of the said minutes Mr Ahmed submits that reasons have been considered by the Commission to come to the conclusion এ অবস্থায় ভোটার তালিক সম্পূর্ন ত্রুটিমুক্ত করা প্রয়োজন।

44. With reference to Annexure-III, at pages 113 to 117 of the paper book Mr Ahmed submits that the file was again put up by the Secretary to the Commission on 5-10-2005 when the Election Commissioner Mr AK Mohammad Ali made observation appearing at page 116 of the paper book.

45. He then refers to Annexure-IV appearing at pages 118-119 in the paper book and submits that upon consideration of the documents including Annexure-I the High Court Division concluded:

"We find from these notes that both the Commissioners (Mr AK Mohammad Ali and Mr MM Munsef Ali) are specific about their intention for preparation of a voter list."

46. He then submits that the High Court Division formulated points for decision as to whether the decision taken in the meeting of the 6th August 2005 was unilateral or was by the Commission and that whether a fresh or new voter list is at all permissible to be prepared under the provisions of the Electoral Rolls Ordinance, 1982 (Ordinance No. LXI of 1982), in short, the Ordinance of 1982 and the Rules framed thereunder.

47. Then Mr Ahmed refers to the following portions of the judgment of the High Court Division:

"The expression, "unless otherwise directed by the Commission" in section 11(1)(a) of the Ordinance is a sufficient indication that other than revision the Commission can follow the foregoing procedure as in sections 5 and 7 for preparation of electoral rolls. We must not loose sight of the chronology of section 7 which puts final roll in section 7(5) and roll afresh of an area or constituency in section 7(7) and updating and revision in sections 10 and 11 respectively of the Ordinance.

It thus follows that the decision in the meeting of the 6th August, 2005 was not unilateral rather it was a decision of the Commission and the Commission is required to have an electoral roll prepared as distinguished from mere corrected, amended or revised taking the list maintained under section 7(6) of the Ordinance as the major basis."

48. Mr Ahmed further submits that "there is no controversy that the decision was taken for preparation of a list and for appointment of Registration Officers, etc on the 6th August 2005 but the 2 other Commissioners started disputing that the decision was taken for revision of the list and appointment of the Registration Officers for that purposes which is belied by Annexure-I of the affidavit of compliance."

49. Mr Ahmed, referring to the above mentioned portion of the judgment, submits that the High Court Division has correctly construed section 7 of the Ordinance but he takes exception to the observation that the Electoral Roll is to be prepared "taking the list maintained under section 7(6) of the Ordinance as the major basis" and emphatically submits that this is an erroneous observation which has also been repeated in the summing up portion in paragraph (III) of the findings and observations. We have considered the submissions made at the Bar and perused materials on record.

<u>106. We have already noticed that the two paragraphs, i.e. paragraphs (III) and (IV), in the impugned judgment of the High Court Division have been challenged by the appellant. The whole question arises as to preparation of a fresh Electoral Roll for the next general election.</u>

107. Mr Amir-ul Islam has rightly placed the preamble of our constitution and the decision in the case of Anwar Hossain vs Bangladesh in order to guide us to take decision in the matter. It is time that after long struggle and costly sacrifice we have achieved our independence pledging in the Constitution, amongst others, democracy and, in the words of Mr Islam, political justice to the citizens.

108. We have also adopted a democratic Constitution but successful working of it requires that those responsible to make the democracy successful should discharge functions in accordance with the Constitution and the law of the land.

109. In order to make a democracy successful election of the representatives in a free and fair way is indispensable.

110. In order to ensure a fair and free election, a flawless Electoral Roll is necessary.

111. Holding of free and fair election at all levels postulates necessity of having Electoral Rolls prepared in accordance with law. For the forthcoming National Election, the Election Commission is required to prepare Electoral Roll. Now the dispute has arisen as to whether Electoral Roll afresh should be prepared or the existing Electoral Roll should be updated. As revealed in the submissions of the parties it is noticed that under Article 122(2) of our Constitution any citizen of Bangladesh, being not less than 18 years of age, not declared by the competent Court to be of unsound mind and being resident of the area or deemed to be so by law is entitled to be enrolled as a voter in the Electoral Roll. The Ordinance of 1982 has provided in section 7 for preparation and publication of the Electoral Rolls embodying almost similar provision. In order to hold the general election the Election Commission appears to have taken decision in its meeting held on 6-8-2005 for preparation of Electoral Roll.

112. Though on behalf of the respondents it has been contended persistently that the decision taken in the said meeting was not taken by the Commission but by the Chief Election Commissioner alone but considering the materials on record the High Court Division held as follows:

"It thus follows that the decision in the meeting of 6th August 2005 was not unilateral rather it was a decision of the Commission."

113. We have already quoted relevant decision of the aforesaid meeting which is again reproduced below:

সিদ্ধান্তঃ ভোটার তালিকা অধ্যাদেশ, ১৯৮২ এবং ভোটার তালিকা বিধিমালা, ১৯৮২ এর আলোকে ইতিপূর্বে ১৯৮৩, ১৯৯০, ১৯৯২, ১৯৯৫ ‍ও ২০০০ সালে যে প্রক্রিয়ায় ভোটার তালিকা প্রস্তুত করা হইয়াছিল ঠিক একই প্রক্রিয়াই আগামী ৯ম জাতীয় সংসদ নির্বাচনের পূর্বে বাড়ি বাড়ি গিয়ে ভোটার যোগ্য ব্যক্তিদের তথ্য সংগ্রহ পূর্বক ভোটার তালিকা প্রস্তুতির কার্যক্রম গ্রহণ করা হউক।

114. From the aforesaid decision taken by the Commission it appears that the Commission decided to prepare the Electoral Roll by collecting information through house-to-house visit. There is therefore, nothing to dispute that Electoral Rolls shall be prepared for the ensuing election to the Ninth Parliament.

115. On consideration of materials on record the High Court Division also found them is no controversy that decision was taken for preparation of a list and for appointment of Registration Officers etc. on 6th August 2005." So, far as preparation of Electoral Roll and appointment of Registration Officer, etc there is therefore, no dispute between the parties. The dispute, as we have already noticed, is whether a fresh Electoral Roll shall be prepared by collecting information, through house-to-house visit or the Roll shall be prepared updated on the basis of existing Electoral Roll maintained earlier.

116. In order to prepare Electoral Roll we cannot be oblivious of the provisions enshrined in the Constitution. Article 122(1) of the Constitution runs as follows:

"122. (1). The elections to Parliament shall be on the basis of adult franchise.

(2) A person shall be entitled to be enrolled on the electoral Roll for a constituency delimited for the purpose of election to the Parliament, if he—

(a) is a citizen of Bangladesh:

(b) is not less than eighteen years of age;

(c) does not stand declared by a competent Court to be of unsound mind: and

(d) is or is deemed by law to be a resident of the constituency."

117. In conformity with the aforesaid Article various provisions have been enacted in the Electoral Rolls Ordinance, 1982. Sections 5 and 7 of the aforesaid Ordinance may be referred to in this connection which are as follows:

"5. Preparation of electoral rolls.—For the purpose of elections to different elective bodies, there shall be prepared electoral rolls for each electoral area or constituency as the case may be, upon registration of the voters.

7. Preparation and publication of electoral rolls.--(1) The Registration Officer for an electoral area or constituency shall, under the superintendence, direction and control of the commission, prepare for that electoral area or constituency in the prescribed manner a draft electoral roll containing the name of every person who, on the qualifying date,

(a) is a citizen of Bangladesh;

(b) is not less than eighteen years of age;

(c) does not stand declared by a competent Court to be of unsound mind; and

(d) is or is deemed by law to be a resident of that electoral area.

118. There are also provisions for amendment and correction of the Electoral Rolls and its revision in sections 10 and 11 of the Ordinance. Pursuant to the aforesaid Ordinance the Electoral Rolls Rules 1982 have also been made providing Rule 4 as to supply of information by occupants of dwelling houses and Rule 10 prescribing the manner of lodging claims and objections, regarding the Electoral Rolls.

<u>119. On perusal of the aforesaid provisions of law we do not find any embargo in preparation of an electoral roll by the Election commission for the ensuing election to the 9th Parliament. There is also no bar in taking into consideration of the existing Electoral Roll prepared under section 7(6) of the Ordinance in preparing such Electoral Roll.</u>

120. Regarding the direction in paragraph III, as already quoted by us hereinbefore, we are of the view that the Election Commission may be given a direction to take into consideration the existing Electoral Roll at the time of preparation of the Electoral Roll for the ensuing election to the 9th Parliament in order to make the Electoral Roll transparent.

121. Both the parties advanced argument on the question of dropping of names of persons from the existing Electoral Roll while preparing the Roll for the next National Election.

122. In this connection the parties referred to section 13 of the Ordinance which runs as follows:

13. Deletion of name from electoral roll—if a person whose name appears on an Electoral Roll ceases to be a citizen of Bangladesh or is declared by a competent Court to be of unsound mind his name shall stand deleted from the electoral roll."

123. The High Court Division considering the provision of the Constitution and the Ordinance of 1982 appear to have made findings and observations mentioned in paragraph IV as to dropping of names of persons from the existing Electoral Roll which we have already quoted hereinbefore.

124. Argument has been advanced that the Election Commission in the directive in paragraph IV has been given the direction for deletion of the names without any legal guideline.

125. We have given consideration to this submission. In this connection sub-rules (3) and (4) of Rule 20 of the Rules of 1982 may be referred to which are as under:

"20. Amendment and correction of the electoral roll.

(3) Where at any time, any clerical, printing or other, error in any entry in any electoral roll for the time being in force comes to the notice of the Registration Officer, he may, on his own motion and after giving notice to the person to whom the entry relates, correct such error.

(4) If an any time it appears to the Registration Officer that the name of any person who has died or is or has become disqualified for enrolment or who ceases or cannot claim himself to be a citizen under the provision of any law relating to the citizenship of Bangladesh has been included in an electoral roll and if he is satisfied after giving notice to the person concerned and after making such enquiry as he may consider necessary that the name should be deleted, he shall amend the electoral roll accordingly.

<u>126. We are of the view that conditions embodied in the aforesaid sub-rules (3) and (4) of rule 20 are required to be complied with in case of deletion/dropping of the names of persons from the existing Electoral Roll.</u>

<u>127. In such view of the matter the directive in paragraph (IV), according to us, should be modified.</u>

<u>128. In view of our decision to make the modifications mentioned hereinafter in the impugned directives we do not think that there is any necessity to allow the appeals.</u>

<u>129. The modifications are as under: Paragraph III of the judgment of the High Court Division (in findings and observations/ directives part) is modified as follows:</u>

<u>The Commission should prepare Electoral Roll taking into consideration of the existing Roll under section 7(6) of the Ordinance. If there is a computerized database the commission should make the best use of it and, if not, a Computerized Electoral Roll with database should always be maintained to avoid future controversy, cost and labour.</u>

<u>130. Paragraph IV of the judgment of the High Court Division (in findings and observations/directives part) is modified as follows:</u>

<u>The persons whose names are already in the existing Electoral Roll cannot be dropped from that Roll unless they are dead or have been declared to be of unsound mind or less than 18 years of age or ceased to be a citizen of Bangladesh; or ceased to be deemed by law to be residents of the electoral area/constituency. The Commission, if occasion arises for dropping the name from the existing Electoral Roll, then shall do the same following the procedure as laid down in sub-rules (3) and (4) of the Rule 20 of the Electoral Rolls Rules 1982.</u>

<u>131. In the aforesaid view of the matter the appeals are dismissed with modification, as above, in the findings and observations/directives given by the High Court Division in the impugned judgment and order.</u>

The parties will bear their respective costs.

End.
