case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated January 11, 1999 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Order No.1451 of 1999).
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: This is a plaintiff's appeal by leave against the order dated January 11, 1999 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Order No.1451 of 1999 dismissing the revisional application summarily. The revisional application was filed against the judgment and decree dated October 18, 1998 of the 3rd Court of Sub-ordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Mymensingh in Other Class Appeal No.202 of 1997 reversing the judgment and decree dated June 8, 1997 of the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Haluaghat, Mymensingh in Other Class Suit No.53 of 1995 decreeing the same. The suit was filed seeking a decree for specific performance of contract for sale of land.

2. The suit was filed stating, inter alia, that Md Abdur Rashid, maternal grandfather of the plaintiff, proposed to sell the land in respect whereof decree for specific performance of contract for sale is sought for consideration of Taka 19,000 and the plaintiff agreed to purchase the land at the price claimed by Abdur Rashid, that in due course plaintiff purchased stamp for drawing up the deed but day following the collection of the stamp, Abdur Rashid became ill and after two months he recovered and on March 8, 1995 upon accepting the price claimed by Abdur Rashid executed the deed of sale and made over possession of the land so agreed to sell, that Abdur Rashid assured the plaintiff that he would register the deed within a week but two days after the execution of the deed Abdur Rashid again became ill having had attack of heart and the right side of his body became paralysed and after prolonged suffering Abdur Rashid died on June 8, 1995, that after the death of Abdur Rashid, the plaintiff approached his daughter defendant No.1 and the grand children through the daughter Salemun Nessa and Amena Khatun (plaintiff is one of the sons of Salemun Nessa and Salemun Nessa's other son is defendant No.2 and the daughter is defendant No.3, Amena Khatun's daughters are defendant Nos.4 and 5) but they refused to execute and register the deed on July 16, 1995. Hence the suit.

3. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos.1 and 3-5 by filing written statement denying the material averments made in the plaint.

4. In was the case of the contesting defendants that Abdur Rashid 5 years before his death became paralysed, that defendant No.1 used to look after him, that through the men of his party the plaintiff has brought into existence the document in question, that defendants as co-sharers are in possession of the land as regard which the plaintiff seeking a decree for specific performance of contract, that plaintiff has created the deed by false personation, that during the lifetime of Abdur Rashid plaintiff did not disclose about the deed, that defendants for the first time on July 27, 1995 came to know about the deed when the plaintiff drove out the defendant No.1 forcibly from the homestead and other land of her father, that plaintiff had never approached the defendants for execution and registration of any deed as regard the land of Abdur Rashid.

5. It may be mentioned that Abdur Rashid was a quite solvent man and he had no necessity of collecting money by selling the land which he had after making gift of 50 decimals of land to the plaintiff.

6. In the plaint it has been averred by the plaintiff that there was certain mistake in the kabala executed by Abdur Rashid as regard the quantity of land of SA Plot Nos.1538, 1539 and 1540 in that in the deed land proposed to be sold from Plot No.1538 has been written 50 decimals but in fact it should have been 21 decimals, from plot No.1539 quantity of land proposed to be sold should have been 35 decimals but in the deed it has been written 20 decimals and in respect of the land of Plot No. 1540 land proposed to be sold should have been 30 decimals instead of 15 decimals. It may be mentioned two other plots i.e. Plot No.1536 comprising 20 decimals of land and Plot No.1537 comprising 25 decimals of land are also in the deed.

7. The trial Court decreed the suit on the finding that the plaintiff has been able to establish, by both oral and documentary evidence, that Abdur Rashid sold the land to the plaintiff and he executed the deed, that plaintiff has established that Abdur Rashid during his lifetime could not register the deed and, as such, plaintiff is entitled to get the decree for specific performance of contract against the defendants.

8. It may be mentioned plaintiff, in support of his case, examined 6 witnesses including himself. Of the witnesses examined by the plaintiff PWs 2 and 3 claimed to be the attesting witness to the deed, PW 4 claimed that he was present at the time of writing and at the time of the execution of the deed. It may be mentioned PW 3 is the brother-in-law of the plaintiff and PW 4 is the full brother of the plaintiff. PW 5 deposed that he was present at the time of execution of the deed and he saw payment of consideration money, evidence of PW 6 is hearsay evidence as to sale of the land by Abdur Rashid to the plaintiff.

9. The contesting defendants went on appeal. The appellate Court observed the discrepancy between the schedule of the plaint and the schedule of the deed on the basis whereof decree for specific performance was sought as to the quantity of land written against some of the plots in suit and the plots mentioned in the deed and thereupon considered the document as not genuine. The appellate Court discarded the evidence of PW 1 since the witness stated that when Abdur Rashid became ill he borrowed money from him. It is the definite case of the plaintiff that Abdur Rashid proposed to sell the land and the plaintiff agreed to purchase the same for the price claimed by Abdur Rashid and accordingly plaintiff purchased stamp for drawing up the deed but day following purchase of the stamp Abdur Rashid became ill. In the background of the said case of the plaintiff the appellate Court observed that had Abdur Rashid agreed to sell the land to the plaintiff prior to his becoming ill there was no occasion for Abdur Rashid to borrow money from the plaintiff to meet the expenses of his treatment. The appellate Court has observed about PW 2 that the said witness stated that he was not present at the time of settlement of price of the land Abdur Rashid proposed to sell and the plaintiff agreed to purchase. The appellate Court considered the PWs 3 and 4 as interested witnesses because of their relationship with the plaintiff as stated hereinbefore and also considered the PW 5 as interested witness since the said witness is plaintiff's "ধর্ম শ্বশুরঃ. The appellate Court noticed in the evidence of PW 6 that Abdur Rashid was quite a solvent man and there was sufficient numbers of valuable trees in the land possessed by Abdur Rashid and the products of the land was also of sufficient quantity. In the background of the evidence of the aforesaid witnesses the appellate Court observed that Abdur Rashid to meet the expense of his treatment was not in the necessity of selling the land or that was not required to approach the plaintiff for lending money to him to meet the expense of his treatment. One striking fact of the case is that the scribe of the deed was not examined by the plaintiff although he cited the scribe of the deed in question as witness and took out summons. No explanation was offered from the side of the plaintiff for non-examination of this vital witness. The scribe of the deed had figured as DW 10 and he had stated that he wrote the deed sitting in the premises of the office of the Sub-Registrar, Haluaghat. It may be mentioned it was the case of the plaintiff that the deed in question was written sitting in the house of Abdur Rashid and the PW 10 wrote the deed sitting in the house of Abdur Rashid. DW 10, as noticed by the appellate Court, has deposed that plaintiff brought into existence the deed in question after the death of Abdur Rashid and that the thumb impressions appearing on the stamp are not of Abdur Rashid.

10. Leave was granted to consider the contentions that the High Court Division was in error in rejecting the revisional application summarily upon misreading and mis-appreciation of evidence though plaintiff proved his case by the evidence of witnesses, that the High Court Division failed to exercise its revisional jurisdiction in not holding that the appellate Court misread and mis-appreciated the evidence of PW 2 and the evidence of other witnesses examined by the plaintiff who proved execution of the deed.

<u>11. Since plaintiff in spite of taking out summons for examining the scribe in support of his case having had not offered any explanation for non-examination of the scribe of the deed a presumption can legally be drawn that the scribe was not examined since he would not have supported the case of the plaintiff. Because of the quality of the evidence of witness Nos. 2-5, as stated hereinbefore, the scribe of the deed was the only independent and disinterested witness through whom the plaintiff could have established the genuineness of the document but did not examine him in spite of taking out summons to examine him and no explanation was offered for non-examination of the scribe of the deed. The scribe figured as DW 10. Evidence of this particular witness has already been stated hereinbefore. From the evidence of this witness it is seen that the document is not a genuine one but the same has been brought into existence for grabbing the land of Abdur Rashid or, in other words, for depriving his heirs although during the lifetime of Abdur Rashid he gifted 50 decimals of land to the plaintiff. The appellate Court, in our opinion, has quite legally considered -the document on the basis of which decree for specific performance of contract for sale of land was sought as not genuine since had the document being genuine the mistake as had crept in the document would not be there and that had the document been written in the presence of Abdur Rashid the papers relating to the land would have been supplied by Abdur Rashid to the plaintiff and the scribe and the document would have been drawn up on consultation of the papers. The mistakes as are in the deed as to the quantity of land of the 3 plots out of 5 plots if considered in the context of the evidence of DW 10 i.e. drawing up the deed sitting in the premises in the office of Sub-Registrar at Haluaghat and not in the house of Abdur Rashid as claimed by the plaintiff, appears to be more acceptable than the claim of the plaintiff that the deed was written sitting in the house of Abdur Rashid. It is in the evidence of DW 10 that the thumb impression appearing on the stamp papers were not of Abdur Rashid. The defendants also pleaded that Abdur Rashid did not execute the deed. In the background of the denial by the defendants as to execution of the deed by Abdur Rashid the plaintiff did not take any step to get the genuineness of the thumb impression ascertained/examined by the Hand Writing Expert.</u>

12. The appellate Court on consideration of the evidence arrived at the finding that plaintiff failed to establish that Abdur Rashid during his lifetime proposed to sell the land and that also failed to establish that Abdur Rashid voluntarily executed the document on the basis of which decree for specific performance of contract for sale of land is sought. One striking fact is, which is also admitted by the plaintiff, that prior to the execution of the deed Abdur Rashid became ill and there is no independent and disinterested witness to establish that he recovered from illness and on such recovery he executed the deed. It is the case of the plaintiff that two days after the execution of the deed in question Abdur Rashid again became ill. This assertion if considered in juxtaposition to the admitted fact that Abdur Rashid was ill before execution of the deed, then it is difficult to consider the assertion that Abdur Rashid became ill after execution of deed as correct.

<u>13. A decree in a suit for specific performance of contract is discretionary one and, as such, where the case of the plaintiff appears to be not genuine or, in other words, where the case pleaded and on the basis whereof decree for specific performance of contract is sought while appears to be tainted the Court is quite competent to refuse the decree asked for. The Court is always reluctant to grant the relief sought in a suit for specific performance of contract when the genuineness of the said contract is doubtful or that the plaintiff has not approached the Court with clean hands or the relief if granted would act harshly on the person against whom the relief is sought. Generally, an act which is not genuine or, in other words, not legal, the character thereof very much is reflected in the result obtained by resorting to illegal means or non-genuine activities. The undenied fact is that an act which is otherwise not genuine is always accomplished by resorting to illegal activities. In the instant case had the document been genuine one or, in other words, had the document in question been written, as claimed by the plaintiff and his witnesses PWs 2-5 in the presence of Abdur Rashid, the mistake as to the quantity of land as regard the land of certain plots would not have crept in the document in question since had Abdur Rashid proposed to sell the land to the plaintiff he would have made available the papers at the time of writing the deed. It is worth to notice that after selling the land, as claimed by the plaintiff, in respect whereof decree for specific performance has been sought, the seller would have no other land. There is nothing on the record to show the fact or circumstances that prompted Abdur Rashid to divest his entire land to plaintiff. In the context of the fact as transpires from the deed in question while the evidence of the scribe of the deed in question would have been the best evidence to establish the genuineness of the document on the basis of which the plaintiff sought for a decree for specific performance of contract, the plaintiff though cited the scribe of the deed as his witness and took out the - summons but ultimately, did not examine him without offering any explanation for not examining him and that also not making any accusation against him, if considered, then the deduction that can logically be made, and that, in our view, the appellate Court quite correctly made, that the document is not a genuine one. In the afore state of the matter we are of the view that the order of the High Court Division rejecting the revisional application summarily and thereby upholding the judgment and decree of the appellate Court cannot be considered unsustainable.</u>

14. In the background of our discussions made hereinabove we find no merit in the appeal.

Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed with cost of Taka 5,000.

End.

full_judgment:
Gour Gopal Saha, J: This Rule is directed against the judgment and decree dated 26.11.1991 passed by the Additional District Judge, Gazipur in Title Appeal No. 144 of 1989 reversing the judgment and decree dated 22.10.1989 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Gazipur in Title Suit no. 248 of 1986 dismissing the suit. Gunjor Ali as plaintiff instituted a suit for partition of ejmali properties in the Court of the Subordinate Judge Gazipur, being Title Suit no. 248 of 1986, claiming 3.85 acres of land in his share. His case is that the suit land belonged to 4 brothers named Omed Ali Bhuiyan, Hasan Ali Bhuiyan, Nowab Ali Bhuiyan and Eklas Ali Bhuiyan and their mother Fazaranessa having 2 annas share. Subsequently, Fazarannessa died leaving the above-named four sons as her only heirs to succeed her. In this way the aforesaid four brothers got 4 annas share each in the said jote. In course of time Nowab Ali died leaving son Asad Ali and 2 daughters named Meljan Bibi and Tolajan Bibi. Thereafter Maljan Bibi died leaving the plaintiff as her only heir, who claims 3.85 acres of land in the suit jote. His further case is that defendant no. 1 falsely claimed that Meljan Bibi by a registered deed dated 13.4.1928 had gifted her entire share in the suit jote to her brother Asad Ali, father of defendant No. 1. Hence the suit for partition with a further prayer for a declaration that the so-called Nadabipatra deed dated 30.4.1928 is fraudulent, collusive, void and not binding upon him.

2. Defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegations of the plaint and contended inter alia that by a registered deed of gift dated 30.4.1928 Meljan Bibi had transferred her entire interest in the suit jote to her brother Asad Ali and thereby she divested herself of all interests in the suit property and as such the plaintiff did not acquire any interest in (he suit land. It was further contended that the SA Khatian and RS Khatian have been rightly prepared in the names of the defendants. The plaintiff has no title and possession in the suit property and as such the suit is liable to be dismissed.

3. The learned Subordinate Judge by the impugned judgment dated 22.10.1928 dismissed the suit finding that the Nadabipatra deed dated 30.4.1928 is, in fact, a deed of gift under section 148 of the Mohammedan Law, by which Meljan Bibi divested herself of all interests in the suit jote and her brother Asad Ali acquired title in the suit land for the entire interest of Meljan Bibi and consequently the plaintiff having not acquired any interest in the suit jote is not entitled to get any saham in the suit property.

4. On appeal by the plaintiff the learned Additional District Judge, who heard the appeal, has been pleased by the impugned judgment dated 26.11.1991 to reverse the judgment of the trial Court and decreed the suit finding that the disputed deed Ext. A was not a deed of gift but it was simply a deed of relinquishment or abandonment of some interest with certain conditions embodied therein, by which no interest was transferred in favour of defendant's father Asad Ali. The learned Court of appeal below further found that Ext. A did not contain the essential ingredients of a valid gift and as such by Ext. 4 the interest of Meljan Bibi in the suit property did not extinguish.

5. Mr. Md. Aminul Islam Mondal, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, submits that the learned Additional District Judge erred in law in reversing the judgment of the trial Court without properly appreciating the legal incidence of Ext. A, a registered deed dated 30.4.1928. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned Court of appeal bellow also erred in law in reversing the judgment of the trial Court without setting aside its material findings with reference to the evidence on record.

6. Mr. A.K.M. Shafiuddin, the learned Advocate appearing for opposite party No. 1 on the other hand supports the impugned judgment and submits that the learned Additional District Judge was perfectly justified in reversing the judgment of the trial Court after setting aside its material findings with reference to the evidence on record. He further submits that the findings of fact arrived at by the learned Court of appeal below, which is the final Court of fact, being based on evidence on record are not liable to be interfered with in revision and as such the rule is liable to be discharged.

7. Mr. Md. Aminul Islam Mondal, the learned Advocate for the petitioners has taken us through the impugned judgments. It appears from the impugned judgment passed by the learned Additional District Judge that he found Ext. A as a simple Nadabipatra deed and not a deed of gift as found by the learned trial Court, Ext A, which is a registered document, on the face of it is a Nadabipatra deed with certain conditions embodied therein. One of such conditions of Ext A, is that Asad Ali, the brother of executrix Meljan Bibi was required to properly maintain the executrix for her life and he was also required to fulfil some other conditions as consideration for abandonment of claim by Meljan Bibi but Asad Ali was not given the right to transfer or alienate the property freely. The learned Court of appeal below referring to the evidence on record, found that Meljan Bibi continued to remain in possession of the suit property and she used to enjoy usufructs thereof at times. In the face of Ext A, which is admittedly a registered document and which has clearly been described and designated as a Nadabipatra deed, it cannot be treated as a deed of gift in a casual manner as has been done by the learned trial Court. The ingredients of a valid gift under the Mohammedan Law are conspicuously absent in Ext. A. The learned Additional District Judge as the final court of fact found on appreciation of evidences that Ext. A was not a deed of gift and no interest was consequently transferred to Asad Ali vide ext. 4 nor interest of Meljan Bibi was extinguished by it. These findings of the learned Court of appeal below are supported by evidence on record and are based on sound reasons and as such are immune from interference in revision.

8. Section 91 of the Evidence Act provides that when the terms of a contract, or of a grant, or any other disposition of property, are reduced to the form of a document, no evidence shall be admissible in proof of the terms thereof except the document itself.

9. Section 92 of the Evidence Act, which is, in fact, a continuation of section 91 prohibits the admission or reiteration of any oral evidence or extraneous evidence to contradict the terms of any condition of the instrument.

<u>10. It is well-settled by consistent judicial pronouncements that oral evidence is inadmissible for the purpose either of construing the terms of a document or of ascertaining the intention of the parties thereto. Thus no oral evidence to transform Nadabipatra deed Ext. A into a deed of gift is admissible in evidence. We get support of our view in the case of Feroza Majid Vs. J.B. Corporation reported in 39 DLR(AD)78.</u>

<u>11. A Nadabipatra deed is usually understood as a deed acknowledging abandonment or relinquishment of some interest in a property by the executant. By itself it does not transfer any interest in the property nor does it confer any title on the recipient. At best, it may be taken into consideration as a piece of evidence to strengthen a claim of title based on other source. Under given circumstances, it may of course, constitute waiver or estoppel but for that it must be clearly shown that the party alleged to have waived his rights had acted in such a manner as to lead the other party to alter his position in respect of the subject-matter of the disputed Nadabipatra. In the instant case, evidence on record shows, as has been rightly found by learned Additional District Judges, that at best the Nadabipatra deed in question could be taken as an amicable arrangement between the brother and the sister for enjoyment of the paternal property. There is no evidence on record to prove that by this Nadabipatra deed the plaintiff or his mother relinquished their claims in the suit property which, is quite a big chunk of land, for all times to come on fulfillment of the conditions embodied in the Nadabipatra deed itself. Under such circumstances, the learned Additional District Judge is found to be perfectly justified in setting aside the judgment of the trial Court on sound reasonings.</u>

12. The only bone of contention between the contending parties is Ext. A. There is no dispute to the fact that the Meljan Bibi as one of the daughters of Nowab Ali Bhuiyan, one of the C.S. recorded tenants, had 1/16th share In the suit jote. There is also no dispute to the fact that the plaintiff is the only heir and son of Meljan Bibi. Since the final Court of fact, on proper appreciation of the evidence on record, found that the plaintiff has title and possession in the suit property, there is no reason why the plaintiff should not be entitled to a decree for partition as prayed for.

13. For the reasons stated above, we find that the learned Additional District Judge did not commit any illegality in passing the impugned judgment and as such the same is sustainable in law. We do not find any illegality in the impugned judgment that calls for our interference in revision. In the result, the Rule is discharged and the judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Gazipur in Title Appeal No. 144 of 1989 are affirmed. There shall be no order as to costs. The order of stay earlier granted by this Court stands vacated.

Send down the lower Court records at once.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. Rafique-ul-Huq, Senior Advocate. (Mr K Z Alam, Advocate with him) instructed by Mvi Md Wahidullah, Advocate-on-Record ----- for the appellants.

Vs
AM Agha Yousuf and others ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
Latifur Rahman CJ: I agree with the final judgment of this Court that the appeal should be dismissed.

Bimalendu Bikash Roy Chowdhury J: <u>I have gone through the Judgment of my learned brother Kazi Ebadul Hoque J. I agree with his conclusion that the appeal should be dismissed. But I differ from the reasonings given by him therefor. The import of Article 114 of the Articles of Association appears to me to be these. No person other than a retiring director or a nominee director shall be eligible for election to the office of the director at any General Meeting unless he is recommended by the directors. This will not apply if a member has left at the office a notice in writing under his hand or under the hand of such agent signifying his assent to his candidature at least 7 clear days before the meeting. The purpose of this provision appears to be that if a general member wants to be elected as director but 'fails to give the requisite notice he will need recommendation of the directors for his eligibility for election.</u>

<u>3. I am unable to agree that the word 'recommendation' occurring in the Article connotes mere scrutiny without any authority to choose. I take the simple dictionary meaning of the word 'recommendation'. I mean speaking favourably of a person for the purpose of election.</u>

<u>4. Yet I hold that the appeal must fail because the appellants have no locus standi to maintain the appeal not being themselves aggrieved by the election.</u>

AM Mahmudur Rahman J: I agree with the view of my learned brother Justice BB Roy Choudhury.

Kazi Ebadul Hoque J: This appeal by leave is from judgment and order dated 25-8-1999 passed by the Company Judge of the High Court Division in Matter No.106 of 1997 disposing of the objection raised by the respondent AM Agha Yusuf against report filed by the Chairman of the Annual General Meeting of the International Finance Investment and Commerce Bank Limited (IFIC Bank) so far as it relates to the election of directors of the said Bank.

7. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, a Senior Advocate of this Court, was appointed Chairman to preside over the Annual General Meeting of the said Bank for the year 1997 and to submit his report by order dated 16-3-1999 passed in the said matter. The said meeting was held on 5th July 1999 presided over by the said Chairman and the said Chairman submitted his report on 4-8-1999.

8. In the said Annual General Meeting four retiring directors of the said Bank namely, 1. Mr ASF Rahman, 2. Mr Salman F Rahman (the appellants), 3. Mr AM Agha Yusuf, (respondent No. 1) and Mr. Saiful Islam representing class 'A' shares retired and offered themselves to be re-elected directors of the said Bank for the next term. Sponsor shareholder Mr. Asaduzzaman (Folio No.0029) nominated Mr A Matin Khan as another candidate for the office of director of the said Bank representing class 'A" shares.

9. Respondent No.1 sent a, Letter to the Chairman of the Annual General Meeting on 5-7-1999 stating that "right up to 27th Board Meeting of the Bank held on 1st July, 1999, no proposal for nomination of any director has been received by the Directors" and further stating that there is no scope for-putting up a candidate for the directorship at the time just before the meeting." But the Chairman overruled the objection raised by the respondent No.1 in the said letter and proceeded to the election of directors of the said Bank. Five shareholders having demanded a poll election was held by the person appointed by the Chairman as Election Commissioner. After the election and counting of votes Chairman, announced the result declaring the appellants, Mr. Saiful Islam and Mr A Matin Khan as directors of the said Bank. Chairman thereafter submitted his report on 4-4-1999 to the company Judge about the Annual General Meeting of the said Bank incorporating the result of the election.

10. Respondent No.1 thereafter submitted a written objection before the Company Judge against the report of the Chairman so far as it relates to the election of directors illegally overruling his objection on the ground that there has been violation of the provisions Of Article 114 of the Articles of Association of the said Bank Company in accepting the nomination of  Mr A Matin Khan as he had not left any notice in writing under his own hand signifying his assent to his candidature for the office of director at the office of the Bank after his nomination by any shareholder nor his name was recommended by the directors for such election.

11. Appellants filed an affidavit-in-opposition controverting the statements made in the said written objection and supporting the report of the Chairman. The Chairman also filed a supplementary affidavit stating that the nomination of Mr A Matin Khan marked Annexure 'X' was not inadvertently annexed with the report.

12. Learned Company Judge after considering the materials on record, hearing the Chairman and learned Advocates of the parties by the impugned judgment and order disposed of the objection and declared the four retiring directors elected as directors of the said Bank.

Learned Company Judge found as follows:

"In the instant case I do not find from the record that the letter of nomination in favour of Mr A Matin Khan vide Annexure-‘X' to the supplementary affidavit was at all placed before the directors nor there was any recommendation by the directors before the AGM was held on 5th July, 1999. No paper has been filed to show that the said nomination letter was at all submitted to the directors at any time before AGM. In this view of the matter, I find that the election of Mr A Matin Khan was not held in due compliance of Article 114 of the Articles of Association of the bank and, as such, the report of the Chairman Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed with regard to the election of Mr A Matin Khan is rejected."

13. Appellants, the two re-elected directors, obtained leave to appeal to consider the submission that the Company Judge completely misunderstood and misinterpreted Article 114 of the Articles of Association of the Bank and thereby committed illegality in declaring a defeated candidate as duly elected candidate. If this interpretation is accepted, then no outsider can ever be eligible to be elected as Director of the Bank in spite of having duly qualified shares unless the Board of Directors recommends his case, which goes against the concept of company law as well as principle of franchise.

14. Following submissions of the caveator were allowed to be considered:

"The petitioners cannot be said to be aggrieved by the impugned decision of the learned Company Judge. Neither the Bank nor Mr A Matin Khan has preferred any petition for leave to appeal from the impugned judgment. The present petitioners have, therefore, no locus standi. That a harmonious interpretation of Article 114 is that, the candidate for election to the office of Directors or his authorised agent shall leave at the office of the Bank at least 7 dear days before the meeting a notice in writing under his hand or under the hand of such agent signifying assent to his candidature for the office of Director and that such nomination needs to be considered by the Board of Directors to determine the eligibility of the candidate and/or his agent and also to make arrangements for holding a vote. This is what is meant by "recommendation" by the Directors. The "recommendation" is not an obstacle but a means to facilitate the election. The letter of nomination of Mr. A Matin Khan never reached the Board of Directors which held its last meeting only three days before the Annual General Meeting. The learned Company Judge, therefore, rightly came to the conclusion that the election of Mr A Matin Khan was illegal."

15. Learned Advocate for the appellants submits that if recommendation of the Board of Directors is considered to be a condition precedent to the valid nomination of a candidate for election of a director in case of a person other than a retiring " director in pursuance of Article 114 of the Articles of Association of the Bank then no outsider could be able to be elected as director. So, the provision of Article 114 is in direct conflict with the provisions of clause (b) of subsection (l) of section 9 J of the Companies Act 1994 and, as such, interpretation of Article 114 as given by the learned Company Judge cannot be sustained. He further submits that the appellants as holders of substantial shares of the Bank has right to see that election of a candidate supported by overwhelming majority of shareholders is upheld and, as such, they contested the objection filed by the respondent No.1 by filing affidavit-in-opposition before the Company Judge and so they have locus standi to file and maintain the appeal.

16. Learned Advocate for the respondent No. 1 submits that the nomination of a candidate for election must be processed through the Board of Directors which has been authorised under the said Article 114 to scrutinize the same and place the same in the Annual General Meeting with its report for consideration of the shareholders and that does not mean that Board of Directors would exclude such nomination. He therefore, submits that there is no real conflict between Article 114 and section 91(1)(b) of the Act. He also submits that Mr A Matin Khan having not felt aggrieved by the impugned judgment and order the appellants as shareholders have no locus standi to challenge the same.

17. Article 114 of the Articles of Association of the said Bank is as follows:

"No person, not being a retiring Director, shall, unless recommended by the Directors for election, be eligible for election to the office of Director at any General Meeting, unless he or his authorised agent has at least 7 clear days before the meeting, left at the office a notice in writing under his hand or under the hand of such agent signifying assent to his candidature for the office of director, Provided however, this Article shall not apply to nominee Directors."

18. From the above provision it appears that no person except a nominee director or a retiring director shall be eligible for election to the office of the director unless he or his authorised agent leaves in the office of the Bank a notice in writing under his hand or under the hand of his agent signifying assent to his candidature for the office of director and unless he is recommended by the directors.

19. In the instant case it appears from Annexure 'X' to the supplementary affidavit submitted by the Chairman on 25-8-1999 that shareholder Mr Asaduzzaman bearing folio No.000029 nominated Mr. A Matin Khan for election to the office of director of the said bank by a letter addressed to the Secretary of the said Bank purported to have been written on 24-6-1999 and at the bottom of the said letter Mr A Matin Khan made the endorsement "I agree" and put his signature under the said endorsement. So, no notice as required under Article 114 was left in the office of the bank by Mr. A Matin Khan under his own hand signifying his assent to his candidature to the office of the director. Admittedly aforesaid letter Annexure 'X' was not placed before the Board of Directors of the said Bank. If it is conceded that the said letter Annexure 'X' is substantial compliance of the requirement of notice under Article 114 the next question is whether there is any necessity of placing the same before the. Board of Directors for its recommendation.

<u>20. Clause (b) of sub-section (1) of section 91 of the Companies Act 1994 provides that directors of the company shall be elected by the members of the company from amongst themselves in a General Meeting. According to the appellants, if recommendation by the Board of Directors under Article 114 is a must for being a candidate for the office of the director and if the Board of Directors do not recommend the name of any candidate then the mandate of the aforesaid provision would be flouted and the provision of the said Article 114 if it comes in conflict with the aforesaid provision of the said Act the same cannot stand. Learned Advocate for the appellant pointed out that in the Articles of Association of almost all the Banks relevant article is in the same language as in Article 114 of IFIC Bank. Why then Banks incorporated articles similar to Article 114 providing for recommendation of the Board of Directors for eligibility of candidature of a person' other than a nominee or retiring director for the office of the director if it is in direct conflict with the said provision of the said Act? It appears to us that such provision has been consciously made to avoid complications in the Annual General Meeting of the Bank in respect of election of directors of the Bank. If the candidature of a person for the office of director is not scrutinized by the Board of Directors before the Annual General Meeting then candidates with defective candidatures would also come to contest in the election and much time would be spent in finding out such defects and-taking decision over the same and thus complications would be created in the Annual General Meeting which has to dispose of important agenda in the meeting. If the Board of Directors scrutinizes the candidatures of such candidates then it would be possible for the Board to find out defect or infirmity in the same, if any, before the Annual General Meeting and would be able to report the same to be considered in the said Meeting. That is why there is the other requirement to submit the candidature in the office of the Bank at least 7 days before the Annual General Meeting. The power of the Board of Directors in the said Article 114 to recommend does not mean power to reject any such candidature. No such power to reject such candidature has been specifically given to the Board of Directors in the said Article or any other Article. So, under the garb of recommendation Board of Directors cannot reject the candidature of any person for the election to the office of the director of the Bank. In our considered view, the word "recommended" means power of the Board to point out defects, if any, in the candidature of a person for the office of director for consideration in the Annual General Meeting to avoid complications in such meeting and not the power to reject any candidature on the ground of defect real or fanciful. It is for the Annual General Meeting to consider defect, if any, in the candidature of a person and to take a decision over the same and not for Board of Directors to do so. So, we find no merit in the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellants that Article 114 does not contemplate recommendation of the candidature of a candidate for the office of director of the Bank by the Board of Directors.</u>

21. Letter of nomination dated 24-6-1999 Annexure 'X' might have been given to the secretary but the same was not submitted in the office of the Bank. Had it been so submitted then the same would have been placed before the court with the report of the Chairman and would not have been placed before the court subsequently as an Annexure to the supplementary affidavit dated 25-8-1999 specially when respondent No.1 raised objection regarding candidature of any person at the time just before the Annual General Meeting. Moreover, no notice in writing either in the own hand of the candidate Mr A Matin Khan nor in the hand of his authorized agent signifying assent to his candidature for the office of director was left at the office of the bank except the letter of nomination Annexure 'X. left with the secretary. In any view of the matter candidature of Mr A Matin Khan was not in conformity with the requirement of the said Article 114 as regards filing of the same in the office of the Bank in writing in the hand of the candidate or his agent. Even if it is conceded that no recommendation of the Board of Directors was necessary there was no valid nomination of Mr A Matin Khan for his election as director. We, therefore, find no illegality in the impugned judgment to interfere with the same.

<u>22. It appears that the appellants filed an affidavit-in-opposition before the Company Judge to contest the written objection filed by respondent No.1 against the report submitted by the Chairman relating to election of directors. Mr A Matin Khan whose election was rejected by the learned Company Judge by the impugned judgment has not preferred any appeal against the same. But the two elected directors who filed the said affidavit-in-opposition preferred the appeal. They are not directly affected by the impugned judgment but it appears that they are indirectly affected by the rejection of election of Mr A Matin Khan who appears to belong to their group holding majority shares. Otherwise they would not have filed affidavit-in-opposition before the Company Judge against the written objection of the respondent No.1. A voter cannot prefer an appeal against setting aside of the election of a successful candidate in an election. But that analogy will not hold good in respect of the election of directors of a company including a Bank Company. In the facts and circumstances of the case appellants representing majority shares having contested the written objection filed by the respondent No.1 challenging election of Mr A Matin Khan before the Company Judge have locus standi to file this appeal. So we find no merit in the objection raised by the learned Advocate of the respondent No.1 regarding locus standi of the appellants.</u>

In the result, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to cost.

End.

caseno: Appeal From Original Decree No. 200 of 1996
lawyer:
Mr. Md. Abdur Rahim with Mr. Ali Imam Khaled Rahim, Advocates ----- for the defendant-appellants. 
Mr. A.B. Mahfuzur Rahman with Mr. Md. Elahi Bakhsh, Advocates ----- for Respondents.
parties:
Md Monir Hossain and others
Vs.
Md Shamsul Hoque Mondal and others
full_judgment:
Md. Abdus Salam, J: This appeal at the instance of defendant-appellants is directed against the impugned judgment and decree passed by Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Jhenidah in Title Suit No. 75 of 1994 mainly on the grounds, among others, that in view of the fact and finding of the Subordinate Judge that the power of attorney in question does not contain the counter signature of the Deputy High Commissioner of Pakistan in Calcutta, the said power of attorney allegedly executed by Shyamapada and others in favour of Shahid Dhabak and Ahar Ali is of doubtful origin; that the Subordinate Judge committed error of law by placing the onus of proving the genuineness and regularity of the auction sale upon the defendant' in utter disregard of the provisions of section 114(E) of the Evidence Act which provides for presumption of regularity and legality of all official acts; that the Court below erred in law in not holding that the auction purchaser purchased the suit property before the alleged exchange and took delivery of possession through Court which is proved by the sale certificate and writ of delivery of possession; that the Subordinate Judge illegally embarked upon an investigation as to the possession of each plot of land without considering that the writ of delivery of possession followed the kabala deed of the defendant and sufficiently proves possession of the plaintiff in the suit land; that Shaheed Dhabak and Ahar Ali did not come forward before that Court to support the case of the plaintiff in view of the alleged exchange of the suit property and the Court below committed error of law in relying upon the false and concocted story of the plaintiffs that the heirs of Shaheed Dhabak possessed plot Nos. 1209, 668, 669, 677, 678, 678, 655 and 682 as their homestead and that after the death of Ahar Ali his heirs plaintiff Nos. 2-6 have been possessing the khaw schedule land through borgader, even though no borgader came forward to depose in support of this claim and that the Subordinate Judge illegally held that the order dated 25.3.1981 passed by Revenue Authority in Miscellaneous Case No.165/IP/69/70 is not binding upon the plaintiff though the competent authority found upon enquiry that the alleged exchange of the plaintiff and the disputed power of attorney are fake and forged.

2. Plaintiff-respondents Shamsul Huq Mondal and others filed Title Suit No. 80 of 1993 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Jhenidah for declaration of title in the suit  land described in schedule 'Kaw' on the basis of power of attorney described in 'schedule 'Gaw'.

3. Defendant No. 1, 3-40 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement date 11.6.95, though the written statement and the verification are signed by only defendant No. 1 Md. Monirul Islam. Defendant No. 45 Deputy Commissioner, Jhenidah on behalf of the Government of Bangladesh did not file any written statement and did not contest the suit. The contesting defendants denied all the material allegations made in the plaint and contended that the suit is not maintainable in its present from and it is barred by limitation and also by constructive resjudicata. It is further contended that the disputed. Ammokternama dated 26.9.62 is not authenticated by any competent Notary Public and not counter-signed by the then Deputy High Commissioner of Pakistan in Calcutta. It is the specific case of the contesting defendant that the suit property was sold by auction in Certificate Case No. 21851/61-62, 21852/61-62 and Certificate Case No. 21853/61-62 and one Amir Hossain and 32 others auction purchased the suit land and they obtained decree in Title Suit No. 223 of 1984 in the Court of Assistant Judge of Mohespur Upazila and the auction purchasers subsequently sold some of the auction purchased land to defendant Nos. 1-40 by Kabala deeds and that the auction purchasers took possession of the land through Court and that the alleged power of attorney and other connected papers of the plaintiff respondents arc forged, fraudulent and not acted upon and as such the suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. The trial Court framed 4 issues including as to whether the suit is maintainable in its present form; whether the suit is barred by limitation; whether plaintiffs have got right, tile and possession over the suit land.

5. The Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Jhenidah Begum Kabita Khanum conducted trial, examined evidence of both the sides and believed the genuineness of the disputed power of attorney, discussed the law points involved therein and ultimately decreed the suit on contest and declared title of the plaintiff-respondents in the suit land by the impugned judgment dated 4.6.96 and the decree signed on 11.6.96. Thereafter this appeal was preferred by the defendant-appellants.

6. Mr. Md. Abdur Rahim, learned Advocate for the defendant-appellants assisted by Mr. Ali Imam Khaled Rahim argued supporting all the grounds mentioned in the Memorandum of Appeal and emphasised that the disputed power of attorney is fake, fictitious and not genuine, on the other hand it has been proved that the suit property was sold in auction, Amir Hossain and others auction purchased the suit property and took delivery of possession through Court and thereafter the contesting defendants purchased the suit land from auction purchasers and they examined witnesses to prove their possession over the suit land and the evidence of the defendants is more dependable, but the trial Court wrongly and illegally believed the evidence of plaintiff-respondents and put undue reliance upon the disputed deed of exchange and the power of attorney and misdirected himself in passing the impugned judgment and decree in favour of the plaintiff-respondents and thereby the trial Court committed error of law and of facts and as such the impugned judgment and decree of the trial Court are liable to be set aside and this appeal has got merit.

7. Mr. A.H. Mahfuzur Rahman, learned Advocate for the plaintiff-Respondents assisted by Mr. Md. Elahi Bakhsh refuted all the grounds of the memorandum of Appeal and all the points submitted by learned counsel for the defendant-appellants and submits that the trial Court discussed the cases of both the sides, properly analysed the evidence on record, rightly and legally believed the power of attorney and the disputed exchange of the suit property and that the trial Court delivered the judgment and decree on the basis of evidence on record without committing any error of law and of facts and as such this appeal has got no merit.

8. We have examined the evidence on record. The original title Suit No. 80 of 1993 was renumbered as Title Suit No. 75 of 1994 by order No. 8 dated 16.7.94 in the 2nd Court Subordinate Judge, Jhenidah. Ext. 1 is the khas Ammokternama in 5 sheets admitted into evidence without any objection. Ext. 1(A) is the disputed power of attorney dated 26.9.62 also admitted into evidence without raising any objection by the defendant appellants at the time of trail. In view of the case law reported in 22 D.L.R. page 858 Sadequr Rahman Chowdhury Vs. Mvi. Abdul Bari, the defendant appellants cannot raise any objection at the time of appeal hearing regarding the disputed power of attorney when the contesting defendants raised no objection against the same disputed power of attorney dated 26.9.62 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Jhenidah when it was admitted into evidence and marked Ext. 1(A). Moreover, the disputed power of attorney is authenticated by the Deputy Commissioner, Jessore with a certificate that the general power of attorney has been duly stamped and the power of attorney is attested by A.B. Mokherjee Notary Public, Calcutta and counter signed by the then Deputy High Commissioner of Pakistan in Calcutta and it bears the official seal of the Deputy High Commissioner. The Subordinate Judge, Jhenidah rightly observed in the impugned judgment that the presumptive value under section 85 of the Evidence Act is applicable to this disputed power of attorney. The disputed power of attorney was executed on 26.9.62. The East Pakistan Disturbed Persons (Rehabilitation) Ordinance No. 1/1964 was made effective from 30th June, 1964, hence the legal bar mentioned in section 4 and section 6 of Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 is not applicable to the instant power of attorney dated 26.9.62 marked Ext. 1 (A). In this connection the trial Court rightly cited a case law reported in 17 D.L.R. page 451, Chitta Ranjan Sutar Vs. Secretary, Judicial Department, Government of East Pakistan that section 4 and 6 of the Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 place unreasonable restrictions on the right of a citizen to acquire property and the same is violative of the fundamental right 13th and as such they are void and are also discriminatory under Fundamental right 15th.

9. In schedule kaw the total area of the suit land has been shown as 21.4.03 acres and this area has been restated as 21.4.03 acres in the valuation statement at the end of the plaint. The Subordinate Judge discussed the documentary and oral evidence on record and came to the finding and decisions that the disputed power of attorney Ext. 1(A) and exchange of the suit property are genuine and the trial Court believed the case of the plain-tiff-respondent and recorded proper reasoning’s in support of its findings and decisions and the trial court decreed the suit in full and declared title of the plaintiff-respondents in the suit property by the impugned judgment and decree; but in page 15 of the original judgment and in the paragraph just before the order portion of the judgment the Subordinate Judge recorded the area of the suit property as 294.58 acres. This area does not correspondent to the total area of the suit property shown in the plaint, schedule kaw and in the valuation statement. Moreover, the total area of the suit property has been shown as 214.03 acres in the decree signed 11.6.96. Hence it is apparent that the area of the suit land has been wrongly typed as 294.58 acres at page 15 of the original judgment.

<u>10. On a careful scrutiny of the documentary and oral evidence on record we find nothing to differ from the finding and observation of the trial Court about the genuineness of the disputed power of attorney Ext. 1(A) and exchange of the suit property. Moreover, according to the principles laid down in the case law reported in 10 D.L.R. page 1, Privy Council, K.M. Perera Vs. H.G. Martin Dias with the observation of Lord Denning and the case law reported in 36 D.L.R.(AD) Page 52 Md. Badruddin Khan Vs. Bangladesh and others in which the Appellate Division of Bangladesh Supreme Court observed that trial Court's findings should not be easily disturbed as a matter of course and before reversing the findings and decisions of the trial Court, the Appellate Court should think twice or more than twice. We do not find any error of law or of facts in the impugned judgment and decree delivered by the Subordinate Judge, 2nd court, Jhenidah. Moreover, in a Civil Matter, all the facts alleged by plaintiff. need not be proved strictly in view of the decision in the case of Jahed Ali Mondal Vs. Jamini Kanta Dey reported in 7 BLD(AD)page 156 and the burden of proof is lightened by presumption, admission and estoppel in view of this case law. It appears that the plaintiffs-respondents have discharged their primary onus to prove the genuineness of the disputed power of attorney Ext. 1(A). The six Govt. rent receipts Ext. 1 (d) upto 1(i) show that the kabala deed dated 13.2.64 executed by Samapada Biswas in favour of Santosh Kumar has been acted upon and the defendant appellants did not take any step for proving possession of the contesting defendants by producing any Govt. rent receipts along with the documentary evidence from Ext. 'A' upto Ext. (J).</u>

11. In the light of our findings and observations made above in the body of the judgment we do not find any error of law and of fact in the impugned judgment and decree delivered by subordinate Judge, 2nd  Court, Jehnidah in Title Suit No. 75 of 1994. Hence, we do not find any merit in this appeal. The area of the suit property will be 214.03 acres as per plaint and the impugned decree. Only on this point the impugned judgment dated 4.6.96 is modified with 214.03 acres as area of the suit property. The trial Court rightly observed that the Govt. and the relevant Revenue Authority may acquire excess of land excluding 100 bighas after payment of proper compensation to the owner.

12. For the aforesaid reasons and only with the above modification regarding actual area of the suit property the appeal is dismissed without cost. The impugned judgment and decree are hereby upheld.

13. Send down the original case records at once with a copy of this judgment to the learned District Judge, Jhenidah and Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Jhenidah for taking necessary action accordingly.

End.

parties:
Abul Kashem Shikder @ Kashem Ali Shikder ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Fazlul Haque Shikder and ors ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Aziz, J: Defendant No. 1 is the petitioner and the rule is directed against the judgment and decree dated 30.11.1997 (decree signed on 1.1.98) passed by the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Shariatpur in Title Appeal No. 45/1995 allowing the appeal reversing and setting aside the judgment and decree dated 18.10.95 (decree signed on 25.10.95) passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Damudya in Title Suit No. 3/1995 dismissing the suit.

2. The opposite party No.1 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 3/95 for declaration of title in the suit land by adverse possession and for permanent injunction against the defendant-petitioner restraining him from entering into the homestead and garden by force and from cutting the tree etc.

3. The plaintiff filed the suit contending, in short, inter alia that, the suit land bearing plot Nos. 1006, 1007, 1008 and 1009 of Khatian No. 1 of Mouza Purba Kandi under P.S: Damudya, District Faridpur was the khas land of the Government, that the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1 are cousins, that the defendant-petitioner took settlement of the entire land of the aforesaid four plots including the suit plots from the Government for their mutual interest at a salami of Tk. 1068/- in Settlement Case No. XIII-M523/66-67 in equal share on payment of equal consideration money. This is alleged that settlement was cancelled under Misc. Case No. XIII-B-25/71-72 and defendant No. 1 petitioner filed a review case being Review Case No. XIII -B-70/73-74 and A.D.0 (Rev.), Faridpur upheld the settlement for 1.13 acres of land of Plot Nos. 1006 and 1007 in their favours and cancelled the settlement of the land of Plot Nos. 1008 and 1009. The plaintiff claimed that he shared the costs of the litigations and proceedings in equal share, that the plaintiff has been possessing the entire .37 decimals of land of Plot No. 1006 and 7½ decimals of Plot No. 1007, out of total .89 decimals of land of these two plots, by metes and bound and raising the land above the flood level, planting trees and by raising houses and have been living there for about 30 years. The plaintiff further alleged that he came to know on 31.1.1401 B.S. that, the defendant opposite party No.1 took the suit land along with other land in his own name only and mutated the same in his name. The plaintiff further contends that he filed Misc. Case No. XIII-B-7/93-94 on 31.5.94 against the said mutation of defendant No. 1 which was rejected and he preferred Case No. XIII/94 to the A.D.C. (Rev.) against the same order and the defendant-opposite party no.1 having threatened the plaintiff with dispossession from the land on 3.4.95, the plaintiff has filed this suit claiming title by adverse possession and prayed for confirmation of possession and permanent injunction.

4. The defendant No.1 petitioner appeared and contested the suit by filing written statements denying the material averments made in the plaint contending, inter alia, in short that, the suit is not maintainable, the suit is defect for parties, the suit is barred by limitation, there are no cause for filing the suit, etc. The main case of the defendant-petitioner, in short, is that he took settlement of over 1.37 acres of land of Plot Nos. 1006-1009 at a salami of Tk. 1068/- but it was cancelled on 4.3.73 and on review the A.D.C. (Rev.) set aside the order of cancellation and upheld the settlement in respect of Plot Nos. 1006 and 1007 and since then he has been in possession in the suit land with wish his minor children raising dwelling house in the suit. The further case of the defendant-petitioner is that, he had minor children and since he lives away from the family due to service, he brought the plaintiff for the security of his family and allowed him (plaintiff) to live in the suit plot by raising a dwelling but for him and that they lived in a joint mess. This is further stated in the written statement that the contesting defendant gifted four decimals of land of Plot No. 1006 and 30 decimals from Plot No. 1007 for setting up a Primary School within the knowledge of the plaintiff, that the plaintiff was living in the suit property on permissive possession and he has no right, title and interests in the same and as such the suit is liable to be dismissed with costs.

5. During trial of the suit the plaintiff examined 6 witnesses and the defence examined two. Both the parties produced some documents which were admitted into evidence and marked exhibits.

6. On consideration of the evidence and the materials on record both oral and documentary the learned Senior Assistant Judge dismissed the suit finding that the suit was bad for defect of parties, that the plaintiff failed to prove the amount of consideration for settlement as well as the costs required in the litigation in equal share, that the plaintiff failed to prove that the settlement was taken in the joint names of the plaintiff and the contesting defendant No. 1 petitioner. The trial court further found that the plaintiff has failed to prove adverse possession in the suit land, on the other hand he has himself admitted in paragraph No. 6 of the plaint that he was living in the suit land with the permission of the contesting defendant-petitioner etc.

7. On appeal by the plaintiff against the aforesaid judgment and decree before the District Judge, Shariatpur the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Shariatpur heard the appeal on transfer and allowed the same reversing and setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial court. The learned Subordinate Judge allowed the appeal on the finding that the plaintiff has proved his possession that the defendant No. 1 miserably failed to prove that he brought plaintiff in the suit land and he was in permissive possession in the same. The learned Subordinate Judge further found that the word "সম্মতিতেই" as inserted in paragraph Nos. 4 and 6 of the plaint was wrongly inserted, it would be "জ্ঞাতসারে" instead of the word "সম্মতিতেই" which is a wrong and  carelessness of the learned Advocate for the plaintiff, etc. The appellate court below decreed the suit on further finding that the plaintiff has been able to prove his case of adverse possession in the suit land, although the plaintiff failed to prove taking settlement of the suit land in their joint name and sharing of the money and the cost for taking settlement and bearing the expenses for litigation etc.

8. Perused the pleadings and the evidence both oral and documentary adduced by both the parties and the judgments passed by the courts below and heard the learned Advocates of both the sides.

9. Mr. M.A. Wahhab Mia, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant-petitioner No. 1 submits that, the plaintiff has not been able to prove his case that the property was taken settlement in their joint names and he shared the money and that he possessed the suit land adversely to the defendant-petitioner. Mr. Wahhab further argued that the plaintiff firstly claimed title and possession of the suit land on the basis of taking joint settlement but when he failed, he took the plea of adverse possession in the suit land but again failed to prove the same. This is further argued that the lower appellate court has erred in law in reading the plaint in a different way and giving a different meaning substituting his own language and as such, the impugned judgment is not maintainable in law etc. This is further argued by him that the learned Subordinate Judge has failed to find that out of the suit plots the defendant gifted 4 decimals of land to local primary school in exercise of his possession as owner of the same and the plaintiff did not oppose the same but admitted, which is also a proof of exercise of exclusive right and possession of the suit land by the defendant-petitioner. This has been further argued that the impugned judgment is not a proper judgment of reversal and the same is totally perversed both in facts and law. On the other hand the finding of the learned Senior Assistant Judge were based on pleadings and evidence of the parties.

10. Dr. Rafiqur Rahman the learned Senior Counsel appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 submits that the plaintiff firstly based his suit on taking settlement of the suit property from the Government in the names of both the plaintiff and the defendant No.1 petitioner jointly and took possession of the same, accordingly. But when the plaintiff found that the suit land was taken settlement in the name of the contesting defendant-petitioner alone, he filed the suit praying his title on adverse possession. Mr. Rahman further argued that the word “সম্মতিতেই” as appeared in the plaint was wrongly inserted instead of "অসম্মতিতেই" and the learned Subordinate Judge has correctly passed the impugned judgment interpreting the word in it's right meaning and spirit and decreed the suit accordingly by setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial court finding adverse possession of the plaintiff in the suit land etc.

11. In paragraph 6 of the plaint the plaintiff has stated that “বাদী নালিশী ভূমিতে ১৯৬৬ সনে বন্দোবস্ত���র সময় হইতেই তদ্মুলে একাধারে নালিশী ভূমিতে এই বিবাদীর সম্মতিতেই continuously  ভোগ দখল করিয়া আসিতে থাকায় নালিশী ভূমি সম্পর্কে বাদী দখল স্বত্ব অর্জন করিয়াছে। This word “সম্মতিতেই” as stated in the plaint by plaintiff has not been amended by his before the trial court or before the appellate court below. The plaintiff examined himself as P.W.1 in the suit and nowhere in his deposition has stated that the said word "সম্মতিতেই" was wrongly inserted by his Advocate. The filing Advocate was also not examined by the plaintiff on this point. But the learned Subordinate Judge has come to a finding that the learned trial court has not considered the total sentence and spirit of the meaning and "সম্মতিতেই" is a careless  insertion by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-appeal". Mr. M.A. Wahhab Miah the learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioner seriously attacked this finding and termed the same as erroneous and beyond pleadings. He submitted that the appellate court below has no authority and jurisdiction to read the plaint in a different way and manner and to give a different meaning and interpretation of the word which is not available in the plaint. He further submits that a court has to read the plaint as it is and cannot read something else which is not in the pleadings or in the evidence and as such the aforesaid finding of the learned Subordinate Judge is erroneous and beyond the pleading and is liable to be set aside. The finding of the lower appellate court shows that, he has discovered a new and different word in the plaint and substituted the word "সম্মতিতেই" by his own word "জ্ঞাতসারে" not in the plaint which he is not allowed to do under the law and the same is unwarranted and uncalled for. No court can give a different meaning of the words and the statements made in the plaint or in the written statement other than the actual meaning nor substitute any word of the plaint or of the written statements by own word and meaning of the court. Mr. Wahhab Miah has rightly submitted that the court has to read the pleading as it is and it has no authority to read something which is to in the pleading or in the evidence. I find substance in his submission and hold that the learned Subordinate Judge has committed an error in finding that the learned Advocate for the plaintiff carelessly inserted the word "সম্মতিতেই" in the plaint which has resulted in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The said finding is not maintainable in law.

12. Regarding possession of the suit land it is admitted than the plaintiff is in possession of the same the case of the plaintiff is that he went into possession of the suit land as back as 1966 when the suit property was taken settlement by the defendant No. 1 petitioner in their joint tames and since then the plaintiff is in possession of the same till he came to know in 1995 that the suit land has been taken only in the name of the contesting defendant-petitioner who threatened to dispossess him resulting filing of the suit. The plaintiff then prayed his title on adverse possession.

13. On the other hand the defendant-petitioner contended that he took settlement of 4 plots including plot Nos. 1006 and 1007 from his paternal money. But on the objection case filed by somebody else the said settlement was cancelled but on review filed by him it was upheld only in respect of plot Nos. 1006 and 107 excluding plot Nos. 1008 and 1009. Thereafter the defendant petitioner raised dwelling hats in the suit plot and his family consisting of minor children used to live in the same, and to ensure security of his family he brought the plaintiff who is his cousin and raised a but for him in the suit land and since then the plaintiff has also been living in the same.

<u>14. Mr. M.A. Wahhab Miah, the learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioner submitted that the possession of the plaintiff is nothing but a mere permissive possession. He further argues that as the defendant-petitioner was living outside due to his service, he inducted the plaintiff who was his cousin to the suit property for the security of his family consisting of wife and minor children. The possession of the plaintiff has not been disputed by the petitioner but the plaintiff has failed to prove that he possesses the suit land adversely against the defendant-petitioner. The plaintiff has also failed to prove that he is possessing the suit land in hostile to the right, title and possession of the defendant and there is no proof of such hostile possession in order to constitute adverse possession by the plaintiff as alleged by him. In support of his submission Mr. Wahhab Miah refers a case between Hazera Begum and others Vs. Roushan Ara Begum and others, reported in 39 D.L.R.(AD)22. In this decision our Appellate Division has held that:-</u>

<u>"Apparent show of adverse possession not sufficient to defeat the title of the real owner.</u>

<u>Whether the possession of the defendants were so hostile and adverse openly so as to justify the claim of the adverse possession. Even if there are apparent show of adverse possession whether those circumstances were sufficient to defeat the title of the real owner only because some lack vigilance can be attributed to the plaintiffs and would in such circumstances relieve the defendant from discharging their onus in support of their claim of adverse possession. The onus is very heavy. It is for the defendant to discharge this so as to build up a claim of adverse possession. A thin veneer of adverse possession or semblance of it viewed from the distance would not be sufficient for the defendants to succeed without dis-charging their heavy onus. They have to do more that their possession was open and hostile to the knowledge of all, that the plaintiff must have known the notorious fact that the plea of adverse possession is being raised up".</u>

<u>Our Appellate Division further held that:-</u>

<u>"As to what constitutes adverse possession subject which formed the topic of some discussion in the case, their Lordships adopt the language of Lord Robartson in delivering the judgment of the Board in Radhamoni Devi Vs. Collectorate of Khulna (27 I.A. 136), where his Lordship said that "the possession required must be adequate in continuity, in publicity and in extent to show that it is possession adverse to the competitor. It is sufficient that the possession should be overt and without any attempt at concealment, so that the person against whom time is running ought, if he exercises due vigilance, to be aware of what is happening".</u>

15. In this case the trial court has found that the plaintiff has failed to make out a case of adverse possession and dismissed the suit. But the learned Subordinate Judge allowed the appeal and decreed the suit on adverse possession. The Appellate Court below found that:-

"So the plaintiff—appellant is not at all a co-sharer with the defendant in the suit jama. Ordinarily question arises how the plaintiff came to the suit land. It is proved earlier that basis neither a permissive possessor of the defendant nor a co-sharer in the suit jama by way of settlement. Taking everything together and in the light of discussion made above I may conclude that the plaintiff appellant adversely possesses the suit land for more than 12 years and I am in opinion to reverse the judgment and decree of the title no. 3/95 passed by the IA. Senior Asstt. Judge of Damudya and the plaintiff-Appellant is entitled to get relief as sought for".

16. In the facts, circumstance and evidence of the case the above finding absolutely erroneous. The appellate court below has failed to answer his own query that how the plaintiff came on the suit land. There is absolutely nothing in the pleading nor in the evidence adduced by the plaintiff-apposite party in that behalf. Nor he specifically pleaded adverse possession in the plaint as required under to law or adduced evidence to that fact, showing that openly and notously is in possession of the suit and in hostile to the defendant-petitioner. There is no such evidence the case. Mr. M.A. Wahhab Miah, the learned Advocate appearing on half of the petitioner submits with reference to his above citation that, the plaintiff has not been able to satiny any of the elements constituting verse possession in the suit. The learned Subordinate Judge has learned in law in decreeing the suit in fact and in law. When attention of Dr. Rafiqur Rahman, the learned Counsel for plaintiff-opposite party was drawn to the above submissions, he found himself in a difficult position to reply excepted conceding the same. On my perusal of the impugned judgment and the evidence and pleadings, I also do not find that the plaintiff has made such specific assertion of hostile possession claiming adverse possession in the suit land in the plaint and led any evidence in support of his case. In that view of the matter, I am of the opinion that the aforesaid finding of the learned Subordinate Judge is erroneous and not maintainable in law. There are also other substantial errors committed by the learned Subordinate Judge in passing the impugned judgment decreeing the suit by setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge.

17. In view of my above discussions, observations and findings I am of the opinion that the impugned judgment is not maintainable in law and is liable to be set aside.

18. In the result, the Rule is accordingly made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge are hereby set aside and the judgment and decree passed by the trial court dismissing the suit are hereby upheld.

The order of stay passed earlier by this court is hereby vacated.

End.
