full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Quddus, J: This civil revision under section 115 C.P.C. at the instance of plaintiff-petitioners is directed against judgment and order dated 29.11.93 by learned Sub-Judge, Comilla dismissing Misc. Case No. 72 of 1992 under Order 22 Rule 9 C.P.C. and recording order of abatement of the Title Appeal No. 244 of 1989 as a whole.

2. The petitioners as plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 30 of 1978 in the Court of the then Munsif 3rd Court, Comilla Sadar against original defendant Nos. 1-6 for specific performance of contract. Government was defendant No. 7 in the original suit. Subsequently at the instance of plaintiff-petitioners some other persons were added as defendants Nos. 8-29 in the suit which was subsequently transferred to the Court of Assistant Judge Muradnagar for hearing and disposal. Therein it was re-numbered as Title Suit No. 29 of 1984. Some added defendants including defendant No. 14 (Ahizuddin) filed joint written statement to contest. After contested hearing the suit was dismissed on contest on 12.10.89. Being aggrieved the plaintiffs-petitioners as appellants preferred Title Appeal No. 244 of 1989 in the Court of District Judge, Comilla wherefrom it was transferred to Sub-Judge, Comilla for hearing and disposal. During pendency of the appeal the respondent by a petition informed the court that respondent No. 29 Ahizuddin (original defendant No. 14) died on 24.4.91 and his heirs were not substituted within the prescribed time.

3. The Plaintiff's petitioners thereafter filed Misc. Case No. 72 of 1992 under Order 22 Rule 9 C.P.C. for substitution of the heirs of deceased respondent No. 29 of Ahizuddin by setting aside the order of abatement as automatically occurred. The heirs of Ahizuddin after receipt of notice of Misc. Case No. 72 of 1992 appeared and filed written objection to contest denying the pleas, grievances and allegations stated in the Misc. Case No. 72 of 1992. At the hearing of the Misc. Case 3 P.Ws. and 3 O.P.Ws. were examined by parties. They were duly cross-examined by the other side. Upon consideration of the evidence learned Sub-Judge disbelieved the pleas and grievances of the plaintiff-petitioners for not having knowledge about death of respondent No. 29 Ahizuddin to substitute his heirs within the prescribed time and accordingly dismissed on contest the Misc. Case No. 72 of 1992 under Order 22 rule 9 C.P.C. vide judgment and order dated 29.11.93 and ordered that Title Appeal No. 244 of 1989 as a whole stood abated.

4. Being aggrieved the plaintiffs-appellants-petitioners preferred this civil revision and obtained the rule.

5. Record was called for. Opposite parties were notified. Record was subsequently received. Some of the opposite parties appeared through engaged Advocate to contest. They filed counter affidavit to deny the allegations and pleas of the plaintiffs-appellants-petitioners. The case being ready was put up for hearing which accordingly took place in presence of both sides.

6. Learned Advocate for the petitioners at the very out set refers to the judgment of court below and has shown there from that opposite party Nos. 29(Ka) to 29(Ga) as heirs of deceased respondent No. 29 Ahijuddin contested Misc. Case No. 72 of 1992. By showing such fact from the judgment of court below, learned Advocate submits that heirs of deceased respondent No. 29 were in the record from before and as such said heirs of respondent No. 29 Ahijuddin were not at all necessary to be brought on record once again to comply the requirements to law. He submits that in that view title appeal was not liable to be abated due to non substitution of the heirs of deceased respondent No. 29 Ahijuddin. In that regard learned Advocate refers to a decision reported in 48 DLR (AD) page 164 w herein it was held:

"A legal representative of a deceased party in a suit if brought on record by substitution in any ancillary or related proceeding arising out of the suit, the substitution of the party will hold good for the suit as well and no fresh application to bring the legal representative of the deceased party on the record of the suit would be necessary.".

He therefore contends that when the heirs of deceased respondent No. 2 Ahijuddin were already on record as evident from the judgment of court below dated 29.11.93 there was no need to being the heirs of the said deceased on record afresh. This court regrets reject such argument and contention of the learned Advocate because on perusal of the original petition of Misc. Case No. 72 of 1992 under Order 22 Rule 9 C.P.C. it will be evident that in the schedule of the said original petition the names of heirs of deceased respondent No. 29 Ahijuddin were mentioned as proposed respondents No. 29 (Ka) to 29 (Ga) and procedurally notices were issued and served on those persons as heirs of deceased respondent No. 29 Ahijuddin in connection with above Misc. Case No. 72 of 1992 under Order 22 Rule. 9 C.P.C. That does not mean that those heirs of deceased respondent No. 29 Ahijuddin mentioned above reasons as 29(ka) to 29 (Ga) were on the record from before the filing of the Misc. Case No. 72 of 1992. After service of notices of Misc. Case No. 72 of 1992 those heirs of deceased respondent No. 29 appeared before court below filed written objection to contest the Misc. Case therein. Thus it is obvious that the cited decision on behalf of petitioner has no manner of application in the present case. Learned Advocate next submits that originally plaintiffs filed O.C. Suit No. 30 of 1978 against principal defendant Nos. 1-6 for specific performance of contract.

Subsequently defendants No. 8-29 were added as defendants by the plaintiff through amendment. According to him respondent No. 29 Ahijuddin was added defendant No. 14 and due to non-substitution of heirs of respondent No. 29 on his death the Appeal No. 244 of 1981 was not likely to be abated as a whole. In this respect he relies on the decision reported in 17 D.L.R. (S.C.) page 536 and submits that the appeal might abate against respondent No. 29 and the appeal should proceed against other respondents as usual.

7. He refers to evidence of 3. P.Ws. and O.P.Ws. He shows that 3 P.Ws. including one of the petitioners stated in deposition that Ahijuddin died while living at Chittagong and as such the plaintiff appellant’s petitioners had no knowledge about the death of Ahijuddin to substitute his heirs within time in the appeal. He also shows that 3 OPWs similarly stated that Ahijuddin never lived at Chittagong. Ahijuddin died at home and his Namaje Janaja was held before he was hurried at village home. He submits that in the face of such contradictory evidence on the point by the parties only best reliable evidence in that regard would have been the copy of death register or the death certificate of Ahijuddin to see where he in fact died. But no such reliable certificate about death of Ahijuddin could be filed at the hearing. He submits that if the petitioners were in fact aware of the death of Ahijuddin in time there was, no reason for them not to substitute his heirs within time as the petitioners filed the appeal on payment of advolaram court fee. He earnestly argues that the petitioners will have not scope for hearing and disposal of the appeal on merit if on mere technical ground abatement of the appeal as whole stands good. He submits that the expression 'sufficient cause' required for setting aside abatement should be liberally construed and court 'need not over strict in expecting such proof. He points out that if the abatement be not set aside the petitioners will be deprived of proving their claim in the appeal. In that regard he refers to decisions reported in 39 DLR page 6 and A.I.R. 1964 (S.C.) page 215. He finally submits that petitioners earnestly want to get hearing and disposal of the appeal on merit. According to him impugned judgment and order suffers from illegality and error of law occasioning failure of justice calling for interference by this Court. He submits that the Rule should be made absolute.

8. In reply to above contentions on behalf of the petitioners, learned Advocate for the opposite parties submits that the suit was for specific performance of contract initially filed against defendant Nos. 1-6, but the plaintiff-appellants-petitioners, subsequently impleaded added defendants No. 8-29 by amendment of the plaint. Deceased respondent No. 29 as added defendant No. 14 who filed joint written statement with other defendants to contest and the suit was dismissed on contest. So respondent No. 29 Ahijuddin was a contesting defendant in the trial court. Due to non-substitution of the heirs of said contesting defendant No. 14 as respondent No. 29 Ahijuddin the appeal as whole would stand abated. In this respect learned Advocate refers to the decision reported in 17 DLR (SC) page 536 in the case of Wali and others Vs. Manak Ali and others where in it was held

"There is only one contract between the parties. The shares of the vendors are not specified in the agreement, but even if they were specified as long as the contract was one. Section 17 of the Specific Relief Act bars a splitting up of the transaction. This is one of those case where the law contemplates only one decision of a dispute.

By 'Total abatement' of a suit or appeal on the death of one of the defendants or respondents is meant that on account of the situation that is created by the abatement of the suit as against a party the suit or appeal cannot for one reason or the other proceed at all. When a suit has abated as against a deceased defendant but for one reason or the other it cannot proceed at all, the proper order to pass would be to dismiss the suit as against the remaining defendants.

Learned Advocate contends that in view of above decision the appeal rightly stood abated as a whole.

9. He next submits that from the evidence of 3 OPWs it was clear to the court below that Ahijuddin died at home and not at Chittagong as disclosed in the evidence of 3 P.Ws. and claimed by the plaintiffs-appellants-petitioners. He shows from the judgment of learned Sub-Judge that plaintiff-appellants-petitioners being men of the same area were quite likely to be aware of the death of Ahijuddin but substitution of the heirs of the deceased was not made within time. He contends that learned Sub-Judge found no sufficient causes as required under the law to set aside the abatement and accordingly learned Sub-Judge rightly dismissed the Misc. Case No.72 of 1992 under Order 22 Rule 9 C.P.C. vide impugned judgment and order which occasioned no failure of justice calling for interference by this court. According to him the Rule should be discharged.

10. It is true that plaintiffs-petitioners filed original O.C. Suit No. 30 of 1978 against defendant Nos. 1-6 for specific performance of contract. But subsequently plaintiff impleaded some other persons as added defendants No. 8-29 by amendment of the plaint due to transfer of some interest in the land by original defendant No. 1-6. It appears that deceased respondent No. 29 was added defendant No. 14 who along with other defendants filed joint written statement and contested the suit which was dismissed on contest by the trial court and against that the plaintiffs-appellant filed O.C. Appeal No. 244 of 1989 in which Ahijuddin was made respondent No. 29. In that view there is no scope for abatement of the appeal against said deceased respondent No. 29 alone due to non-substitution of his heirs within time. The decision reported in 17DLR(S.C.) page 536 as cited on behalf of the opposite parties will be appropriately applicable in this instant 'case and according to above decision the appeal must abate as a whole.

11. Now to see whether sufficient causes required under law for setting aside abatement could be shown by the plaintiff-appellant-petitioners in Misc. Case No. 72 of 1992 before learned Sub-Judge, Comilla. From the evidence of 3 P.Ws. including some of the petitioners it appears that Ahijuddin died at Chittagong while he was living there. But from the evidence of 3 O.P.Ws. it appears that Ahijuddin died at his village home. His Namaje Janaja was held in the village and he was burned at his village Home. Learned Sub-Judge believed the evidence of 3 O.P. Ws. about death of Ahijuddin at his village home and being hurried therein. Learned Sub-Judge observed that the residence of the plaintiffs-appellants-petitioners being in the same area they were quite likely to be aware of the death of Ahijuddin at the village home but they did not substitute his heirs in the appeal within time. With such observation learned court below disbelieved and rejected the plea of ignorance of the death of Ahijuddin as disclosed in evidence of 3 P.Ws. and dismissed the Misc. Case accordingly vide impugned judgment and order. In view of claim of petitioners about death of Ahijuddin at Chittagong making thereby the plaintiff-petitioners unaware and ignorant of the death in time and denial of the same by the 3 O.P.Ws. disclosing about death of Ahijuddin at his village home, there should be some more reliable evidence on the point. Most reliable evidence on the said point would have been the death certificate or copy of the death register regarding death of Ahijuddin to see or prove as to where and when Ahijuddin in fact died. But no such reliable evidence could be produced by either side. If in fact the plaintiffs-appellants-petitioners were in the know of the death of Ahijuddin in time there was no reason why they would set idle and would not substitute the heirs of the deceased respondent No. 29 Ahijuddin in time to save the appeal from being abated when they filed the appeal on payment of advolorum court fee. Learned Sub-Judge did not properly consider such aspect.

<u>12. In such regard reference may be made to the decisions reported in 39 D.L.R. page 6 and A.I.R. 1964 (S.C.) page 215. In the case of Azemon Nesa Vs. Rup Gazi reported in 39 DLR page 6 it was held.</u>

<u>"Unless there is gross negligence etc the expression 'sufficient cause' may be liberally construed. If these abatement is not set aside the applicant is deprived of proving his claim. Courts power in dealing with such application is discretionary and the court when exercising it may afford to be liberal. But the expression 'sufficient cause' occurring in rule 9(2) of Order 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure seems to have always been liberally construed so as to advance substantial justice unless there is gross negligence or want of bonafides on the part of the party seeking the relief.</u>

<u>" In the case of Union of India vs. Charon reported in AIR.1964 (SC) page 215 it was held,</u>

<u>"the court in considering whether the applicant has established sufficient cause for applying for setting aside of the abatement within time, need not be over strict in expecting such proof of tie suggested cause as it would accept for holding certain fact established.</u>

<u>It the abatement is not set aside the applicant is deprived of his proving claim on account of his culpable negligence or lack of vigilance of course that does not mean the court should readily accept whatever is alleged to explain away the default."</u>

<u>13. In view of above two decision when the court of law is expected for ends of justice to be liberal in construing the sufficient cause to be shown for explaining the delay and when court need not be 'over strict' in such respect to expect such proof of suggested cause and when in case of not setting aside the abatement the present petitioners will be deprived of proving their claim in the appeal filed by them on payment of advolorum court fee, linient proof of the default in question by sufficient cause in as much as the Courts power in dealing with such prayer under Order 22 Rule 9 CRC is discretionary and the court when exercising it may offered to be liberal.</u>

<u>14. Moreover from facts noticed above reliable best evidence about the place and time of death of said Ahijuddin would have been the copy of death register mentioned under the law or death certificate of said Ahijuddin by competent recognized authority and when no such best reliable evidence as above was not produced at the court below liberal construction to the cause shown by the plaintiff  petitioners to explain the delay or default may be given for ends of justice when the petitioners as appellants filed the appeal on payment of advolorum court fee earnestly desiring for hearing and disposal of the appeal on merit.</u>

<u>15. In such view as above this court is of the opinion that impugned judgment and order of learned Sub-Judge Comilla will have legal infirmity and error of law resulting in an error occasioning failure of justice calling for interference by this court. There is merit in the Rule.</u>

16. In the result the Rule is made absolute without cost. Impugned judgment and order dated 29.11.93 be set aside. Misc. Case No. 72 of 1992 under Order 22 Rule 9 C.P.C. be accordingly allowed on contest and the heirs of deceased respondent No. 29 Ahijuddin be accordingly substituted and brought on record having set aside automatic abatement of the O.C. Appeal No. 244 of 1989 as a whole restoring it to its file and number. I.C. record along with copy of the judgment be set down at once.

End.
